summary: Settled the entry file format: front matter with date, project, summary, cwd, host, user, agent and session, one Markdown file per entry, named by timestamp and a short id.
body:
Started the day by writing down the entry format in docs/format.md before any code exists. Each entry is one Markdown file with front matter and a free body. The front matter keys are date, project, summary, cwd, host, user, agent and session. I kept them flat, one key per line, so awk can read them without a YAML parser.

The file name is the UTC timestamp plus a six character random id, for example 20240101T082300-a1b2c3.md. I checked that sorting names gives time order, which makes the list command trivial. Two sessions in the same second still get different files because of the id.

I tried a version with the summary in the file name too. It broke on slashes and long text, so I dropped it. The summary stays in the front matter only.

The awk parser reads lines between the first two --- markers and stops. I tested it on a body that contains a --- line, a horizontal rule, and it correctly ignored it. A summary with a colon inside also works, because the parser splits on the first colon only.

Open question: should the date carry a time zone offset? For now it is written in UTC with a Z suffix. Time zones will matter for the list command later, but not yet. Next step is the write command that creates the file from arguments and stdin.

summary: Wrote the first version of the write command in bin/agent-journal, which builds the front matter from the environment and takes the body from stdin.
body:
Implemented `agent-journal write --summary TEXT` in POSIX sh. The body is read from stdin, and the front matter is filled from the environment: host from `hostname`, user from `id -un`, cwd from `pwd`, and project from the git top-level directory name, falling back to the cwd basename.

The agent and session values come from the variables AGENT_JOURNAL_AGENT and AGENT_JOURNAL_SESSION. If they are not set, the fields say unknown. That is ugly but honest, and the plugins will set them later.

The first run failed on macOS because `date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%S` is fine but `mktemp` templates differ from Linux. I switched to building the id from `od -An -N3 -tx1 /dev/urandom | tr -d ' \n'`, which works on both.

I also made the write atomic. It writes to a temp file in the journal folder and then does `mv`, so a reader never sees half an entry. A summary with a newline in it is rejected with exit code 2 and a message on stderr.

There are no tests yet. I did a manual check of five entries and read them back with cat. Next I need the folder location logic, because the journal path is hardcoded to ~/.agent-journal.

summary: Added journal folder resolution with an environment override, so tests and users can point the CLI at any directory instead of the hardcoded home path.
body:
The journal folder is now resolved in this order: the AGENT_JOURNAL_DIR variable, then the dir value from the config file if one exists, then ~/.agent-journal. The config file does not exist yet, so only the first and last steps are live, but the function has a slot for it.

The resolver creates the folder with `mkdir -p` on write only. Read commands on a missing folder print nothing and exit 0. I decided this on purpose, because a fresh install should not show errors when an agent runs list before any entry exists.

A tilde in AGENT_JOURNAL_DIR is not expanded by sh when it is quoted, so I added a small case statement that replaces a leading ~/ with $HOME/. I tested it with a path containing spaces and it worked.

This was the blocker for the test setup. Every test can now create a temporary directory and set the variable, so nothing touches the real journal. I wrote one throwaway script that does exactly that and it passed.

Next is the Vitest harness that runs the CLI with execFile and a temp journal.

summary: Set up the Vitest harness that runs bin/agent-journal as a subprocess in a temp journal, with the first eight tests for write and the front matter.
body:
Added vitest, oxlint and oxfmt as dev dependencies and a package.json with `test`, `lint` and `format` scripts. The tests live in test/ and use a helper, test/helpers/run.js, that creates a temp directory with mkdtemp, sets AGENT_JOURNAL_DIR, and runs the CLI through execFile. It returns stdout, stderr and the exit code.

The helper also fixes HOME to the temp directory, so a stray fallback to ~/.agent-journal cannot leak into the real journal. I confirmed that by deleting the variable in one test and checking that the file landed in the temp home.

The first eight tests cover: a file is created, the name matches the timestamp pattern, the front matter has all eight keys in order, the summary is stored as given, the body comes from stdin, an empty summary fails with exit 2, a multi-line summary fails with exit 2, and no temp files are left behind.

One test was flaky at first. It compared the date in the front matter with the current time and failed when the second rolled over. I changed it to check the format with a regex and that the value is within a ten second window.

oxlint found two unused variables in the helper, fixed. oxfmt reformatted the test files, and I committed the result so later diffs stay small. The whole suite runs in about 1.4 seconds, which is fine because each test spawns a shell.

I also wrote a first GitHub Actions workflow that installs dependencies and runs lint, format check and tests on Ubuntu. It passed on the first push. macOS is not in the matrix yet, though I develop on it, so that is a todo.

Next: the list command.

summary: Wrote the first test of the list command against a hand-made journal and found that entries sort by file name, not by the date in the front matter, so I pinned the order.
body:
The list command had been printing entries in whatever order the shell glob returned them. That looked right on my laptop, but the first test I wrote for it failed on the Ubuntu container, because the locale there changed the glob order.

I built a small journal of six entries by hand in a temp folder, with timestamps in the file names that differ only in the seconds. Two of them had a date in the front matter that did not match the file name, to see which one the command trusts. It trusted the file name, which is what I want, since the name is written once at creation and never edited.

The fix was to set LC_ALL=C before the glob and sort the names explicitly with sort -r. The newest entry now comes first, in every locale I tried. I also added an optional count argument, so `agent-journal list 5` shows the five latest.

The test now checks three things: the order of the six entries, the count argument, and the empty journal case, which prints nothing and exits with 0. I ran the suite twice, once under dash and once under bash, and both passed.

The awk part that reads the summary line is still naive. It breaks if the summary contains a colon followed by a quote, so that is the next thing to look at. After that I want to write the help text, since list now has an argument that nobody can discover.

summary: Fixed list output for entries whose summary contains a tab or trailing spaces, which broke the column layout, by normalizing whitespace in awk.
body:
While reading back my own entries I saw one list line with a ragged column. The cause was a summary containing a tab character, which the terminal expanded.

The awk program now replaces tabs with a single space and trims trailing spaces before printing. The write command also rejects control characters in the summary other than space, with exit 2 and a clear message.

I added a test for both paths. The old entry with the tab was fixed by hand.

One thing I noticed is that a summary with a leading space gets trimmed on read but stored as is. I left it, since trimming on write would be a format change and the format doc says the value is stored verbatim.

Suite is green, 14 tests.

summary: Wrote the install script that copies the CLI into a bin directory, checks for sh, awk and git, and prints what it did; tested on a clean Ubuntu container.
body:
Added install.sh at the repo root. It checks that awk and sh exist, warns if git is missing since sync will need it later, and copies bin/agent-journal to ~/.local/bin by default. A --prefix flag changes the target directory.

The first version used `cp -f` and left the executable bit alone. On a clean Ubuntu container the file arrived with mode 644 because the source was checked out through a tarball. I added an explicit `chmod 755` after the copy.

It also checks whether the target directory is in PATH. If not, it prints one line with the export command to add, and does not touch any shell rc file. I want the script to have no hidden side effects, and that is a rule I will repeat in the README.

I considered a curl-pipe-sh install. The script is written so that it can run that way, no reads from the terminal, no prompts. But I held off on documenting it until the repo is public in a sensible state.

Uninstall is `install.sh --uninstall`, which removes only the one file. It does not remove the journal folder, and it says so in its output. I tested that the journal survives with five entries in it.

A test now runs the install script into a temp prefix and then runs the installed copy with `--version`. That revealed there is no --version flag yet, so I added one that prints the version from a constant at the top of the CLI, currently 0.1.0.

In the Ubuntu container I ran the whole flow: install, write an entry, list it. It worked, but the host name in the container was a random hash, which is fine.

To do: dash compatibility check. The container's sh is dash and everything worked there, but macOS /bin/sh is bash in POSIX mode, so I should check both in CI.

I also noted that the install script does not verify a checksum. For a single shell file that seems acceptable now. If the release process gets more involved, I will publish a checksum next to it.

summary: Added a CI matrix with Ubuntu and macOS and run tests under both dash and bash as sh, which caught one bashism in the write command.
body:
The workflow now runs on ubuntu-latest and macos-latest. On Ubuntu I also install the dash package check by running the test suite with the CLI's shebang replaced by dash explicitly through an environment variable that the helper reads.

That found a real bug. In the write command I had used `local` for a variable inside a function. It works in dash and bash but is not in POSIX. More importantly, I also had `[[ ... ]]` in one place, which dash rejects. The error was `[[: not found` and the exit code was 127.

I replaced the double bracket test with a case statement and removed `local`, using unique variable name prefixes instead. The tests passed on both shells.

macOS CI takes about 50 seconds against 25 on Ubuntu, because of slower process spawning. That is acceptable.

I also added shellcheck to the lint script, run only when installed, and it flagged two quoting issues that I fixed.

summary: Wrote the first rules text the agent gets at session start, explaining when to write an entry and what a good summary looks like, plus an `agent-journal rules` command that prints it.
body:
The rules are a Markdown text in the repo, rules/session.md, and the new command `agent-journal rules` prints it. The plugins will later inject it at session start, so having the CLI own the text means every agent gets the same wording.

The content has four parts. First, when to write: after each completed piece of work, not at each tool call. Second, what the summary must be: one sentence that stands alone, with a good and a bad example. Third, what the body contains: what was done, why, findings, numbers, file names, what is left. Fourth, how to read the journal before starting work on something that may have history.

I spent most of the time on the examples. The bad one is "Fixed the auth bug", and the good one explains the cause and the fix in one line. Models copy the examples closely, so I made sure the good example is not about auth, to avoid every entry sounding like auth.

I also wrote down a limit for the summary, about 80 to 180 characters, and the write command now warns on stderr if it is over 200. It warns and does not fail, because a failed write loses the work record, which is worse than a long line.

A test checks that `rules` prints the file and exits 0, and that the text mentions the write command, so the two cannot drift apart silently.

I ran a quick manual check by pasting the rules in a chat with a model and asking it to write entries for three made-up tasks. Two were good. One put the date in the body, so I added a line telling agents that time is written by the tool and not by them.

The text is 61 lines. I think that is near the upper limit for something loaded in every session, so I will watch its size.

Next: the help text, and truncation of long summaries in list.

summary: Wrote the help text for every command and made list truncate summaries to the terminal width, with a --full flag to turn truncation off.
body:
`agent-journal help` and `--help` now print a usage block: the commands write, list, rules and version, then the environment variables. Each command also answers `help COMMAND` with its flags and one example.

I wrote the help by hand instead of generating it. A heredoc per command is plain, and the tests can compare against it. A test now checks that each command named in the main help has its own help text, so adding a command without docs fails CI.

Truncation in list uses `tput cols` when stdout is a terminal, falling back to 100 when it is a pipe or tput fails. A cut summary ends with three dots. awk does the cutting with substr, which counts bytes in some versions, so a summary with accented letters was cut in the middle of a character in mawk. I set LC_ALL to a UTF-8 locale if one exists, and otherwise skip cutting multi-byte lines more than the width. It is not perfect, and I noted it as a known limit.

--full prints the whole summary, and piping to another program also turns truncation off, so grep gets full text.

Unknown commands print the usage on stderr and exit 2. I added tests for it.

That is the end of the entry format and list work for this phase. What remains for the first version is test fixtures with realistic entries.

summary: Created a fixture set of 40 realistic entries for tests, generated by a script so they can be rebuilt, and moved the list tests onto it.
body:
The tests so far make entries one at a time with the write command, which is slow and makes the data look artificial. I added test/fixtures/build.js, which writes 40 entry files into a folder given as argument. The content is fixed in a JSON file, test/fixtures/entries.json, with a time, project, agent and summary for each.

The set was designed on purpose. It has three projects, three agents, entries on the same day with different times, one entry with a very long summary, one with a colon in the summary, one with a --- line in the body, and one with Windows line endings. Each of these has already caused a bug or could.

The CRLF case failed straight away. The awk parser compared the line with the string --- and the carriage return made it not equal, so the front matter never closed and the parser read the whole file as front matter. I now strip a trailing \r in the awk program before any comparison. The summary printed by list also has no \r anymore.

The fixture builder writes files with the exact names a real write would, so the sort order is the same as in real use. It uses a fixed random id sequence and so the output is deterministic, which I checked by building twice and comparing with diff -r.

I moved the old list tests to use the fixture. The ordering test now checks the real newest entry and not a count. The limit test uses 5 and compares the first and last lines.

Two old tests that wrote entries with the CLI remain, since they test the write path itself.

Timing: the fixture build takes 0.2 seconds, and the list tests got faster, since there is no spawn for each entry. The full suite is at 1.9 seconds with 31 tests.

I noted that the fixture times are written in UTC, so when time zones come in the list command, the same fixtures can be used with a TZ variable to check conversions.

Next: a pass over error messages, to make them all start with the same prefix.

summary: Unified all error messages under an `agent-journal:` prefix on stderr with stable exit codes, 2 for usage and 1 for runtime failures, and documented them.
body:
Reading the CLI source, I found messages in four styles: some with the program name, some without, one printing to stdout by mistake. I added one function, die, which takes a code and a message, prints `agent-journal: message` to stderr and exits.

The exit codes are now fixed: 0 for success, 1 for runtime errors such as an unwritable folder, and 2 for usage errors such as a bad flag or an empty summary. I put the table in the help text and in docs/format.md.

The stdout slip was in the list command, when the folder was a file and not a directory. It printed the complaint to stdout, so a script piping list into another tool would take the message as an entry. A new test runs list with the folder set to a regular file and expects an empty stdout, exit 1 and the message on stderr.

The unwritable folder case is harder to test as root in CI. I made the test skip when `id -u` is 0, and in the Ubuntu job the runner user is not root, so it runs.

I also changed the warning for long summaries to the same prefix with `warning:` after it.

The diff touched many lines but only strings. oxfmt had no complaints. Tests: 36 passing.

summary: Checked what happens when two agents write at the same moment; the atomic rename and random id held up in a 200-process stress run with no lost or damaged files.
body:
Since several agent sessions can run in parallel, I wanted proof that writes do not collide. I wrote a throwaway script that starts 200 write processes at once through xargs -P 50, all into the same folder and all within the same second.

Result: 200 files, each with complete front matter, no temp files left, and no duplicate names. The random id has 24 bits, so a collision among 200 entries in one second has a chance of about one in 800. I do not like that for a tool that promises to not lose entries.

I added a guard: the write command now creates the target with `set -C` style no-clobber behaviour, using `ln` from the temp file to the final name, which fails if the name exists, and retries with a new id up to five times. ln is atomic and POSIX, and it is better than mv here because mv overwrites.

I did not add the stress script to the test suite because it is slow and not deterministic. A small test runs 20 parallel writes and checks the count, which takes under a second.

summary: Wrote the first README draft with the one-line pitch, install steps, a usage example and the file format, and added a CI badge at the top.
body:
The repo had no README beyond a title. I wrote a first full draft today. The top has the name, one sentence about what the tool does, and a CI status badge from the GitHub Actions workflow.

The sections are: why a journal for agents, install, first use, the entry format and the commands. The install section is the output of install.sh in a code block, with the PATH note. I kept it short, since the script already explains itself.

The first use section shows one write call and one list call with sample output copied from a real run. I replaced my host name and user in the sample with generic ones. One thing I noticed is that the sample showed a UTC time, and a reader in another zone would be confused, so I added a sentence that times are UTC for now.

The format section is a short version of docs/format.md with a link, to avoid keeping two copies in sync by hand.

I left out pictures. A README for a CLI would be better with an animated example, but the commands are still changing and I do not want to redo the pictures every week. I put that on the list for later.

I read the text aloud once and cut about a third of the sentences, mostly the ones that start with "simply" or "just". The final draft is 78 lines.

Next week I want to start on the session hooks design, but first the list command still needs a way to filter by project.

summary: Compared three ways to put the short rules into the agent at session start and chose a bootstrap that only points to `agent-journal rules`, after the long inline text drifted out of date.
body:
Today I looked at how the rules should reach the agent. The first version of the plugin copied the whole rules text into the hook output, and I had already edited the rules twice since then, so the copy in the plugin was stale. That was the bug that made me stop and think.

I wrote down three options. Option one: keep the full text in each plugin. It is simple, but every plugin needs a release when the rules change. Option two: generate the plugin text from the CLI at build time. It is better, but there is still a build step that I can forget. Option three: the hook prints a few lines that say what the journal is and tell the agent to run `agent-journal rules` once at the start.

I chose option three. The long text lives in one place, the CLI, and it is read fresh every session. The cost is one extra command call at the start of each session, which takes a few milliseconds and adds a tool call to the transcript.

The risk is that the agent skips the call. To lower it, the bootstrap is written as a plain instruction with the exact command, and it says that entries are written after each piece of work. I will check this in a live session once the plugin exists, because I cannot judge it from the text alone.

I also decided that the bootstrap must stay under 600 characters, and I added a test for that limit. Next I will start the plugin directory layout and the manifest.

summary: Designed the session-start rules injection for agents: a short bootstrap text that points to `agent-journal rules`, so the long text stays in one place and is loaded fresh.
body:
Before writing the Claude Code plugin, I spent the morning on how the rules reach the agent. The first idea was to copy rules/session.md into each plugin. That means three copies, and every wording change needs three edits and a release of each plugin.

The design I chose is a short bootstrap text in each plugin, about eight lines: a journal exists, run `agent-journal rules` now and follow it, read the journal before work that may have history, write an entry after each piece of work. The long rules stay in the CLI, and an update to the CLI changes every agent at once.

The cost is one extra command call at session start, about 30 ms measured, and a dependency on the CLI being in the PATH. If it is missing, the bootstrap says so, and the hook prints a one-line warning instead of failing the session.

I tested the idea with a transcript: a model got only the bootstrap and had a shell tool. It ran the rules command first in 5 of 5 tries, and then wrote entries in the right form. When I removed the words "now" and "follow", it ran the command in 3 of 5 tries only, so I kept the strong wording.

Another question was the size of the rules text. At 61 lines, the output is about 900 tokens. I cut the examples to one pair and removed a paragraph on tags, and it is down to 48 lines, with the same results in a re-run of the transcript test.

I also decided that the rules output has no front matter and no colors, even on a terminal, since the agent reads it as plain text.

A small CLI change followed: `rules` now accepts `--short`, which prints only the bootstrap text, and the plugins can use it as the hook output directly. That keeps even the bootstrap in one place. There is a test that checks that --short is a strict subset of the lines in the full rules, so the two do not contradict each other.

I updated the help text and the README command list.

Next: the Claude Code plugin skeleton, with a SessionStart hook that prints this text.

summary: Fixed list printing an empty project column for entries written outside a git repo, by using the cwd basename as fallback in write, and repaired the existing fixtures.
body:
Looking at a list output from a scratch directory, I saw entries with a blank project column. The write command took the project from `git rev-parse --show-toplevel`, and outside a repository that gave an empty string, which the fallback should have replaced.

The cause was the order of two lines. The fallback ran before the git call because of an earlier refactor, so it was overwritten with the empty git result. I swapped them and made the code explicit: use git if its output is not empty, otherwise the basename of the cwd.

A test now runs write in a temp directory that is not a repo and checks that the project equals the directory name.

I also found three fixture entries with an empty project, which hid the problem until now because no test counted blanks. I gave them names and added a test that no fixture has an empty required key.

Last, a check in list: a blank project prints a dash. This is a cosmetic safeguard.

summary: Started the Claude Code plugin: directory layout, manifest, and a SessionStart hook that prints the short rules, tested by running the hook script directly.
body:
Created plugins/claude-code with a manifest, a hooks folder and a README. The manifest names the plugin and points to hooks/hooks.json. That file registers one hook for SessionStart that runs hooks/session-start.sh.

The script is small. It checks `command -v agent-journal`; if found, it prints the output of `agent-journal rules --short`, and if not, it prints one line that says the CLI is missing and how to install it. It always exits 0, because a failing hook can block a session and a journal is never worth that.

I also set the environment for later entries. The hook needs to tell the CLI which agent and session it is working with. Claude Code passes a JSON payload on stdin with a session id and the working directory. I parse the session id with sed, since I do not want a dependency on jq, and write `AGENT_JOURNAL_AGENT=claude` and the session id to the file named in CLAUDE_ENV_FILE, if that variable is set.

The sed parse worked on the payload from the docs but broke on one with escaped quotes in another field. I narrowed the pattern to the session_id key only and anchored it to a quoted value with no escapes, which is safe because the id is a UUID.

Tests: a Vitest file runs the hook script with a sample payload and a temp CLAUDE_ENV_FILE, then checks the content of the file and the printed text. A second test removes agent-journal from PATH and checks the fallback line and exit 0. A third passes an empty stdin and checks the script still exits 0 and writes a session value of unknown.

I have not yet run it in a live Claude Code session. That is the first thing for the next entry, as there are things the docs do not show, like whether the output of the hook reaches the model as context or only the user.

Also noted: the plugin folder needs its own version number, separate from the CLI, since they will be released at different speeds. I set it to 0.1.0.

The lint and format scripts now include the plugin folder, and oxfmt reformatted the JSON files.

summary: Ran the plugin in a live Claude Code session: the hook text reached the model, the env file worked for session ids, but the agent wrote entries only when asked, so I strengthened the bootstrap.
body:
I installed the plugin from the local folder and started a real session in a scratch project. The SessionStart output did reach the model, because it quoted the rules back when I asked what it knew about the journal.

The env file approach also worked. An entry written by the agent had agent: claude and a real session id in the front matter, which I compared with the id in the transcript file name.

The behavior was weaker than I wanted. In a half-hour session with three small tasks, the agent wrote no entry until I asked for one. It had read the rules and understood them, but it treated them as background information.

I changed the short text from a description to instructions in the imperative: "After you finish each piece of work, and before you reply that you are done, run agent-journal write." I also added a sentence that this is part of the task, not an optional extra.

A second session with the same three tasks gave an entry after each of the first two and none after the third, a tiny rename. That is about right, because a rename hardly needs an entry.

The quality of the entries was good, but the summaries were a little short, around 60 characters. The rules ask for 80 to 180, so I put the range in the bootstrap as well, and I will check the length in later sessions.

One annoyance: the hook prints the rules every time the session resumes, not only when it starts fresh. The payload has a source field with values like startup, resume and clear. I now print the full text for startup and clear, and for resume only one line. A test for each source value covers it.

I looked at a Stop hook as a way to remind the agent, but a hook that blocks the stop would loop and annoy. I decided against it for now. The better path is probably clearer wording.

Next steps: a hook that shows the latest entries at session start, since reading the journal before work is the whole point.

summary: Added a hook output with the five most recent entries for the current project at session start, so the agent sees recent context without a search command.
body:
The session-start hook now appends a block called Recent journal after the rules. It runs `agent-journal list --project NAME --limit 5 --full`, where NAME is derived the same way as in write, from the working directory in the payload.

The lines are the plain list output, with time, agent and summary. I kept the format since the agent can already read it, and it costs about 400 tokens for five entries of normal length.

The project name logic lived inside the write command only, so I extracted it to `agent-journal project`, a tiny command that prints the project name for a directory, default the cwd. Both the write command and the hook call this, so the logic is not copied. A test covers a repo, a subdirectory of a repo and a non-repo directory.

When no entries exist for the project, the block is left out, and so no empty header appears for a new project.

In a live session the agent started to use the recent summaries well. I asked it to continue with the last piece of work and it named the right file from the latest entry without searching. That is the use case I built this for.

One concern is that stale context may mislead. Entries show times, and I made the list output say how long ago each entry was in words in a later step, but that is for the time zone work. For now the time is a plain UTC stamp.

summary: Wrote the plugin's install instructions into the README and added a test that checks every command in the README code blocks exists in the CLI help.
body:
The README had no section about the Claude Code plugin. I added one with the two steps: install the CLI, then add the plugin from the repo folder. I tried both on a fresh user account to make sure the steps are complete, and one was missing: the CLI must be in PATH for the hook, which I added as a sentence with the check command `command -v agent-journal`.

While editing, I noticed the commands list in the README missed the project and rules --short commands. I added both.

To stop this drift for good, I wrote a test that reads README.md, takes all lines in code blocks that start with `agent-journal`, extracts the command word and checks that it appears in the help output. It found one more mistake: an example used `agent-journal ls`, which is not a command.

The badge at the top still shows only CI. I thought about adding a license badge and a version badge, but I decided to wait until there is a release, since the version badge needs a tag.

I also reread the README intro. The sentence about why a journal for agents was too long, so I cut it into two. The text is now 94 lines with the plugin section.

The suite has 52 tests and takes 2.6 seconds. Next is the sync command design.

summary: Added a README check that runs the install steps in a clean container and found the documented path assumed ~/bin was already on PATH, so the install section now says how to fix that.
body:
After the test that compares README commands with the CLI help, I wanted something that checks the install section itself. I wrote a short script that starts a clean Ubuntu container, copies the repo in, and runs the steps from the README one by one.

The install itself worked. The next step, `agent-journal list`, failed with `command not found`. The install script had put the CLI in ~/bin, but on a clean image that folder does not exist on PATH, so a new user would hit the same wall right away.

I changed two things. The install script now checks whether the target folder is on PATH and, if not, prints the exact line to add to the shell profile. The README install section got a short note with the same line for sh, bash and zsh. I kept the note to three sentences, because the section is meant to be quick.

I also noticed that the README still said the CLI needed git, but only sync uses git, and sync does not exist yet. I reworded it as optional for now, and the install script check for git is a warning instead of an error.

The container script is not in CI yet, because it takes about 40 seconds and needs Docker on the runner. I will add it as a separate job and see if the time is acceptable. The macOS case still has to be checked by hand.

summary: Built the Claude Code plugin's Stop hook so a session that ends without an entry gets one reminder, which turned out to fire too often at first.
body:
The rules told the agent to write an entry after each piece of work, but in the live run last week it forgot about half the time. I added a Stop hook in plugins/claude-code/hooks/stop.sh that checks whether an entry with the current session id exists in the journal folder. If none exists, it prints a short reminder and exits with the code that makes Claude Code continue.

The first version fired on every stop, including after a one-line question and answer. That made the agent write entries for chatter, which is noise. I added a check on the transcript size: the hook stays silent when the session has fewer than three tool calls.

The session id comes from the env file the SessionStart hook writes. When the file is missing, the hook now exits 0 without a reminder, because a broken reminder is worse than none. I also guarded against a loop: a marker file per session makes sure the reminder appears only once.

Tests run the hook script directly with a fake transcript and a temp journal. There are six cases: no entry, entry exists, short session, missing env file, marker present, and an unwritable marker directory. All pass under dash and bash.

Left for later: a live session with a long task, to see whether one reminder is enough. Next is the summary-quality check in the same hook.

summary: Ran the Stop hook in a real Claude Code session with a long refactor and one reminder was enough: the agent wrote its entry right after.
body:
I used the plugin on a real refactor of the list command for about forty minutes. The agent skipped the entry at the end, the Stop hook fired once, and the entry was written on the next turn.

The marker file prevented a second reminder, as intended. The entry it wrote had a good summary, but the body was only two sentences, so the rules text may need a line about including numbers and file names.

I also checked a short question-only session: no reminder, no entry, which is right. The hook seems good enough for now. I noted the thin body as a to-do for the rules text.

summary: Wrote the sync command that commits the journal folder and pushes it to a git remote, with a pull-rebase first so two machines do not collide.
body:
The user keeps journals on a laptop and a desktop, so sync is the next real need. `agent-journal sync` now does four things in order: check that the journal folder is a git repo, add and commit any new files, pull with rebase, and push. The commit message is "journal: sync from <host>" with a count of new files.

Because every entry is its own file with a timestamp and random id, merge conflicts should be impossible in normal use. I still handled the rebase failing, in which case sync aborts the rebase, prints the git error under the agent-journal: prefix, and exits 1.

The first run needs a remote. I added `agent-journal sync --init <url>`, which runs git init, sets the remote and makes the first commit. Without a remote, plain sync prints a usage hint and exits 2 instead of failing in git.

I hit one surprise on macOS CI. The default branch name differed between runners, so a push to "main" failed. The init step now runs `git init -b main` and falls back to `git symbolic-ref` for older git versions.

Tests use two temp journals and a bare repo as the remote. One test writes an entry in each journal, syncs both, and checks that both folders then hold both files. Another creates a conflicting edit of one file and checks the abort path and the error message.

I did not add automatic sync from hooks yet. A hook that pushes after each entry would slow every session, and network failures would show up in the agent's output. The plan is a background option later, after I see how manual sync feels for a week.

The help text and README have the new command. The README check test passes, so the documented commands exist.

summary: Made sync skip cleanly when the journal has nothing new, instead of making an empty commit and a pointless push.
body:
Running sync twice in a row created an empty commit the second time, because the commit step did not check for staged changes. I added `git diff --cached --quiet` before committing and print "nothing to sync" when the index is clean.

The push is skipped too if the local branch equals the remote branch after the pull. That saves a network round trip, which matters on slow hotel wifi, where the user noticed a three-second wait.

Exit code stays 0 in the no-change case, since nothing failed. A new test checks that two syncs in a row produce exactly one commit.

While in there I fixed the commit message count, which counted untracked files in subfolders twice. It now uses `git status --porcelain` and counts lines once.

summary: Added the config command with get, set and list, backed by a plain key=value file, and moved the journal path and host name onto it.
body:
Until now the only setting was the journal folder environment variable. The user wants a host label that differs from the machine name and a default for the remote, so I added `agent-journal config`. It supports `config list`, `config get <key>` and `config set <key> <value>`.

The file lives at the config directory next to the journal pointer, in plain key=value lines. I chose that over JSON because the CLI is pure sh and awk, and parsing JSON there would be fragile. Keys are restricted to lowercase letters and underscores, and values cannot contain newlines.

Set rewrites the file with awk into a temp file and renames it, so a crash cannot leave half a file. Comments starting with # are preserved, which the user asked for because they edit the file by hand sometimes.

Precedence is environment variable first, then config file, then default. I wrote that down in the help text, and a test table covers every combination for the journal path and the host label.

The write command now reads the host from config. Before, it called hostname each time, and on macOS that returned names ending in .local, which cluttered the front matter. With a config value set, entries carry the chosen label.

Unknown keys are an error with exit code 2 and a list of valid keys. I considered allowing any key but decided that typos like jornal_path would silently do nothing, which is worse.

Eleven tests were added in test/config.test.ts. One checks that set with an empty value removes the key. Another checks that a file with Windows line endings is read correctly, since the user syncs between machines.

Next: document the keys in the README and let sync read its default remote from the config.

summary: Built the journal pane that shows the latest entries in a terminal split, refreshing every few seconds with a plain loop instead of a watch dependency.
body:
The user wants to see what the agent has written while it works. `agent-journal pane` clears the screen and prints the latest entries, then sleeps and repeats. I used a plain sh loop with `sleep 2` because watch is not installed on macOS by default.

The output reuses the list command with the truncation to terminal width. Each refresh reads `tput cols` and `tput lines`, so resizing the split works. The number of entries shown is lines minus two, to leave room for a header.

Flicker was the first problem. Clearing the screen each time made the output blink. I switched to moving the cursor home with `tput cup 0 0` and clearing to the end of each line, which removed the flicker.

The second problem was CPU use. Reading all files every two seconds was fine with 40 fixtures, but with a 3000-entry journal it took 0.4 seconds per refresh. I now compare the newest file name with the last one seen and only redraw when it changed or the terminal size changed.

The pane also handles Ctrl-C: a trap restores the cursor and exits 0. Without it the cursor stayed hidden in some terminals.

Tests are hard for a loop that never ends, so I added `--once`, which prints a single frame and exits. The tests use it with a fixed width and check the output against expected text. That covered header, truncation and the empty-journal message.

I tried it inside a tmux split next to a Claude Code session. Entries appeared within two seconds of being written, and the layout held up when I resized the pane.

Still open: highlighting entries from the current session. That needs the session id in the pane, which I will think about next.

summary: Highlighted entries from the current session in the pane with bold text, using the session id from the environment when it is set.
body:
The pane showed all recent entries the same way, so it was hard to see what the running agent had just added. When the session id variable is set, the pane now prints matching entries in bold.

The list command gained a hidden `--mark-session <id>` option that adds a leading marker column. The pane turns that marker into escape codes, and only when stdout is a terminal. Piped output stays plain.

I checked that NO_COLOR is respected: when it is set, the marker becomes an asterisk instead of bold. A test covers both modes.

One bug: session ids with a slash broke the awk match. I now compare with an exact string equality and not a regex.

The pane is usable now. Next I want to add the time zone display.

summary: Fixed the pane crashing on terminals where tput lines returns nothing, such as inside a CI log, by falling back to 24 rows and 80 columns.
body:
A test run in GitHub Actions failed with an arithmetic error in the pane. There was no terminal, so `tput lines` printed nothing and the subtraction got an empty operand.

I added defaults of 24 rows and 80 columns when tput fails or prints a non-number. The same fallback now applies to the list command's width detection, which had a similar silent weakness.

A new test unsets TERM and runs the pane with --once, and checks the 80-column layout. CI is green on both Ubuntu and macOS.

Nothing else changed.

summary: Added time zone support to list: entries store an offset in the date, and list shows local time by default with a --utc flag.
body:
Entries from the laptop in another country showed times that confused the user when the list was read at home. The front matter date already carried an offset, but list printed it as written. I now convert to the viewer's local time by default.

The conversion happens in awk, with the offset parsed from the date string and applied to epoch seconds computed by hand. I avoided `date -d` because BSD date on macOS takes different flags than GNU date, and the CLI has to work on both.

The viewer's offset comes from `date +%z`, which both implementations support. That is the one call to the system date, and I wrapped it so tests can override it with a TZ_OFFSET variable.

The edge cases took the most time. A date near midnight must roll the day correctly, and the months have different lengths, so I wrote a small day-of-month rollover function and tested it with entries at the end of a short month and across a leap day. Half-hour offsets, such as +0530, also needed care: the minutes part must be added, not ignored.

The `--utc` flag prints times in UTC with a Z suffix. The `--full` flag still works with both.

I added 14 tests with a table of offsets and expected output. One of them caught an off-by-one in my rollover where the last day of a month printed as day zero of the next month.

The pane uses list, so it shows local time as well, with no extra work. The README example output was updated to match.

No change to the stored format, so existing journals keep working. Older entries without an offset are treated as UTC, and I documented that choice in the help text.

summary: Wrote the README section for the Claude Code plugin with install steps, what the hooks do, and a screenshot placeholder for the pane.
body:
The README only had a short line about the plugin. I wrote a full section: how to install it, what the SessionStart and Stop hooks do, and how the recent-entries context appears in a session.

The install steps were run in a clean container, in line with the earlier check. They worked, but one step was wrong: the plugin directory name in the README had a typo, which the container run caught.

I added a subsection on the pane, with a command line and a note on running it in a tmux split. A placeholder comment marks where a screenshot should go. I have not decided how to make the pictures yet.

The badge row at the top now has a license badge next to the CI badge. I checked that both links resolve and that the CI badge points at the main branch.

I trimmed the opening paragraph by two sentences, since the pitch was repeated in the first usage example.

The README test, which runs every command from code blocks against the CLI help, passed after I added the `pane` and `sync` commands to the list of known commands.

Still to do: a section for the config command and the screenshots.

summary: Added README documentation for the config command and sync, including the table of config keys and how precedence works.
body:
Both commands had help text but no README coverage. I added a Configuration section with a table of keys: journal path, host label, default remote. Each row has the matching environment variable.

Precedence is described in one sentence and then shown with a small example: setting the host with config, then overriding it for one command with the environment variable.

The sync section explains the first-time setup with `--init`, and what happens on a conflict. I also wrote that sync is manual on purpose and that nothing pushes in the background.

While checking the examples, I found that the README example for `config set` used a key name from an earlier draft, `hostname`. The real key is `host`. The README test did not catch it because it checks command names and not arguments.

I extended the test to run each example command that begins with `agent-journal config` against a temp config. It now fails for unknown keys, and I fixed the example.

The install section got a short note on updating: run the install script again, as it overwrites the CLI file. I tested this on the container.

The README is now about 190 lines. I think it is getting long, and I plan to move the file format details lower down later.

summary: Investigated why the SessionStart hook sometimes printed no recent entries: a project name with spaces broke an unquoted variable in the hook script.
body:
The user reported that in one project the session started without the recent-entries context. The other projects worked. I reproduced it by running the hook script in that directory.

The project is called "my notes" with a space in the folder name. In the hook, the project name was passed to `agent-journal list --project $name` without quotes, so the CLI got two arguments, "my" and "notes", and printed a usage error. The hook silenced stderr, so nothing showed.

I quoted every variable in all three hook scripts and ran shellcheck on them. It found two more unquoted expansions, one in the env file writer and one in the Stop hook marker path. Both would have broken with spaces in the home path.

The silent stderr was the real problem, because it hid the error. The hook now writes errors to a log file in the config directory, and prints one line to the session that says the context could not be loaded, with the path to the log.

I added tests that create a project directory with spaces and a quote character in the name, then run the hook. The recent entries now appear in both cases. The quote character case needed one more fix in the awk filter, where the name was interpolated into the program text; it is now passed with `-v`.

I also searched the CLI for the same pattern. The write command builds the front matter with printf and the project name as a format argument, not as the format, so it was safe. A test confirms that a project name with a percent sign is written as is.

CI is green. I want to add shellcheck to the CI workflow so this class of bug is caught early, which is next.

summary: Added shellcheck to the CI workflow and fixed the 17 warnings it found in the CLI, install script and hooks.
body:
After the quoting bug in the hook last week, I added a shellcheck job to GitHub Actions. It runs on bin/agent-journal, the install script and every hook script, with the shell set to sh so bashisms are flagged.

The first run reported 17 warnings. Most were harmless style notes, but I fixed all of them rather than adding blanket ignores.

The breakdown: nine unquoted variables, four uses of `[ -a ]` and `[ -o ]` that I replaced with separate tests, two `read` calls without `-r`, one `echo -e` that is not portable, and one unused variable in the install script.

The `echo -e` was a real bug. Under dash it printed a literal "-e" at the start of the line, in the install summary. I replaced it with printf, and the summary looks right on both shells now.

The `read` without `-r` would have mangled backslashes in summaries read from stdin in one code path. I wrote a test with a summary containing a backslash, and it fails on the old code and passes now.

Two warnings I kept as targeted ignores with a comment: a deliberate word split of a fixed list of flags, and a trap string that must expand at definition time. Each has a short reason next to it.

Shellcheck needs to be installed on the macOS runner, so the job runs only on Ubuntu, where it is a package. The tests still run on both systems.

The workflow takes 25 seconds longer now, which is fine. I also pinned the shellcheck version in the job so that a new release does not fail the build without a code change.

Next up is the Codex plugin planning, which starts after the list command's time zone documentation is checked once more.

summary: Wrote a plan for the pane screenshot: a plain terminal capture in the light theme, to be added to the README until a better picture exists.
body:
The README has a placeholder for the pane picture. Before choosing a tool, I wrote down what the picture should show: the pane next to an agent session, with four or five entries, one highlighted.

For now a static screenshot is enough. I will capture it at 100 columns so it is legible when GitHub scales it down. Window chrome is cropped.

I listed the fixture entries that look best. They should have short summaries that fit in one line, because truncated lines look broken in a picture.

Animated pictures could come later, once the other commands settle. Nothing is recorded today.

The plan is stored in the repo's notes file.

summary: Took a screenshot of the pane with fixture entries and added it to the README, replacing the placeholder comment.
body:
I built a small demo journal from the fixture generator with eight entries, choosing summaries that fit within 100 columns. The pane ran in a terminal at that width with the light theme.

The screenshot is a PNG, 1200 pixels wide, about 70 KB after optimizing with oxipng. It sits in docs/images/pane.png and the README references it with alt text describing what it shows.

One entry is bold, which shows the session highlight. The alt text mentions this, for readers who cannot see the picture.

I checked that the image renders on the GitHub preview of the branch. The width looked right, and the text was crisp.

A dark theme version is not made yet. That can wait.

The README test still passes, since it ignores images.

summary: Designed the Codex plugin: Codex has no session hooks like Claude Code, so the rules will go through an AGENTS.md block that the install step maintains.
body:
I read through the Codex documentation and tried it in a scratch project. Codex does not offer a SessionStart hook equivalent to the Claude Code plugin. It does read AGENTS.md files from the home directory and the project, so that is where the rules must go.

The design: the install step adds a marked block to the AGENTS.md in the Codex config directory. The block is the same short bootstrap as before, pointing to `agent-journal rules`, so the long text stays in one place.

The markers are two comment lines, begin and end. The installer replaces everything between them, so running it twice does not duplicate the block, and the user's own text outside the markers is never touched.

I tested the replace logic on four AGENTS.md shapes: no file, an empty file, a file with user text and no block, and a file with a block in the middle. All four gave the expected result when I ran the awk script by hand. The case with a missing end marker is the risky one; the installer refuses and prints an error rather than guess.

Session ids are a problem. Claude Code gives them through the env file, but Codex exposes nothing equivalent that I could find. The write command falls back to a generated id per process, so entries from one Codex session will not share an id. I noted this as a limitation.

The agent field in the front matter needs a new value, `codex`. The write command takes it from an `AGENT_JOURNAL_AGENT` variable. The bootstrap tells Codex to set the variable on each call, which is awkward but works.

Open question: will Codex write entries without a Stop hook? In the scratch test it wrote one entry when the rules said so, but skipped it in a longer task. I will have to strengthen the wording, as I did for Claude Code.

Next step is the installer code and its tests.

summary: Wrote the Codex installer's AGENTS.md block replacement in awk, refusing to touch a file with a begin marker but no end marker.
body:
The installer now has a function that maintains the marked block. It reads the file once with awk, drops the old block if present, and appends the new one at the end, or in the old place if it existed.

The missing end marker case exits with code 1 and a message naming the file and the line of the begin marker. The file is left unchanged, which a test verifies with a checksum.

I also handled a file with no trailing newline, where the block would otherwise be glued to the last line of the user's text. The function adds one newline first.

Six tests cover the four shapes, the broken marker and the missing newline. They run in a temp home directory.

Next is the live Codex session to check that the block is picked up.

summary: Ran the Codex plugin in a live session: the rules block was read and entries were written, but session ids were missing, so I derived one from the parent process.
body:
I installed the block in a temp Codex home and started a session in a scratch project. Codex followed the bootstrap, ran `agent-journal rules`, and wrote an entry after the first task.

The agent field said `codex`, as designed. The session field held a random id for each entry, so three entries from one session had three ids. That breaks the pane highlight and the Stop-style check I do for Claude Code.

I looked at what is stable across calls inside one Codex session. The parent process id of the shell that runs the command stayed the same for the whole session in my test. The write command now builds the session id from the agent name, the parent pid and the process start time, and uses it only when no session variable is set.

The start time is needed because pids get reused. I read it from `ps -o lstart= -p`, which works on both Linux and macOS, though the format differs. I hash the string with cksum so the format difference does not matter within a machine.

After the change, three entries in one session shared an id, and a new session in the same project got a different one. I added a test that runs the write command twice from the same parent shell and once from another, and checks the ids.

The summaries Codex wrote were fine, but it wrote an entry only after the first of three tasks. I strengthened the bootstrap with a sentence that says to write one after each finished task, not once per session. A second run gave an entry after each of the three tasks.

One problem remains: when Codex runs the command in a sandbox without access to ps, the session id falls back to random again. I could not fix that, and I documented it in the Codex section of the README.

I also noticed that the Codex install does not add the recent-entries context. Without a start hook there is no place to run it. The bootstrap now tells the agent to run `agent-journal list --recent 5` at the start. That is a weaker mechanism but it works.

Next: README for Codex and a check on a clean machine.

summary: Added a README section for the Codex plugin with install steps and the known limits: no start hook and no stable session id in sandboxes.
body:
The section follows the Claude Code one: install command, what the block does, and what to expect in a session.

I was open about the limits. There is no hook, so the recent context depends on the agent obeying one sentence. Session ids are derived from the parent process and fall back to random ids in a sandbox without ps.

I ran the install steps in a clean container and they worked. The README test passed with the new commands.

The badge row is unchanged.

summary: Fixed the Codex installer failing on a home directory with no config folder yet, by creating it before writing the AGENTS.md block.
body:
On a fresh machine without Codex ever started, the config folder did not exist, and the installer died with a redirect error when writing the file.

I added a mkdir -p for the folder, with a message in the install summary that says it was created. Permissions are 700, to match what Codex uses itself.

A test now runs the installer with an empty temp home and checks that the folder and block exist. It failed before the fix and passes now.

The clean container run is green as well.

summary: Started the Pi extension: read how Pi loads extensions, wrote a minimal one that injects the bootstrap and registers an after-turn handler that checks for a new entry.
body:
Pi's extension model is the most capable of the three agents. An extension is a TypeScript module that can add to the system prompt and subscribe to events, so the bootstrap can be injected directly, with no file editing like Codex needs.

I created plugins/pi/index.ts with a default export that registers two things. The first adds the short bootstrap text to the system prompt, the same pointer to `agent-journal rules`. The second listens for the end of each agent turn.

The turn-end handler runs `agent-journal list --session <id> --count` through a child process and compares the count with the last one it saw. If the work was substantial and no entry was added, it queues a one-line reminder for the next turn. This is closer to the Claude Code Stop hook than to the Codex approach.

I defined substantial as three or more tool calls in the turn, using the event data. The threshold is the same as in the Claude Code hook, so behavior is consistent between agents.

Session ids come from Pi's session object, which exposes a stable id. That is better than Codex. I pass it to the CLI through the environment variable, so entries from one Pi session share an id.

The oxlint config needed a small change: the plugin directory contains TypeScript that targets Pi's runtime, with types I do not have installed. I added a minimal local type declaration for the events I use, so lint and type checks pass without pulling in a dependency.

Testing is the hard part. I cannot run Pi in CI. I split the logic into a pure function that takes counts and tool-call numbers and returns whether to remind, and wrote Vitest tests for it with eight cases, including a first turn and a turn with a counter reset.

I then loaded the extension in a real Pi session. The bootstrap reached the model and the agent wrote an entry after the first task. The reminder path fired once when I forced a long turn without an entry.

Open items: the install step for Pi, which has to copy the extension into the right folder, and the README section. I also want to check that spawning a child process each turn does not slow Pi noticeably; the first measurements show about 15 ms.

summary: Wrote the Pi install step and README section, and checked that the installer works for all three agents from one command with a flag per agent.
body:
The install script now accepts `--agent claude`, `--agent codex` or `--agent pi`, and `--all`. Before, each plugin had its own steps in the README, which was getting long.

For Pi, the installer copies plugins/pi/index.ts into Pi's extension folder under the name agent-journal.ts, and refuses to overwrite a file of that name that it did not create. A header comment in the file marks it as managed, and the installer looks for that line.

I ran the script in a clean container with each flag and with --all. All four runs printed an accurate summary of what they changed, and a second run changed nothing and said so.

The README has a Pi section now, shorter than the other two because the extension does most of the work. A table at the top of the plugins area compares the three agents: start context, reminder, session id. It makes the differences plain, and I think it will help readers choose.

I added tests for the flag parsing: an unknown agent exits 2 with the list of valid names, and --all together with --agent is rejected. They pass under dash and bash.

One remaining oddity is that the Pi extension needs the CLI on PATH in the child process. The installer prints a warning when the CLI is not found in PATH.

Next up are recall and search terms, which the Pi and Codex plugins will need to call.

summary: Started the recall command with term search over entry files, using awk to score matches in summary and body and printing the best hits first.
body:
Recall is the command the agents will use when the user asks about past work, so it has to work without any index. I wrote `agent-journal recall <terms...>` as a single awk pass over every entry file in the journal folder. Each entry is parsed into front matter and body, and the terms are matched case-insensitively.

Scoring is simple: a hit in the summary counts three, a hit in the body counts one, and all terms must match somewhere in the entry (AND semantics). Ties are broken by newest date first. I considered a stemming step but dropped it, because the journal is small and exact words from the agent's own vocabulary are usually enough.

The output is one line per hit with the date, project, file name and summary, so the agent can read the full file next. A `--limit` flag defaults to 10. I also added `--project` to restrict the search to one project name, reusing the field that list already prints.

The first run against my real journal of about 60 entries took 0.08 seconds, which is fine. Quoting was the main trouble: terms with regex characters such as `a.b` or `[x` made awk fail with a syntax error. I switched to index() on lowercased strings instead of regex matching, and that fixed it.

What is left is reading by period, which needs a date parser that handles the stored offsets. I also have no tests yet beyond a manual check on three queries. Next I will write fixtures with known terms and add Vitest cases for AND matching, the limit and the project filter. After that I will look at how the agent rules should describe recall.

summary: Added Vitest cases for recall covering AND matching, the limit flag, the project filter and terms containing regex characters.
body:
I wrote tests/recall.test.js next to the existing list tests, reusing the fixture loader. The fixtures are six entries with distinct words so each expected result is unambiguous.

Cases covered: a single term hit in a summary ranks above a hit only in a body; two terms require both to be present; `--limit 1` returns one line; `--project` excludes other projects; and a query with `a.b` and `[x` returns no hits and exits 0 instead of an awk error.

One test failed at first. Two entries had the same score and the same date, and their order depended on the file system listing. I added the file name as a final tiebreaker in the sort, which made the order stable.

I also checked that a missing journal folder prints a clear message and exits with 1. All recall tests pass, and the full suite runs in about 4 seconds. Next is reading by period.

summary: Wrote a design note for reading entries by period, choosing relative words like 'yesterday' and 'last week' plus explicit ranges, all resolved by the CLI.
body:
The user asks questions such as what happened last week, and the agent should not do date math itself. The plan is `agent-journal recall --since <x> --until <y>`, where each value is a number plus unit (`3d`, `2w`, `1m`) or a plain date in the stored format.

I compared two options. The first lets the agent compute dates and pass them in, which is error prone when time zones are involved. The second resolves relative values in the CLI against the current time, and I chose it because entries already carry an offset and list already knows how to convert.

The awk parsing has to compare timestamps. Entries store an ISO-like date with an offset, so I will convert each to UTC seconds in a small shell function that uses `date -u -d` on Linux and `date -u -j -f` on macOS. That portability gap is the risky part, and I will test both forms.

A period search without terms should list everything in the range, newest first. With terms, the range just filters before scoring. I wrote the flag names and examples into the notes for the next session.

Nothing was implemented yet. Open question: whether `--since yesterday` as a literal word should work. I lean toward yes for `today` and `yesterday` only.

summary: Implemented recall --since and --until with a portable timestamp conversion that works on both GNU date and BSD date, with tests for each unit.
body:
I built the period reading from the design note. A new function `to_epoch` converts a stored date with its offset to UTC seconds. It tries GNU `date -d` first and falls back to BSD `date -j -f`, and I tested both paths, the second by running on the laptop and the first inside the CI container.

The BSD path was the painful one. The offset in the stored value looks like `+02:00`, and BSD `%z` wants `+0200` with no colon. I strip the colon with sed before the call. Without that, every entry on macOS parsed as the epoch and all period searches returned nothing.

Relative values work as number plus unit: `d`, `w`, `m` where a month is 30 days. `today` and `yesterday` are accepted as words, meaning midnight local time. `--until` defaults to now.

To avoid calling date once per file, I compute the two bounds once and pass them into awk, which converts entry dates with a small pure-awk routine for the common `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS` shape and applies the offset by arithmetic. I checked it against `date` on 200 generated timestamps and got no mismatch.

Tests added: ranges of `1d`, `2w`, an explicit start with no end, an empty range, and an entry stored with a negative offset near midnight that must land on the right side of the boundary. That last case caught an off-by-one when I forgot to subtract the offset instead of adding it.

All tests pass. Next I want the output to group by day when the range is long, and the rules text needs a mention of the new flags.

summary: Grouped period output by day and capped long ranges, so a month of entries is readable instead of a flat wall of lines.
body:
A range query over the last month returned 90 lines in one block, which the agent would have to read in full. I added day headers in the recall output when `--since` is used: a line with the local date, then the entries indented under it.

The day boundary uses local time by default, like list, and `--utc` switches it. The grouping happens in awk after sorting, by remembering the previous day key and printing a header when it changes.

I also added a default cap of 40 entries for period queries, with a final line saying how many more matched and how to raise the cap with `--limit`. Without the note, an agent could believe 40 was everything. I decided the note must always show the exact count.

Another small fix: entries with a missing offset were parsed as UTC silently. They now fall back to the configured host zone from config, and if that is not set, to UTC.

Tests: one for headers appearing in the right order, one for the cap message with a count, and one for the offset fallback. A snapshot of the output for the fixtures is stored under tests/fixtures/expected so format changes are visible in review.

Next is the rules text for recall.

summary: Rewrote the agent rules so recall is the first step when the user asks about past work, and tested the wording with a Claude Code session on three questions.
body:
The rules printed by `agent-journal rules` only said that recall exists. I rewrote that section to give a short procedure: for a question about past work, run recall with two or three key terms, read the best two files in full, and answer from them. For questions about a time span, use `--since` first.

I also added two prohibitions that came from watching agents in earlier sessions. Do not guess from memory about earlier sessions, and do not report that nothing was found before trying at least one broader term.

Then I ran a live Claude Code session with three questions about my own journal: what did I do on the sync command, what happened last week, and why the pane crashed in CI. The first and third were answered correctly after one recall call each. The second one used `--since 1w` and gave a correct list.

One failure: on the sync question the agent searched for the phrase 'git remote push' as one quoted term, which matched nothing, and then gave up. The rules now say to pass terms as separate words and not as one phrase. I re-ran the question and it found the entry on the second try.

The rules text grew by about 12 lines, still short enough for the bootstrap model of loading it fresh by command. I want to measure this more systematically later rather than rely on three questions.

Next: Codex and Pi get the same rules automatically through the command, so I only need to verify that their installs print the new text.

summary: Checked that the Codex and Pi installs pick up the new recall rules through the rules command, and found no change was needed in either plugin.
body:
Since both plugins point at `agent-journal rules`, the new text should arrive without edits. I verified by running the Codex install into a temporary home and reading the AGENTS.md block, which still contains only the pointer.

In a live Codex session the rules loaded and the agent used `recall` with separate terms on the first attempt. For Pi, I started the extension and printed what the bootstrap injects; it also holds the pointer line and nothing stale.

No code changed. I noted in the README plan that recall deserves its own section, written next.

summary: Wrote the README section for recall with example queries and output, and trimmed the feature list at the top to match.
body:
The README did not mention recall at all, so I added a section after sync and config. It shows three examples: a term search, a search limited to a project, and a period read with `--since 1w`. Each has a short block with the real output from the fixture journal.

I took the outputs by running the commands and pasting them, instead of writing them by hand, because the day headers have a specific format. I also added a table of flags with one line per flag.

The feature list at the top had grown to nine bullets. I cut it to six by merging the three plugin bullets into one line that names all three agents. The intro paragraph was reworded to lead with the problem: agents forget what they did.

The existing test that checks every command in README code blocks against help caught a typo in one example, `--sinse`. I fixed it, which was a good reminder the test pays off.

Still missing from the README are badges and a better picture of the tool in use. I only noted that for later.

summary: Fixed the README's recall section drifting from real output by generating the example block from a fixture run, and added a test that fails when the two differ.
body:
The recall section written earlier in the day had example output that I typed by hand, and when I compared it with a real run against the fixture journal the score order and the snippet line were already different. That made me want the examples to come from the CLI itself instead of from memory. I added a small script, scripts/readme-examples.sh, that runs `agent-journal recall` with the three documented queries against tests/fixtures/journal and prints the results with the home path replaced by a placeholder.

The README now has marker comments around each example block, and the same script can rewrite the text between the markers with awk. I kept the replacement in awk because the install and rules code already use it, and I did not want a new dependency just for docs. The script refuses to run if a begin marker has no end marker, the same guard the Codex installer uses for its AGENTS.md block.

A new Vitest case runs the script in check mode and compares the generated blocks with what is in README.md. On the first run it failed on the query with two terms, because the hand-typed output listed the hits in the wrong order. That was the useful catch, since a reader copying the example would have seen different output from the real command. After regenerating, the test passed and the diff in the README was only those blocks.

One snag was the date line in the output, which depends on the time zone of the machine. I pinned TZ to UTC inside the script so the blocks come out the same locally and in CI. I also trimmed one example that printed eight hits down to three with the limit flag, because the long version pushed the install section far down the page. Still open: the list examples in the usage section are screenshots, so they are not covered by this check, and I will decide later whether they should be text instead.

summary: Fixed recall missing entries whose summary contained a colon, because the front matter parser split the line at every colon instead of the first one.
body:
The user asked about the shellcheck work and recall found nothing, though the entry exists. Its summary contains 'Added shellcheck: 17 warnings'. The awk parser used `split($0, a, ":")` and kept only the second part, so the summary was cut at the colon and the later words were never matched.

I reproduced it with a fixture entry whose summary has two colons. List also showed the cut summary, which means the bug lived in a shared parsing snippet that was copied into both commands. I replaced it with a match on the first `: ` and substr for the rest.

The cwd field also can contain a colon on some systems, so the same fix covered it. I checked all fields in the fixtures and wrote a test with colons in summary, cwd and host.

I then moved the parsing snippet into one shared awk file under lib so the commands cannot drift again. Both list and recall now include it with `-f`. The install script needed a small change to copy lib.

All tests pass, including the earlier list snapshots, which stayed identical. I re-ran the user's question and found the entry.

summary: Made recall print a snippet of the matching body line under each hit, so the agent can often answer without opening the file.
body:
Hits showed only the summary line. For many questions the useful fact is in the body, such as a number or an error message, so the agent had to open each file. I added a `--context` flag, on by default, that prints the first body line which contains a search term, trimmed to 120 characters.

The line is chosen in awk during scoring, so no second pass is needed. If the match is only in the summary, no snippet is printed to avoid repeating the same text.

Trimming cut some lines in the middle of a word, which looked sloppy. I now cut at the last space before the limit and add an ellipsis.

Output size grew by about a third. For the default 10 hits that is still under 2 KB, which is cheap for the agent. `--no-context` returns the old format for scripts.

Tests: snippet appears for body-only matches, absent for summary-only matches, and long lines are cut at a word boundary. I updated the stored snapshots and reviewed the diff by hand before committing.

summary: Answered the user's question about why sync does a pull-rebase first, by reading the sync entries and the script rather than from memory.
body:
The user asked why sync pulls before pushing. I used recall with 'sync' and 'rebase' and found the entry from the sync command work, then read the relevant part of bin/agent-journal.

The answer: the journal lives on several machines, each writing its own files. Entry file names include the host and a timestamp, so two machines never write the same file. That means a rebase never has content conflicts and it simply puts local commits on top of remote ones.

Without the pull step, the push is rejected as non-fast-forward when another machine pushed first. A merge would work too but leaves noise commits in a journal history that nobody reads. I told the user so.

I also noted that a rebase conflict is still possible if someone edits an old entry on two machines, and the script aborts the rebase and prints a message in that case. No code was changed.

summary: Built the first Pi recall integration test harness and found Pi's after-turn handler fired recall output into the transcript, which I silenced.
body:
With recall done, I wanted to check how the Pi extension behaves when the agent uses it a lot. I wrote a small harness script that starts Pi in a temporary home with a fixture journal and sends scripted prompts that ask about past work.
