The first run worked, but the after-turn handler, which checks for a new entry, called `agent-journal list --since 5m` and printed its output into the session. The agent then treated that output as new information and sometimes mentioned it. The handler should check silently.

I changed the handler to call a new quiet mode, `agent-journal recall --since 5m --count`, which prints only a number. The extension compares it to zero and decides whether to remind. Adding `--count` to recall took about ten lines and a test.

I ran five scripted prompts. Four correct answers came from recall with separate terms, and one question about last week used `--since 1w`. One prompt used a very vague term, 'that bug', and the agent answered that it could not find it, which is acceptable behavior under the rules.

The reminder fired once at the end of a session with no entry, as planned. The harness now lives under tests/pi and is not part of CI because it needs the Pi binary.

I also noticed that the extension has no timeout on the command call. If the journal folder is on a slow mount, a turn could hang. I added a three-second timeout and a skip on failure.

Next I will try the same kind of harness for Codex, though it has no after-turn hook, so the test will be simpler.

summary: Wrote a Codex smoke test that runs scripted questions through recall and checks the answers mention the right entry, without needing hooks.
body:
Codex has no after-turn hook, so the check is only about reading. I wrote tests/codex/smoke.sh that runs `codex exec` with a prompt about a fixture entry and greps the answer for a marker word that appears in only one entry.

Three prompts were used: a term question, a project question and a period question. The first two passed on the first run. The period question failed because the sandbox clock differs from the fixture dates, so 'last week' held no entries.

I fixed that by making the fixtures relative: the smoke script generates entries with dates computed from the current time. This is also better for the rest of the tests, and I noted that for a later cleanup.

The script is skipped when codex is not on PATH. It is not run in CI.

summary: Fixed recall treating a leading dash in a search term as a flag, so searching for '-1' or '--utc' now works after a double dash separator.
body:
While looking for the entry about the --utc flag I typed `agent-journal recall --utc` and got an unknown option error, which is correct, but there was no way to search for a term that begins with a dash. Agents can run into this with error messages such as `-bash: command not found`.

I added support for `--` as the end of options. Everything after it is a term. The option loop in the CLI had a case for unknown flags that exited; I put the `--` case before it.

I also updated the help text for recall with one line explaining the separator and an example. The rules text got a short hint so agents know about it.

Tests: a term with a leading dash returns the entry that contains it, and an unknown flag without the separator still fails with exit code 2. A third test checks that the separator works together with `--project`.

The README recall section got one line about it too. The command-check test accepted the new example.

summary: Planned a better set of README pictures: which three views to show, which fixture entries to use, and the tools to compare, without recording anything yet.
body:
The README still has only one static screenshot, of the pane. I wrote a plan for pictures that show the tool in use: the agent writing an entry, list and recall output, and the pane refreshing.

For each view I picked a fixture so the content is stable. The entries should show believable work, not lorem ipsum, and I selected six from the test fixtures and rewrote two to be less cryptic. Terminal size is fixed at 100 columns by 28 rows so text stays readable on GitHub.

I listed requirements: sharp text at the displayed size, small files under 1 MB each, a dark and a light version because the README is viewed in both themes, and a way to rebuild the pictures from a script when output formats change.

Tools to compare later: screenshots with the terminal app, a scripted recorder, and a rendering tool driven by a text file. I did not try any of them today. The plan is stored in the repo notes.

Open question: whether animation is worth the file weight or two good static images are enough. I will decide after seeing a sample.

summary: Took fresh static screenshots of list and recall in a 100-column terminal and put them in the README under the usage section.
body:
As an interim step I captured two screenshots with the terminal app: one of list, one of recall with a period query. I used the fixture journal and a font size that stays readable when GitHub scales the image to 800 pixels.

The first capture had my real hostname in the prompt. I retook it with a plain `$ ` prompt and a clean shell. Files are about 90 KB and 110 KB as PNG.

They sit under docs/img and the README references them with relative paths and alt text that describes the content. The light theme only for now.

The pictures are static and will need retaking when output formats change, which I accept for now.

summary: Added a --json output to recall after a script consumer needed stable fields, writing the escaping in awk and testing quotes, backslashes and newlines.
body:
A pull request from another contributor asked for machine-readable output, so a status script can read recall results. I agreed on the idea but wanted the implementation to stay in the CLI. I added `--json`, which prints one JSON object per line with date, project, file, summary and score.

The hard part is escaping in awk. I wrote a small function that escapes backslash, double quote, tab and the control characters, and replaces newlines with `\n`. Summaries are single lines, but cwd values can hold odd characters.

I tested with an entry whose summary contains a quote, a backslash and a unicode character. The first version double-escaped backslashes because I applied the replacements in the wrong order: quote first, then backslash. Putting the backslash step first fixed it.

I validated the output with node's JSON.parse inside the Vitest test, which is simple because tests already run under node. Every line must parse and the fields must equal the fixture values.

The snippet option is ignored in JSON mode unless `--context` is explicitly passed, and then it adds a `snippet` field. I wrote that into the help text.

I replied on the pull request with the design and thanked the author, since the original patch had a nice test idea that I reused: a round trip through JSON.parse.

README flag table updated. Next I want to look at list, which should probably get the same flag for consistency.

summary: Gave list the same --json flag as recall by moving the JSON escaping into the shared awk library, and added the matching tests.
body:
After the recall change, list lacked a JSON option, which would be an odd gap. I moved the escaping function from the recall script into the shared awk file under lib, the one I made when fixing the colon bug, and used it from both commands.

List prints more fields than recall: cwd, host, user, agent and session. All are included in the objects. Missing fields are empty strings rather than absent keys, so a consumer does not need to check for undefined.

The list tests use the same JSON.parse round trip. I wrote one parameterized test that runs both commands over the same fixtures with odd characters and checks that each line parses.

One snag: list formats times in local zone by default, and JSON output should be stable. I decided that JSON always prints the stored date string with its offset, and ignores the local conversion unless `--local` is given. This is documented in help.

The pane uses list internally, and I confirmed that it is not affected because it does not pass the new flag.

Suite passes with 58 tests in about 5 seconds. README table updated for both commands.

Remaining: a note in the rules text so agents prefer plain output for reading and use JSON only when writing scripts.

summary: Looked into why recall ranked an old entry above a newer one on the same score and confirmed the date tiebreaker was correct, but the sort key used local time.
body:
The user noticed that two entries with an equal score were listed with the older first. I checked the sort: it used the formatted local date string. Across a daylight saving shift, local strings can sort wrong, and entries with different offsets are compared as if they were the same zone.

The fix was to sort by the UTC epoch that recall already computes for period queries. I now compute it for every entry, not only when a range is given. That adds little time: 200 entries still take about 0.1 seconds.

I built a test with two entries 30 minutes apart, one stored with +02:00 and the other with -05:00, where the string order and the real order differ. It failed before the fix and passes after.

No output format change, so the snapshots stayed intact.

summary: Wrote the eval plan for the recall rules: twelve questions with known answers, a scoring script, and a baseline run before changing any wording.
body:
I want to stop judging the rules text by three live questions. The plan is a small eval that asks an agent twelve questions about a fixed fixture journal and checks the answers.

The questions cover four kinds: a fact in a body, a count of entries, a period question, and a question where the right answer is that nothing was recorded. For each there is an expected marker string. The fixture journal has 40 entries, written to include near misses, such as two entries about similar topics with different numbers.

The scoring script runs the agent non-interactively, saves the transcript and counts a pass when the marker appears and a wrong marker does not. It also records the number of recall calls, because an answer that needed eight calls is a sign of unclear rules.

The baseline run comes first, with the current rules, so that later changes can be compared. I wrote the question file and the scoring script but did not run the baseline yet, because it costs agent time.

I expect the 'nothing recorded' type to be the weakest, since agents tend to answer anyway. Next I will run the baseline with Claude Code and Codex.

summary: Ran the baseline eval of the recall rules on Claude Code and Codex: 10 of 12 and 8 of 12 passed, with the failures mostly on the not-recorded questions.
body:
I ran the twelve question eval with the current rules, once per agent. Claude Code passed 10 and Codex passed 8. Each run took about 11 minutes.

The two Claude failures were both of the not-recorded kind. For a question about a feature that was never built, the agent found a related entry about a planned feature and presented the plan as done. Reading the transcript showed it did read the entry but did not check its wording.

Codex failed the same two and two more. In one, it passed a quoted phrase as a single term, which the rules forbid, but the wording was in a different place than the recall procedure. In the other, it answered from the snippet only and the snippet was from a different entry that used the same words.

The average number of recall calls was 1.9 for Claude and 2.6 for Codex. That seems fine.

I wrote down three candidate changes: say explicitly that plans are not results, tell the agent to read the file before answering numeric questions, and move the single-term rule up to the first line of the recall section. I did not change the rules today so that each change can be measured alone.

The variance of one run is unknown, so I also queued a second baseline run for tomorrow to see if the scores are stable. Transcripts are saved under evals/baseline for comparison.

I also fixed a bug in the scoring script: a marker found inside the question text echoed by the agent counted as a pass. It now strips the echoed question before matching, which changed one Codex result from pass to fail.

summary: Tried the first rules change from the eval, saying plans are not results, and it fixed both Claude failures on the not-recorded questions.
body:
I added two sentences to the recall section of the rules: an entry that describes a plan or an idea is not evidence that the work was done, and if only a plan is found, say so. Nothing else changed.

I ran the eval again on Claude Code. It now passes 12 of 12, where the baseline passed 10. Both former failures answered that the feature was planned but not built, quoting the entry.

Because one run is thin evidence, I ran it a second time and got 11 of 12. The miss was a count question where the agent reported 4 entries instead of 5. That is a different kind of failure and was not in the baseline, so it is probably noise, but I will keep watching it.

summary: Second rules change from the eval, a not-recorded wording for Codex, lifted Codex from 8 to 10 of 12 but broke one previously passing question
body:
Continued the recall rules eval with Codex, which had failed four questions in the baseline. The Claude fix of last night, saying plans are not results, was copied into the AGENTS.md block with no other change.

Codex went from 8 to 10 of 12. Both not-recorded questions that failed before now pass: the agent says nothing was recorded instead of describing the plan entry as if it were done.

But question 7, about the last sync change, started failing. The agent now answers that nothing was recorded, because the sync entry used the word 'planned' in its summary and the rule made it too cautious.

I read the transcript twice to be sure it was the rule and not noise. The answer text quoted the plans-are-not-results sentence back almost word for word, which is a good sign that the wording caused it.

I did not fix it yet. One run per question is thin, so I want three runs per question before changing any more wording. The scoring script already takes a --runs flag, but it only reports the mean, so I added a per-question pass count to its output.

Next is a rerun with three runs on both agents, then a decision on whether to add a sentence saying that an entry which describes finished work counts even if it mentions a plan.

summary: Looked at the eval's remaining failure after the second Codex rules change and found the broken question depended on a sentence the new wording had pushed out of view.
body:
The second rules change lifted Codex from 8 to 10 of 12, but question 4 started failing, and today I went looking for why. I reran question 4 five times on Codex and it failed four of them, always with the same shape of answer. Codex said the work was not recorded, although recall returned the right entry with a clear summary.

I compared the transcripts from the baseline run and from the new run. In the baseline, Codex read the recall output and quoted the summary. In the new run it read the same output and then ignored it. The new not-recorded sentence sat directly after the recall instruction, and it said to answer that nothing was recorded whenever the hits did not name the exact thing asked about.

Question 4 asks about the sync lock, and the matching entry says 'stop two syncs running at once' without using the word lock in its summary. Codex judged that as not naming the thing. So the wording was too strict about exact matches, and that is a rules problem, not a recall problem.

I tried three rewordings in a scratch copy of the rules. The first said to answer from the hits when the summary or the snippet is about the same topic. That fixed question 4 but brought back one of the old not-recorded failures. The second added that plans are not results, which was already in the rules from the first change, so it did nothing new.

The third wording separated two cases: a hit that is about the same work counts as an answer, and a hit that only shares a word does not. With it, question 4 passed in five of five runs and the not-recorded questions stayed at their level of 10 of 12 overall. I have not put it into the real rules file yet, because one more pass over all twelve questions on Claude Code is needed to be sure it does not move anything there.

Next step is that Claude run, then a Pi check, since the rules text length is limited there. I also want to add the sync lock phrasing to the fixture so the question does not depend on a lucky summary.

summary: Checked the rules text length against the Pi bootstrap limit and found the new sentence fits with 140 characters to spare
body:
The Pi extension injects the rules into its bootstrap, and I had set a soft length limit there earlier. The rules had grown with the two recent changes, so I checked.

The rules command output is now 3,860 characters, against a limit of 4,000. The extra sentence about finished work adds about 120, so the final size is 3,980 characters, just under it.

That is too tight to keep growing. I did not raise the limit. Instead I noted in the eval plan that any further rule change has to remove words as well as add them.

I also added a small Vitest case that fails if the rules output exceeds the limit, so the next change cannot go over without notice.

summary: Eval with the finished-work sentence fixed Codex question 7 and put both agents at 11 of 12 or better over three runs
body:
Reran the three-run eval with the extra sentence about finished work added to the rules.

Claude Code reached 36 of 36 passes. Codex reached 34 of 36, and question 7 now passes three of three. The two Codex misses were on question 3 and question 9, one each, neither repeated.

The sentence did what I wanted without hurting the not-recorded questions. Questions 5 and 8 still pass on all runs for both agents.

I am calling this wording good enough for now and committing it. The commit message lists the eval numbers before and after so I can find them later.

What remains is a Pi run, because Pi was not in the baseline. The harness for it is the one I built for the recall integration test, so it needs a small adapter.

summary: Added Pi to the eval runner and found Pi passes 9 of 12, failing mostly because its transcripts hide the recall output from the scorer
body:
Wrote the adapter that runs the twelve questions through Pi and feeds the answers to the scoring script. It reuses the harness from the recall integration test, with a scripted session per question.

First result was 9 of 12. Looking at the failures, three of them were not wrong answers. In those, the agent ran recall and answered correctly, but the scorer checks the final message for the entry summary text, and Pi had paraphrased it.

The other Claude and Codex runs quote the summary more often, probably because the rules say to cite the entry. Pi seems to weight the rule less, since the bootstrap sits in a different place in its prompt.

To separate the two causes I added a second check to the scorer: a question also passes if the transcript shows that recall returned the right entry file and the answer does not contradict it. With that check Pi scores 11 of 12.

I am keeping both scores in the report, strict and lenient, because they measure different things. Strict tells me how well the agent cites, lenient tells me whether it found the right entry.

The one real Pi failure is question 8, a not-recorded question, where Pi invented a plausible answer. I will look at that one separately.

I also reran Claude and Codex with the lenient scorer. Their numbers did not change, which fits with them quoting well.

Nothing was changed in the rules today. Next is the Pi question 8 transcript.

summary: Pi invented an answer on a not-recorded question because the recall output was empty and the rule for that case sat at the end of the rules
body:
Read the Pi transcript for question 8, which asks about a change that was never recorded. Recall returned no hits, and Pi then answered from a guess about how the sync command probably works.

The rules say to state that nothing was recorded when recall is empty, but that sentence is the last one in the text. Pi's bootstrap seems to get less attention at the end.

I moved the empty-recall sentence up next to the sentence that says recall is the first step. To stay under the length limit I cut two examples from the section about writing entries, which were repeated in the README anyway.

The rules are now 3,940 characters. Ran question 8 five times on Pi: it said nothing was recorded four times and guessed once.

That is better but not solid. I will run the whole set again tomorrow rather than draw conclusions from one question.

summary: Full Pi eval after moving the empty-recall sentence gives 11 of 12 strict, and Claude and Codex stay where they were
body:
Ran all twelve questions three times on each of the three agents after the rules reordering.

Pi scored 33 of 36 strict, up from 27, with question 8 now passing two of three. Claude held at 36 of 36 and Codex at 34 of 36.

The move did not cost anything on the other two agents. That was the risk, because the order changes what they see first.

I committed the reordered rules and wrote the three scores into the eval notes.

summary: Added the config command's get and set paths with a small awk rewrite of the key=value file, and tests that cover missing files, repeated keys and values containing equals signs.
body:
The config file is plain key=value lines in the journal's state folder, and I wanted set to change one line without touching the others. The awk script reads the file, replaces the first line whose key matches, and appends the key if none matched. It writes to a temporary file in the same folder and moves it over the original, so a crash cannot leave half a file.

Get prints only the value and exits 1 when the key is missing, so shell scripts can test it. Values may contain equals signs, so the parser splits at the first one only, the same mistake I fixed in recall last week for colons. Repeated keys are handled by taking the first occurrence on get and collapsing the rest on set.

I wrote Vitest cases for a missing file, an empty file, a repeated key, a value with an equals sign, and a key with regex characters in it. The last one failed first, because the key was used as a regex in awk, and I switched to a plain string comparison. All cases pass now. Next is list, which shows every key with its value, and the journal_dir and host keys.

summary: Started the config command: a get/set/list interface over a small key=value file, with the journal path and host name as the first keys
body:
Began the config command that the Claude Code plugin will need. Until now the journal path came only from an environment variable, which is awkward when a hook runs in a clean environment.

The design is a plain file at ~/.config/agent-journal/config with one key=value per line. The CLI reads it with awk, and the environment variable overrides it when set.

The subcommands are config get KEY, config set KEY VALUE and config list. The first keys are journal_dir and host_name, where host_name replaces what hostname returns in new entries.

config set rewrites the file through a temp file and mv, so a crash in the middle cannot leave a half-written file. It keeps unknown keys and comments untouched, which took a few lines of awk to get right.

I refused keys with spaces or an equals sign in them, with an error to stderr and exit status 2. Values may contain an equals sign, because the awk split is at the first one only, which is the same lesson as the colon bug in recall.

Added Vitest cases for get on a missing key, set on a new file, set over an existing key, comments kept and the environment override. All pass.

Still to do is the help text for config and the use of journal_dir in the install script.

summary: Wired the install script to write journal_dir through the config command and made it fall back to a default when the config command fails, with a test for a read-only home.
body:
The install script used to print an export line for the journal directory and ask the user to put it in a shell profile. That was easy to forget, so I changed it to call config set journal_dir with the chosen path. The CLI reads the value from config on every run, and an environment variable still wins when it is set, which keeps the tests simple.

The risky part was the failure case. If the config folder cannot be created, for example in a sandbox with a read-only home, the install used to abort with a vague error. Now it prints one line saying config could not be written, continues with the default folder, and exits with 0 so an agent plugin install does not break.

I also made the CLI itself tolerate a missing config file. Reading a key from a file that does not exist returns the default and writes nothing, so nothing is created as a side effect of a read. This matters for Codex, where the first run may happen in a sandbox.

The tests run the installer with a temporary HOME in three states: normal, no config folder yet, and a read-only home. All three pass, and the read-only case checks the printed warning text. I updated the install section of the README to drop the export instruction. What is left is the host key, which should be filled at install time from the machine name.

summary: The install script now writes journal_dir through config instead of exporting a variable, and falls back safely when config is missing
body:
Changed the install script so it calls agent-journal config set journal_dir with the chosen path, instead of telling the user to export a variable in the shell profile.

The old instructions are still printed when the shell has the variable set, because that value would win over the file and the user should know.

On a re-run the installer keeps an existing journal_dir unless a flag asks to replace it. I tested that by running it twice with different paths.

One problem came up: the installer runs before the CLI is on PATH on some systems. I made it call the CLI by its path inside the checkout, not by name.

The install test covers a clean home directory, a home with a config file and a home with the variable set. All three pass.

summary: Built the first Claude Code hook: a session-start hook that prints the rules and the latest five entries, with a timeout guard
body:
Started the Claude Code plugin with its first hook, which runs at session start and prints the rules plus the latest five entry summaries into the context.

The hook is a short sh script that calls agent-journal rules and then agent-journal list --limit 5. Output goes to stdout, which Claude Code adds to the session.

The first version hung when the journal folder was on a slow network mount. I wrapped the list call in a timeout guard of two seconds, using a background process and a kill, because the timeout command is not on every system.

When the guard fires, the hook prints only the rules and a line saying the journal could not be read in time. The session still starts, which matters more than the list.

I checked the hook in a live session. The rules showed up and the agent wrote an entry after a small change, with the right session id from the hook input.

The session id comes in as JSON on stdin. I parse it with awk instead of adding a dependency, picking the value after the session_id key with a regex that tolerates spaces.

I also tested a missing config, an empty journal and a journal with a broken entry whose front matter has no summary. The hook handled all of them without errors, and the broken entry was shown as 'no summary'.

Plugin manifest and hook registration are written, but the stop hook is not done. That is next.

summary: Built the Claude Code session-start hook that prints the rules and the latest five entries, and added a timeout guard so a slow disk cannot delay the start of a session.
body:
The hook is a short shell script that the plugin registers for session start. It calls the CLI rules command, then the list command with a limit of five, and prints both as one block that Claude Code adds to the context. I kept the output compact: the latest entries show as one line each with time, project and summary.

The first version hung once when the journal folder sat on a network mount that was asleep. I added a timeout guard around the list call, using a background process and a kill after three seconds, since the timeout command is not on every system. When the guard fires, the hook prints the rules alone and a line saying the latest entries were unavailable.

I checked the hook in a live session in this checkout. The rules showed up at the start, and the agent mentioned the latest entry when I asked what happened last. A test now runs the hook script with a fake CLI that sleeps and confirms the output arrives within about four seconds. Next is the stop hook.

summary: Added the stop hook that reminds the agent to write an entry when work happened without one, and tuned it to avoid nagging
body:
Built the stop hook for Claude Code. It runs when the agent finishes a turn and checks whether files in the working tree changed since the last entry in this session.

If they did and no entry was written, the hook prints a short reminder. The first version fired after every turn, including pure question turns, and that was annoying in testing.

To find out whether work happened, the hook runs git status --porcelain and compares a hash of its output with one stored in a temp file for the session. If the hash is the same, nothing changed, so no reminder.

Outside a git repository the hook cannot check, so it stays silent. I thought about falling back to file times, but that would give false reminders in folders with build output.

The second problem was loops. A reminder makes the agent write an entry, which changes the journal repo if the journal sits inside the working tree. I made the hash ignore the journal directory.

I also added a limit of one reminder per ten minutes per session, kept in the same temp file.

Tests in Vitest run the hook script with a fake git repo: clean tree, changed tree, changed tree after a reminder, and a journal-only change. All four give the expected output.

A live test in Claude Code worked: after a small edit the agent got the reminder once and wrote an entry. A follow-up question about the code got no reminder.

Open question is whether to block the stop instead of just reminding. I decided not to, because blocking would trap sessions on quick questions.

Next I want to write the README section for the hooks.

summary: Wrote the README section for the Claude Code plugin and hooks, with an install block and a table of what each hook does
body:
Added a README section for the Claude Code plugin after the Codex and Pi sections, to keep the three in the same order and style.

It has the install command, a table with the two hooks and when they run, and the config keys they read.

I also wrote the known limits: the hooks need a POSIX sh, the stop hook only works inside git repositories, and the timeout guard is two seconds.

The feature list at the top of the README now mentions all three agents in the same sentence.

I checked every command in the section by running it in a clean shell. One example used an old flag name, which I fixed.

The README test that compares the generated examples with real output still passes. The new section has no generated block, so it is not covered, and I noted that as a gap.

I also fixed the badge row, where the CI badge pointed at a workflow file name I had renamed last week. It showed 'no status' until I corrected the path.

The install section got a sentence on how to uninstall each plugin, which was missing.

summary: Wrote the sync command's first version: init, push and status against a git remote, with a lock to stop two syncs running at once
body:
Started the sync command, which pushes the journal folder to a git remote so entries survive a lost laptop.

Three subcommands for now: sync init URL, sync push and sync status. init turns the journal folder into a git repository if it is not one yet and adds the remote called origin.

push stages all entry files, commits with a message that names the host and the number of new entries, and pushes. If there is nothing new, it prints that and exits with status 0.

I added a lock using mkdir on a lock folder inside .git, since mkdir is atomic in POSIX sh. A stale lock older than ten minutes is removed with a warning.

The first test run showed that commit failed in a clean CI environment because no git user was set. I set a local user.name and user.email in the journal repo at init time, using the host name from config.

status prints the number of entries not yet pushed, the last push time, and whether the remote can be reached. For reachability I use git ls-remote with a five-second guard, similar to the hook timeout.

The tests use a bare repository in a temp folder as the remote. They cover init, a first push, a push with nothing new, a locked push and a stale lock.

A question I left open is conflicts. With one machine they cannot happen, but with two they will, and the entry file names include the session, which makes name clashes unlikely but not impossible.

The pull side is not written. That is the next step, along with the rebase behavior.

I also let sync read its remote URL from the config file, as a sync_remote key, so a hook could call push later without arguments.

The help text and the README are not updated yet.

summary: Added sync pull with a rebase so a second machine can fetch entries, and tested it with two clones of a bare remote
body:
Wrote sync pull, which runs git pull --rebase and then reports how many entries arrived.

Push now does a pull first, so that a second machine pushing after the first does not get rejected as non-fast-forward.

The test creates two clones of the same bare remote, pushes from one, then pushes from the other, and checks that both sets of entries end up on both sides.

A conflict stops the rebase, and the command prints how to resolve it and exits with status 3. I tested that by editing the same file in both clones.

Help text for sync is still pending.

summary: Added a sync hook to the Claude Code plugin that pushes in the background at session end and never blocks the exit
body:
Wired sync into the Claude Code plugin with a session-end hook that runs sync push in the background.

The hook starts the push with nohup and redirects output to a log file in the config folder, then returns at once. The session can end without waiting for the network.

It only runs when sync_remote is set in config, so people who do not use sync are not affected.

The first live test failed quietly: the push ran, but the lock folder from the previous test was still there and was less than ten minutes old, so the push was skipped. I cleared it and the next run worked.

That made me change the log to include a line for a skipped push with the reason, so I would have seen it directly.

I also checked that the hook does nothing when offline. The push fails after the five-second guard and writes one line to the log.

A test runs the hook with a fake remote and checks that it returns in under a second while the push is still going.

The log has no rotation yet. At one line per session this will take a long time to matter, but I noted it.

Next is documenting sync in the help text and the README.

summary: Added a sync hook to the Claude Code plugin that pushes in the background at session end, using a detached process so the exit is never delayed, and tested it against a slow remote.
body:
The sync command already worked by hand, and the next step was to run it without anybody remembering. I added a session-end hook to the Claude Code plugin that starts a push and returns right away. The push runs detached with its output sent to a log file in the state folder, so Claude Code does not wait for the network.

The hook first checks whether sync was ever set up. If no remote is configured it does nothing and prints nothing, so people who never use sync see no change. It also relies on the lock from the first version of sync, so two sessions ending together cannot run two pushes at once; the second one exits quietly when it sees the lock.

I tested with a bare remote whose pre-receive hook sleeps for ten seconds. The session-end hook returned in under 100 milliseconds, and the push finished later in the background. The log showed one clean push and, for a second session that ended during it, a single line saying a sync was already running.

One problem showed up: a failed push left no trace unless one looked into the log. I made the hook write a short status file with the time and the result, and sync status now reads it. A Vitest case covers the no-remote path, the lock path and the failure path. Next is the README section for sync.

summary: Added a README section for sync with a setup walkthrough and a warning that the journal remote should be private
body:
Wrote the README section on sync, with a three-step setup: create a private remote, run sync init with its URL, and run sync push.

The warning is in bold at the start of the section. Entries can contain paths, host names and bits of code, so the remote should not be public.

I described the session-end hook and how to turn it off by removing the sync_remote key.

The conflict case has a short paragraph with the exit status 3 and the commands to resolve it.

As before, I ran each command in a clean shell. The init example used a URL form that git accepts but my status check did not handle, so I fixed the check to use ls-remote on whatever URL is configured.

The feature list at the top now has sync as its own bullet.

The README test still passes.

summary: Answered the user's question on why sync commits one file per entry instead of squashing, from the sync entries and the script
body:
The user asked why sync keeps one commit per push with all new entries, and whether squashing would make the remote smaller.

I read the sync entries from the last days and the push function before answering. The commit per push is by design: it names the host and the count, which gives a readable history without one commit per file.

Squashing would rewrite history, which breaks the pull side on a second machine, because rebase would then replay old commits that no longer exist on the remote.

Size is not an issue: entries are small text files, and the whole journal after a few months is well under a megabyte of packed objects.

I told the user that, and that if the remote ever grew large, a shallow clone on the second machine would help more than squashing.

No code was changed.

summary: Started the journal pane: a script that clears the screen and shows the latest entries, refreshing when the folder changes
body:
Began the journal pane that shows the latest entries in a terminal split next to the agent.

The first version is a sh loop that clears the screen, runs agent-journal list --limit 10 and sleeps. To avoid flicker it only redraws when the output hash changes.

Change detection uses the newest file's modification time in the journal folder, checked every second. That is cheap and does not need fswatch.

Long summaries are cut to the terminal width, read from tput cols at every redraw so a resized pane still looks right.

I hit a bug on macOS: stat flags differ between BSD and GNU, so the mtime check failed on one of them. I used ls -t and took the first name, which is portable, instead of stat.

A SIGINT trap restores the cursor, which I had hidden during drawing. Without the trap, Ctrl-C left the terminal without a cursor.

The pane works for me in tmux. I have not tested it with the agents' own split views.

The command is agent-journal pane for now, with no options. Colors and a title line are next.

summary: Gave the journal pane a title line and dim colors for the time column, with a NO_COLOR switch
body:
Added a title line to the pane showing the journal folder and the number of entries.

The time column is dim and the project name is bold when stdout is a terminal.

NO_COLOR set in the environment turns all color off, and so does a non-terminal output, which keeps the pane testable.

I wrote a test that runs the pane once with a --once flag, which I added for this purpose, and compares the output with a fixture. The flag also helps with debugging.

Columns are aligned with awk printf and a fixed width for the time. The project column uses the longest name in view.

A wide character in a summary broke alignment by one column in one case, and I left it, since it only affects the cut position.

summary: Fixed the pane showing stale entries after a sync pull, because pulled files kept an old modification time
body:
A pull brought in entries from the other machine, but the pane did not redraw and showed the old list.

Cause: change detection uses the newest file by modification time, and git sets the time of a pulled file to the moment of checkout in most cases, but one of my test files kept the time from the clone step, which was older than the newest local entry.

I changed the check to also include the number of files in the folder. Any new file changes the count and forces a redraw.

The hash of the output remains the final gate, so redraws still do not flicker when nothing visible changed.

I reproduced it with two clones, pulled in one and watched the pane. After the fix it refreshed within a second.

A test with the --once flag covers the count, using a folder where I add a file with an old time using touch -t.

The pane also sorts by the date in the front matter, not by file time, so the order on screen was right all along; only the redraw trigger was wrong.

summary: Added time zone handling to list with a --utc flag and a tz config key, converting stored timestamps with portable awk and date
body:
Entries store the timestamp with an offset, but list printed them as written, so entries from another machine in another zone looked out of order.

I added a --utc flag that converts every timestamp to UTC, and a tz config key that sets a zone name used for display when the flag is absent.

The conversion uses date with TZ set in the environment, which works on both GNU and BSD date, and reads the epoch value computed by the same function that recall uses for --since.

The sort already used the epoch value, so order is correct. Only the display changed.

Tests cover an entry with a positive offset, one with a negative offset, one at the date boundary after conversion and an invalid tz value, which prints an error and falls back to UTC.

The help text and README mention the flag and the key. The README example block is generated from a fixture run, so I regenerated it, and the test comparing the two passes.

summary: Added a --utc flag test matrix for list covering midnight boundaries, and found one entry shown under the wrong day when the tz key was set to a negative offset.
body:
Wrote a table-driven Vitest file for the time zone handling from earlier today. It runs list with tz set to UTC, a positive offset and a negative offset, against fixtures with timestamps at 23:30 and 00:30.

The negative offset case failed. An entry stored at 00:30 UTC showed under the previous day, which is correct, but the day header grouping still used the stored date, so the header and the time disagreed.

The cause was in the awk that groups by day: it read the date from the front matter instead of from the converted timestamp. I changed it to derive the header from the converted value. All nine cases pass now. Still open: the half-hour offsets, which the fixtures do not cover yet.

summary: Added half-hour and 45-minute offsets to the list time zone tests and fixed a rounding slip in the awk offset parser that shifted Kathmandu-style zones by 15 minutes.
body:
Followed up on the open item from this morning and added fixtures for +05:30 and +05:45. The +05:45 case failed by 15 minutes.

The parser split the offset string and divided the minutes by 60 with integer arithmetic, which truncated 45 to 0.75 and then to 0 in one branch. I rewrote it to compute total minutes first and only then convert to seconds for date.

After the change all eleven time zone cases pass on both the macOS and the Linux runner image I tested locally with date flags checked for each. The help text for --utc still says nothing about offsets, so I noted that as a small follow-up.

summary: Started the recall command's period reading by adding --since and --until parsing, with relative words like yesterday, and found that BSD and GNU date disagree on the syntax.
body:
The plan is for the user to ask for work from a period, so list needs a way to cut by time. I began with --since and --until in the shared awk library.

Absolute dates were easy, but relative words such as yesterday and last week turned out to depend on date. GNU date takes -d yesterday, BSD date wants -v-1d. I wrote a small function that tests which one exists once and caches the answer in a variable.

The function now handles yesterday, today, N days ago and N weeks ago. Months are left out on purpose because their length makes the result vague.

Tests cover the four forms on both date flavors by stubbing date with a script in the test PATH. One stub case was wrong at first, because it did not mimic the BSD error on an unknown flag, which hid a real bug in the detection. I fixed the stub and the detection together.

Next step is to apply the cut to the file list before awk parses the entries, so large journals stay fast. I did not measure that yet. The help text has not been updated either.

summary: Made the period filter select files by name before parsing, measured it on a 5,000-entry journal, and cut list time from 2.1 seconds to 0.3 seconds for a one-week window.
body:
Entry file names start with a timestamp, so the period cut can be done by comparing names and never opening files outside the window. I implemented that in the list path today.

Before the change I generated a synthetic journal of 5,000 entries with a small script in test/tools. list --since with a one-week window took 2.1 seconds, because every file was read by awk. After the change it took 0.3 seconds.

The filename comparison is a plain string comparison in sh, using a case pattern on the prefix. That is portable and avoids spawning a process per file. I first tried a loop with expr, which was slower than reading the files, so I dropped it.

One problem came out of the time zone work: file names carry UTC, while the user thinks in local time. A window that starts at local midnight must be converted to UTC before comparing. I reused the offset code from the list tz handling for that.

The edge case is a file whose name was written with a different clock, for example after a sync from another machine with a wrong time. These files would be missed or included wrongly. I decided to accept this and document that the name is the truth.

Tests added: window inside one day, window across midnight with a negative offset, empty window, and since later than until, which now prints a clear error and exits with 2.

The synthetic journal generator is kept as test/tools/make-journal.sh with a size argument. The performance test is not part of the normal suite, since it is slow, and runs with an env switch.

Remaining work: term search, which comes next, and the help text for the period flags.

summary: Wrote the help text and README lines for the new --since and --until flags, and fixed the usage line of list that still listed a flag removed last week.
body:
With the period filter in place I updated the help output. The list and recall usage now show --since and --until with examples using yesterday and 2 weeks ago.

While reading the help I found the usage line of list still mentioned --local, a flag removed when the tz key arrived. I removed it and added a test that compares each flag in the help to the flags the parser accepts, so this drift gets caught.

The README got a short section under usage with three example commands. I kept it to the commands and one sentence each, since the longer rewrite is planned for later.

The help test failed once because the example used a tab. I replaced it with spaces. All tests pass.

summary: Built the first version of term search for recall: AND matching over summary and body, case-insensitive, ranked by number of hits, with newest first on ties.
body:
Started the search part of recall. Terms given on the command line must all appear in an entry, in the summary or the body, ignoring case.

The awk script reads each entry in two parts, front matter and body, and counts hits per term. An entry that misses any term is dropped. The score is the sum of hits, with summary hits counting three times as much as body hits.

Ties are broken by timestamp, newest first. I remember the earlier question about the sort key using local time, so this sort uses the UTC name prefix.

Quoted phrases work by joining the arguments with a single space and matching it as one term. Terms with regex characters such as a dot or a bracket are matched literally. I used index() in awk instead of match() for that reason.

I tested with the fixture journal: single term, two terms, a phrase, a term with a dot, no match and empty term list. The empty list prints the usage and exits with 2.

One surprise: tolower() on non-ASCII text differs between awk implementations. mawk on the Linux runner left accented capitals alone, while macOS awk changed them. I did not fix it, and wrote a note in the test file that case folding is ASCII only.

Output is the same format as list, with the score in --json. Next I want to limit output with --limit and show a snippet.

summary: Added --limit and a context snippet to recall results, then found the snippet cut multi-byte characters in half on macOS awk and switched to cutting at word boundaries.
body:
Recall prints only the summary line now, which is not always enough to tell why an entry matched. I added a snippet of about 120 characters around the first body hit.

The first version used substr with byte offsets. On macOS awk this worked for ASCII, but a fixture entry with an en dash was cut in the middle of the character and printed a broken byte. The terminal showed a question mark.

I changed it to cut at the nearest space before and after the hit, so the snippet always starts and ends on a whole word. That avoids the splitting for any awk, since spaces are single bytes in UTF-8.

The snippet marks the match with nothing special in plain output, and with bold in a terminal unless NO_COLOR is set. In --json it is a separate field named snippet.

--limit N defaults to 10. I put the limit after ranking, not before, which was wrong in my first try: the limit was applied while reading, so the first N files that matched were kept, not the best N. A test with 15 matching fixtures and a better score in the last file caught it.

I also made the summary hit case show no snippet, since the summary is already printed.

Tests added: snippet near the start, near the end, a multi-byte fixture, limit 1, limit 0 which prints an error, and the JSON field. Total tests are now 94, all passing.

A remaining idea is stemming, so that fix and fixed match. I decided against it for now, since it adds language rules to a POSIX shell tool.

summary: Checked how recall behaves when the journal folder is empty or missing and made both print a clear not-recorded message with exit code 1 rather than an awk error.
body:
The eval work showed that agents handle empty recall output badly, so the CLI should say so itself. I tried recall with an empty folder and with a missing one.

The empty folder printed nothing and exited 0. The missing folder printed an awk error about a file that does not exist, which an agent might read as a result.

Now both cases print a line such as No entries match, and a missing folder prints the path that was checked. Exit code is 1 for no match so scripts can tell, and 2 for a missing folder.

I also made a search without hits print the terms that were used, so the agent can see what was searched.

Three tests were added, one for each case. The rules text mentions the empty case already, and I did not change it. I will run the eval again once the whole recall command is done.

summary: Combined term search with the period filter in recall and fixed a bug where --since silently dropped the search terms when given before them.
body:
Recall should accept both a period and terms in one call, for example recall --since 2 weeks ago sync. Until now the two parts were tested separately.

The first combined run returned entries from the period with no term filter. The argument parser took everything after --since as the value, so 2 weeks ago consumed the word sync as well, and the term list was empty.

I changed the period value to be a single argument, so it must be quoted when it has spaces, or written with a dash such as 2-weeks-ago. I also accepted the form --since=2weeks. The help text shows the quoted form.

This is a trade-off. Parsing a free-form number of words is fragile, and agents quote arguments well anyway. The error message now says when a value looks like it swallowed a term.

The order of options no longer matters. I rewrote the parser loop as a case statement that collects terms into a list separated by a newline character, and all options set variables.

I added tests for both orders, for the equals form, and for a value that is not a period, which gives exit 2 and a clear message.

I measured the combination on the 5,000-entry journal: 0.4 seconds with a one-week window and two terms. A search over the whole journal without a period took 2.6 seconds, which is acceptable for now.

Next: reading a full entry by name, so the agent can open a hit.

summary: Added recall --show to print one full entry by file name or unique prefix, with an error listing candidates when the prefix is ambiguous.
body:
After a search, the agent needs the whole body of a hit. I added --show, which takes the file name or a prefix of it.

The lookup uses a glob in sh and counts matches. One match prints the file without the front matter by default, and with --raw it prints everything. No match gives exit 1.

An ambiguous prefix lists up to five candidate names and exits with 2. Without this, the first try printed whichever file sorted first, and that was wrong in a test with two entries made in the same minute.

I kept the prefix check from matching in the middle of a name, so it cannot select another folder through a path. A name with a slash is rejected, and a test covers a dot-dot path.

The tests cover exact name, short prefix, ambiguity, missing, raw and the slash case. All pass.

The output of --show starts with the summary as a line, so the agent sees the key point first.

summary: Wired recall into the Claude Code plugin rules with the exact commands for terms, period and show, and checked the rules fit the length budget with 90 characters to spare.
body:
The recall command is complete enough to be taught to the agent. I wrote the commands into the rules that the session-start hook prints.

The text shows three patterns: search by terms, read by period, and open one entry with --show. Each has one example line. I kept the explanation short because the rules are read on every session start.

The length budget matters for Pi, whose bootstrap limit I checked in the eval work. The new text leaves 90 characters free, less than the 140 before, so I will not add more without cutting something.

I also kept the sentence that says plans are not results, and put the recall commands before it so it does not move to the end, where the eval showed it was weaker.

The hook was run in a scratch session and printed the rules and the five latest entries in 0.2 seconds. The test that checks the rules length passes.

I noted for later that Codex and Pi get the same text from a shared file, so one edit covers all three agents. Their plugins are not built yet, so I only changed the file and the Claude hook test.

Next step is the same check from the user's side: ask a question about past work in a real session and read the transcript.

summary: Ran a real Claude Code session asking what changed in sync last week and found the agent used recall --since correctly but did not open any entry with --show.
body:
I tested the new rules in a normal session. The question was: what did we change in sync last week.

The agent ran recall with --since 1 week ago and the term sync. The command worked and listed six entries. It then answered from the summaries alone.

The answer was right but shallow. It missed that the lock was added in the first version, which only appears in the body. It did not use --show.

I think the cause is the rules: they say that --show exists but not when to use it. I added one sentence, saying that summaries can be incomplete and that details need the full entry.

I repeated the session. The agent opened two entries and the answer included the lock. This is one try, not a measurement, so I added the question to the eval list as number 13 with the lock as the known answer.

The length budget is now 31 characters free for Pi. That is tight, so the next wording change will need a cut elsewhere.

summary: Shortened the rules text by 120 characters without losing eval results, after the extra --show sentence left Pi with only 31 characters free.
body:
The added sentence about opening entries used most of the room under the Pi bootstrap limit. I wanted a margin back before more changes.

I looked for the longest sentences in the rules. Two of them said the same thing about not inventing answers when recall is empty, one in the intro and one near the end. I merged them into one sentence, kept it in the early position and removed the later copy.

I also cut the example for period reading from two lines to one, and replaced three words in the install note. The total saving was 120 characters, so the margin is 151 now.

Then I ran the eval on all three agents with the 13 questions, three runs each. Results over three runs: Claude 13 of 13 on two runs and 12 on one, Codex 12 of 13 on all three, Pi 12 of 13 on two runs and 11 on one.

The Codex miss was question 13, the lock question, where it read summaries only. Claude and Pi use --show more often. The wording says details need the full entry, but Codex seems to treat the summary as enough when it looks complete.

I do not want to add a sentence for one agent while the margin is this thin. A different fix would be for recall to print the first body line under each hit, so a summary-only answer has more to work with. I will think about that.

I saved the three run transcripts in the eval folder. The earlier results for the 12 questions are unchanged, so the cut did not hurt them.

Next: decide between the body line in recall output and a stronger rule, then repeat the Codex runs.

summary: Tried printing the first body line under each recall hit, and Codex then passed question 13 on all three runs without any change to the rules.
body:
I chose the output change over a new rules sentence, because it costs no characters in the bootstrap text.

Recall now prints the first non-empty body line under each hit, indented by two spaces and cut at 160 characters at a word boundary. In --json it is a field named lead.

The snippet still appears when the hit is deeper in the body, so one hit can have a lead and a snippet. That looked noisy at first, so I print the snippet only when it differs from the lead.

Three Codex runs on the 13 questions gave 13 of 13 each time. Claude stayed at 13 and 12, and Pi at 12 and 12 and 12.

Tests were updated for the new output format, 11 of them, mostly through the fixture helper. Two needed hand edits.

summary: Looked at why Pi still misses one question and found it is question 9, whose answer is in an entry that recall ranks eleventh, just beyond the default limit of ten.
body:
Pi keeps failing the same question in the eval, question 9, about the choice of the date tiebreaker. I read the transcripts to see why.

Pi ran recall with the right terms. The matching entry exists but the hit count is low, because the entry says tiebreaker once. Ten other entries match the term sort more often, so it ranked eleventh and was cut by the default --limit 10.

An agent cannot know there is more. I made recall print a line at the end when results were cut: 3 more matches, use --limit to see them.

Pi then ran again with a larger limit and answered correctly in one of two tries. The other time it did not follow the line.

The rules do not mention the line, but the line is self explanatory. I will check it again in the next eval round.

summary: Started the Codex plugin by reading how Codex loads instructions and hooks, and wrote a first install path that places the rules in the Codex instructions file.
body:
I began the Codex plugin today with reading. Codex takes instructions from an AGENTS file in the home config folder, and has no session-start hook like Claude Code does.

That changes the design. The Claude hook prints the latest entries at start, but with Codex the rules must tell the agent to run list itself at the start of a session. I wrote that as a short rule: at the start of work, run agent-journal list --limit 5.

The install script gets a new step for Codex. It looks for the Codex config folder, and if it is there, it adds a block between two marker comments in the instructions file. The markers let a second install replace the block rather than append another.

I tested the replace logic with three cases: no file, a file without the block, and a file with an old block and text on both sides. The third case had a bug, where the end marker was matched lazily and removed a line after it. I changed the awk to track state with a flag.

Uninstall removes the block in the same way, and leaves the rest of the file intact. A test checks that the file is byte-identical to the original after install and uninstall.

The rules block is generated from the same shared file as the Claude one, with one added line for the start of session. The length check includes this line.

I could not yet test the end-of-work reminder. Codex has a notify setting that runs a program when a turn ends, and I plan to look at it next.

I also noted a risk: if the user already has long Codex instructions, our block adds to the load. The block is about 1,900 characters now. I will keep it that way and mention it in the README later.

summary: Used the Codex notify setting to build a reminder that fires when a turn ends without a journal entry, after finding that notify gets its payload as a JSON argument and not on stdin.
body:
Codex can run a program at the end of each turn. I wanted the same reminder as the Claude stop hook: if work happened and no entry was written, say so.

I first assumed the payload came on stdin, as with Claude hooks. The script waited on read and hung. After checking the Codex docs and a trace, I saw the payload is passed as the last command-line argument, as a JSON string.

Parsing JSON in POSIX sh is awkward. I only need two fields, the type and the cwd, so I used a small awk that finds the keys with a pattern. It is not a general parser, and I put a comment on the limits.

The logic is this: on agent-turn-complete, look at the files changed in the cwd since the session start, and at the newest entry time. If files changed and no entry is newer than the start, print the reminder.

Here Codex differs from Claude. Notify output is not shown to the agent, only run as a side effect. So the reminder cannot reach the agent directly.

My workaround is to write a small marker file in a state folder. The rules tell the agent to check for the marker with agent-journal status at the start of each turn, and to write the entry if the marker is there. That costs one more rule line.

I added a status subcommand that prints pending when the marker exists, and clears it when an entry is written. Entry writing was already a file creation, so I added the clearing to the same function.

The tests cover the argument payload with escaped quotes, a payload with no cwd, a turn with no changes, a turn with changes and no entry, and a turn with changes and an entry. All five pass, with the first version failing the escaped quotes case.

I then ran a real Codex session. The agent edited a file, the notify ran, and at the next turn it ran status, saw pending and wrote the entry. That worked on the first real try.

One doubt remains: the agent may skip the status check when the user's next message is long. I will watch it in the eval.

The rules margin for Pi does not matter here, since this line goes only to Codex. The shared file now has a section marker for agent-specific lines.

summary: Added the Codex plugin to the eval runner and got 12 of 13 on three runs, with the one miss caused by the agent not running list at session start.
body:
The eval runner knew Claude Code, Codex by plain prompt, and Pi. I changed the Codex path to use the installed plugin, so the rules block and the notify setup are the real ones.

The runner makes a temporary home folder, runs the install script with it, and then starts Codex with the question. This also tests the install on a clean home, which found a small bug: the script assumed the Codex config folder existed, and failed under set -e when it did not. It now creates the folder only if the user passed a flag, and skips otherwise with a message.

Three runs of 13 questions gave 12, 12 and 12. The miss was always question 4, about what was done at the start of the journal pane.

In the transcripts, the agent did not run list at the start of the session, and the question was answered through recall alone. Recall found the entries, but a ranking issue pushed the pane entry down, since the question used the word screen and the entries use pane.

That is a vocabulary gap, not a Codex issue. Claude passes it only because the session-start hook prints recent entries that include a pane entry. Over three runs, it does not use recall for that question at all.

I considered synonyms in recall, and decided against it. A fixed synonym list will always be incomplete and hides how ranking works. The agent can try again with other words, and the rules could say so.

So I added a sentence to the rules: if a search finds nothing useful, retry with other words before saying it is not recorded. The margin for Pi is 118 characters after this.

I ran the three runs again. Codex gave 13, 12 and 13. The remaining miss was the agent stopping after one search again.

The eval results are saved in the eval folder with the plugin version in the file name. I plan to keep one run per change from now on, to see which sentence did what.

Next is the Pi extension, which has its own way of loading rules, and I expect more work there than for Codex.

summary: Began the Pi extension and found Pi loads TypeScript extensions that register hooks as functions, so the session-start behavior is written in a small TS file that calls the shell CLI.
body:
Pi takes extensions as TypeScript modules, not as config files or shell scripts. That is different from the other two agents, and I wanted to keep the logic in the shell CLI.

The extension is a thin file of about 60 lines. It exports a function that registers a handler for session start and one for session end. Both handlers run the CLI with child_process and return the output.

At session start, the handler runs agent-journal list --limit 5 and puts the result plus the rules into the system prompt addition. At session end, it runs the sync push in a detached process, so the exit is not delayed.

I built it in the plugins/pi folder with its own package file. It has no dependencies, since child_process comes from Node. oxlint and oxfmt run on it with the repo config, and oxlint complained about an unused parameter, which I prefixed with an underscore.

The rules text is read from the shared file at build time. I wrote a tiny script that copies it into the extension folder, so the extension works without access to the repo after install. The copy is checked by a test that compares both files.

The install script gets a Pi step. It copies the extension folder to the Pi extensions directory and does nothing if Pi is not installed. A second install replaces the folder, so old files do not stay behind.

I tested the handlers with Vitest by importing the module and calling them with a fake context. The CLI path is passed through an env variable in the test, pointing at a stub script that prints a fixed text. Four tests pass: start output, start with a failing CLI, end handler spawns, and end handler does not wait.

The failing CLI case matters. If agent-journal is missing from the PATH, the handler returns an empty addition and logs one line, and the session starts as usual. I do not want a journal problem to block work.

I have not run it in real Pi yet. I read the Pi docs about the handler return values, and one point is not clear: whether the returned text is appended to the system prompt or replaces a part. I will test it tomorrow.

There is also the eval point from before. Pi hides tool output from the transcript, which made the scorer fail. The extension runs list itself, so that output now reaches the model as part of the prompt, and this should help the scorer too.

summary: Ran the Pi extension in a real session, found the returned text replaces the system prompt addition of other extensions, and changed it to append through the documented context field.
body:
I tested the Pi extension in a real session today. The first result looked fine: the agent knew the rules and the latest entries.

Then I turned on a second extension that adds its own text, and the agent no longer knew the journal rules. The return value of our handler was set as the whole addition, and the order of loading decided which extension won.

The Pi docs describe a context field, where each extension adds a block and Pi joins them. I had missed it, since the examples use the older return value. I changed the handler to push a block named agent-journal into the context.

With both extensions on, the agent saw both blocks. I checked it by asking it to repeat the rules it was given.

The tests changed too. The fake context now has a blocks array, and the assertions check that exactly one block with the right name was added, and that nothing else in the array was touched. Four tests pass again.

I found one more thing in the same run. The session end handler ran the sync push, but the detached process kept the Pi terminal open for two seconds on a slow remote. The spawn used stdio inherit. I set stdio to ignore and called unref on the child, and the exit became instant. I tested it with a remote that sleeps ten seconds.

The Pi eval runner now uses the real extension in a temporary home, like Codex. First run: 12 of 13, and the miss was question 9 again, the date tiebreaker one. The cut line from the earlier change did not help this time. The agent saw it and still answered from the hits it had.

I looked at the question text. It asks why the date was chosen as the tiebreaker, and the answer is in the body of one entry. The search terms the agent chose were date and tiebreaker, and the entry ranked fourth, so it was in the output. The agent read the summaries and picked a wrong one.

The summary of the right entry says the tiebreaker was correct but the sort key used local time. The agent may have read that as the answer to a different question. That is not a tool problem, and I will not change the rules for it. I marked the question as a known flaky one for Pi.

Next I want to write the README section for the Codex and Pi plugins, since both are installed by the same script now.

summary: Wrote the README sections for the Codex plugin and the Pi extension, with the notify limitation and the status check explained in two sentences each.
body:
The README had a section for Claude Code only. I added two more under it, one for Codex and one for Pi.

The Codex section says what the install changes: a marked block in the instructions file, and the notify setting. It explains that notify cannot show text to the agent, so the reminder works through the status check. I kept this to two sentences, since the reader mostly wants to know what files are touched.

The Pi section says the extension is a small TypeScript file that calls the CLI, and that it adds a block to the context, so other extensions keep working.

I wrote a table at the top of the plugin part that compares the three agents: what runs at session start, what reminds the agent, and what runs at session end. It has three rows and three columns.

I also fixed the install block, which still said the script supports Claude Code only. The command is the same for all three, and it skips agents that are not installed.

The README is getting long, around 260 lines. I added a short list of contents at the top. A larger rewrite is on the plan for later, with better pictures.

summary: Found that the install script printed success for Pi even when the extensions folder was not writable, and made it report the failure and exit with 1.
body:
While writing the README I ran the install script on a copy of my home with read-only permissions on the Pi folder. It printed Installed Pi extension and exited 0.

The copy command failed, but its status was lost because it ran inside an if with a pipe to a log function. The pipe returns the status of the last command only.

I removed the pipe and checked cp directly. On failure, the script prints which path failed and continues with the other agents, but at the end it exits with 1 and lists the steps that failed.

I added a test with a read-only folder, which runs as the normal user. The same test for Codex passes without changes, since that step already checked the status.

Summary lines are now printed per agent: installed, skipped or failed.

summary: Reviewed the README install section against the real script and fixed three wrong statements: the default folder, the config key name and the flag for skipping Pi.
body:
After the install bug I read the README install part line by line and ran each statement against the script.

Three were wrong. The default journal folder was written with an old name from the first version. The config key was named journal_path in the text, while the code uses journal_dir. The flag to skip Pi was written as --no-pi, but the script knows --skip pi.

I corrected all three. I also added the exit code behavior from this evening, one sentence.

To avoid this drift, I wrote a small test that extracts the code blocks of the install section and checks that each flag and key it names exists in the script or in the config defaults. It is crude, using grep, but it caught all three errors when run on the old text.

The test is in the normal suite and runs in under a second.

summary: Added a recall eval for the Codex status check, found the agent skipped it on 4 of 10 long prompts, and fixed it by moving the check into the first rule line.
body:
I worried that the Codex agent would skip the status check on long user messages. Tonight I measured it.

The test makes ten prompts of different length, from one line to about 40 lines of pasted text. Each asks the agent to do a small edit in a scratch repo. After the edit, the pending marker is set by notify, and the next prompt is a short follow-up. The check is whether the agent runs agent-journal status and writes an entry.

For the five short prompts, the agent ran the check five times. For the five long ones, it ran the check once, so four skips in ten in total, all on long prompts.

In the rules the status line is the eleventh line. I think the long prompt pushes the rules far from the end of the context, and the model gives more weight to the text near the user message.

I moved the status check to the first line of the Codex block and made it a single imperative sentence: at the start of every turn, run agent-journal status and follow the result. The old explanatory text stayed below it.

I ran the same ten prompts again. The agent ran the check on nine of ten. The one skip was the longest prompt, with 40 lines.

I tried a second change, adding the word every in bold. Markdown bold made no difference in a second run: nine of ten again, with the same skip. I reverted that, since it changes nothing.

Another approach is to have notify write the reminder into a file that Codex reads as part of its instructions. That would make the reminder part of the prompt, rather than something the agent has to fetch. I did not try it, since the instructions file is the user's and changing it at runtime seems too intrusive.

So the current state is nine of ten. I decided that is enough for now, and that the reminder is a help, not a guarantee. The README says so in the Codex section: the reminder is best effort.

I added the ten prompts as a script in the eval folder, with a note about how to run it, since it uses real Codex calls and takes about 12 minutes.

The unit tests for the rules file now check that the status line is the first line of the Codex block. All tests pass.

For tomorrow: look at the Pi equivalent. Pi has no notify, but the session end handler can set the same marker, so the status approach may work there without new code.

summary: Made Pi use the same pending marker as Codex through its session end handler, and verified with the ten-prompt script that the agent wrote an entry on 8 of 10 follow-ups.
body:
Pi has no notify, but its extension can run code on each turn end. I used the turn-end event in the extension to run the same check as the Codex notify script: files changed since session start and no newer entry.

The check is a CLI subcommand now, agent-journal check-pending, which takes the cwd and the session start time. Codex notify and the Pi handler both call it, so the logic lives in one place. This also removed about 30 lines of duplicate shell from the Codex script.

For Pi the result does not need the status trick. The handler can add a block to the context for the next turn, so the reminder text reaches the model directly. I wrote it to add the block only when the check says pending, and to remove it after an entry was written.

I ran the ten-prompt script against Pi. It wrote an entry on 8 of 10 follow-ups, one skip on a short prompt and one on a long one. That is lower than I expected for a direct reminder, so I read the two failing transcripts.

In both, the agent saw the reminder and replied that it would write the entry after finishing the current request. The follow-up asked for another small edit, and the agent finished it and never came back to the entry. That looks like a reasonable reading of the text, so I changed the wording from you should write an entry to write the entry before anything else.

A second run of ten gave 10 of 10. I ran a third time to be sure and got 9 of 10, with one skip on a long prompt.

Unit tests: the Pi handler has three new tests for pending, not pending and cleared after writing. The shell side has tests for check-pending with changed files, with none, with a newer entry, and with a missing cwd. The missing cwd gives exit 2.

I also updated the README sections for Codex and Pi, since the notify script now calls the shared command. The Pi section mentions the reminder as a block in the context.

The next thing in the plan is the README rewrite, with a new top section and pictures of the CLI. I want to start with the text and decide later how to show the commands.
