summary: Added a Pi status check that reports whether the extension is loaded and the rules fit, after a silent failure left an agent without journal rules
body:
A user report last night described a Pi session that wrote no entries at all. The cause was an extension file that failed to compile after a Pi update, and Pi skipped it without a visible message. The agent then ran with no journal rules.

I added a status subcommand to the Pi side, run as agent-journal status --agent pi. It checks that the extension file exists in the extensions folder, that it is readable, and that the rules text inside it matches the current rules in the CLI.

The third check was the interesting one. The extension embeds a copy of the rules at install time, so after a CLI upgrade the copy can go stale. I compare a checksum of both texts using cksum, which exists on both macOS and Linux.

Output is one line per check, with ok or FAIL at the start. The exit code is 1 if any check fails. I kept the format the same as the Codex status check so the rules can describe both with one sentence.

I also tried to detect the compile failure itself. Pi has no dry-run command for extensions, so I could not do it cleanly. Instead the status command prints the path of the extension and tells the user to start Pi once and look at its startup output.

Tests were added in the Vitest suite for the three cases: missing file, unreadable file, and stale rules. The stale case writes an old rules text into a temp extensions folder and expects exactly one FAIL line.

The suite now passes with 3 new tests. What is left is to mention the check in the Pi README section, which I will do together with the next README pass.

summary: Fixed list printing entries from the wrong host when two machines shared a synced journal and their clocks differed by a few seconds
body:
While testing sync between my laptop and the desktop, I saw list show two entries in the wrong order. Both were written within the same minute, but the desktop clock ran about 40 seconds behind.

The list command sorted by the timestamp in the file name only. When two names had the same minute prefix, the order fell back to the host part of the name, which has nothing to do with time.

I changed the sort to use the full timestamp including seconds from the front matter date field when the name prefixes match. That needs one extra awk read, but only for the tied files, so the speed measured on the 5,000-entry journal did not change. It was 0.3 seconds before and after.

I did not try to fix the clock skew. A journal cannot know which clock is right, and entries are only ever compared in their own written time.

A regression test creates two entries with the same minute and different seconds and different hosts, and checks the order. It failed before the change and passes now.

One more thing found: the date field is sometimes written with a trailing Z and sometimes with an offset, depending on the tz config key. The tie-break strips both before comparing. That matches the conversion code from the time zone work.

summary: Answered the user's question on why list output has no host column by reading the format entries and the list script
body:
The user asked why list does not show the host, since the journal is synced between two machines. I read the early entry-format entries and bin/agent-journal.

The host was put into the front matter on purpose, for filtering later, but list was kept to time and summary so lines fit in a narrow pane. The first version decided that the pane width matters more than the host.

I suggested a --host flag that filters, and a --long flag that adds the column, rather than showing it by default. The user liked the filter and said the long flag is not needed yet.

No code was changed. I noted the filter idea as a possible next step after the Pi README text.

summary: Added a --host filter to list and recall so entries from one machine can be selected, with the match done in the awk pass
body:
Following the question from three days ago, I built the host filter. Both list and recall now take --host NAME and show only entries whose front matter host equals NAME.

The match happens inside the existing awk program that reads the front matter, so there is no second pass. A file is skipped as soon as its host line is read and does not match. That keeps the speed on the large journal.

I first tried to filter by the host part of the file name. That broke for names where the host contains a dash, because the name uses dashes as separators. The front matter field is the only reliable source.

Host names are compared exactly, not as a pattern. A pattern would need escaping of dots, and I saw no use for it.

If the host matches nothing, the command prints the same not-recorded message as an empty journal and exits with 1. That is consistent with recall, which already does this.

I updated the usage lines in the help text for both commands. A check in the tests compares the help output against the flags that the parser accepts, which has caught stale usage before, so it would have caught a miss here.

New tests: one host with two entries, one with none, and the combination with --since. All pass.

The README flag list still needs the new flag. That goes into the README work later today.

summary: Reworked the README install section to lead with the one-line install and a short table of what each plugin adds
body:
The install section had grown into a long list of steps that mixed the install script with manual plugin setup. A new reader had to scroll through Pi details before finding out how to start.

I moved the one-line install to the top, followed by two sentences about what it does: copies the CLI, creates the journal folder, and installs plugins for the agents it finds.

Below that I added a small table with one row per agent. The columns are the agent, where the rules go, and how the reminder works. For Claude Code it is the hooks, for Codex the notify setting, for Pi the session end handler.

The manual steps moved into a section called Manual install further down. I kept the three statements fixed in the last review and checked them again against the script: default folder, config key name, skip flag for Pi. All were still right.

I also added the new --host flag to the flag list, as planned this morning.

One thing I noticed is that the badges at the top wrap onto two lines on narrow screens. The CI badge and the license badge could be merged into one row but I left it, because it looks fine on GitHub itself.

The README is now 18 lines shorter. The user read it and asked for the table to include the status check command per agent. I will add that tomorrow.

summary: Added the status command per agent to the README install table after the user asked for it
body:
The user wanted the table in the install section to show how to check each plugin. I added a column with the exact command: agent-journal status --agent claude, codex and pi.

I ran each command on my machine first to be sure the output matches what the text says. The Claude Code one printed an extra warning about a missing hooks entry, which turned out to be a leftover from an old test install, so I removed it and ran again.

The table is now four columns wide. On GitHub it renders without a scroll bar. The change touches only README.md.

summary: Found that the install script overwrote a user-edited rules file silently and made it keep a backup with a .bak suffix
body:
A user on an issue wrote that he had edited the rules file for Codex by hand and lost the edit after running the installer again. I could reproduce this. The script used cp without a check.

The fix compares the installed file with the new one using cmp. If they are the same, nothing happens. If they differ, the old file is moved to the same name with .bak added, and a line tells the user where it went.

I considered asking the user for a yes or no. The installer is often run in a script, though, and a prompt would hang it, so a backup is safer.

If a .bak already exists, it is replaced. Keeping many numbered copies seemed too much for a small text file.

Tests cover the three cases: identical, changed, and changed with an existing backup. I also answered the issue with the reason for the choice. A note about the backup went into the install section of the README.

summary: Built the first version of a doctor command that runs all plugin status checks plus folder and git remote checks in one report
body:
There were three separate status checks by now, plus the sync setup, and the user had to remember each of them. I added agent-journal doctor to run all of them and print one report.

The report has four groups: CLI, journal folder, sync, and agents. The CLI group shows the version and the path of the script that is running, which helps when two installs exist on the PATH.

The journal folder group checks that the folder exists, is writable, and counts the entries. It also warns when a file has no front matter date, since list would skip it. I found two such files in my own journal, both from the first week, and fixed them by hand.

The sync group checks whether the folder is a git repository and whether a remote is set. It does not contact the remote, because that would make doctor slow and fail without a network. It prints the remote URL and the number of unpushed commits.

The agents group calls the existing status code for each agent that is installed. I refactored the three status checks into functions in the script so doctor and status share the same code. Before that, doctor would have had to call itself as a subprocess and parse the output.

An agent that is not installed is shown as not installed and does not count as a failure. Only an installed agent with a failing check sets the exit code to 1.

I chose the plain format of one line per check, with ok, warn or FAIL in front. Colors are used only when stdout is a terminal and NO_COLOR is not set, like in the pane.

The first run on the desktop machine showed a warning that the Pi extensions folder did not exist. That was right, since Pi is not installed there, and the agent check had to detect Pi by the folder. I changed it to look for the pi binary on the PATH first.

Tests use a temp HOME with fake agent folders. Five new tests pass, and the whole suite takes 11 seconds now. Next I need to write the help text and the README line for doctor.

summary: Wrote the help text and README line for doctor and fixed the top-level usage that did not list the status command
body:
Doctor now has its own help text with the four groups named and the meaning of the exit code. I kept it to 12 lines like the other commands.

While writing it I saw that the top-level usage listed list, recall, sync and config but not status. That had been the case since the Codex work. I added both status and doctor.

The README got one line in the command overview. The test that compares help output with the parser caught nothing this time, since the subcommands list is separate. I added a second check that every word in the top-level usage line is a known command and the other way around.

summary: Investigated why the journal pane flickered on the desktop machine and replaced the full clear with cursor positioning and line-wise redraw
body:
The pane showed a visible flicker every time the folder changed. It was not noticeable on the laptop but clear on the desktop terminal, which is slower to draw.

The script used clear and then printed everything again. Between the two steps the terminal showed an empty screen for a moment. I measured this by recording the output with script and counting the clear sequences: one per refresh.

The new version moves the cursor to the top left with a printf of the escape sequence, prints the lines, and then clears only the rest of each line and everything below. No blank screen appears.

There was a catch. If a new line is shorter than the old one, the leftover characters stay on the screen. So each line gets the clear-to-end-of-line sequence added before the newline. The final clear-below handles the case of fewer entries than before.

I also hit a problem with long summaries that wrap. A wrapped line takes two rows, so the row count differs from the line count. The pane now cuts each line to the terminal width, which I read with tput cols once per refresh. The cut uses the same word boundary code as recall snippets, so multi-byte characters stay whole.

I checked the width in a narrow window and found that the time column plus the dim color codes counted against the width. The color escape sequences have no visible width. I changed the cut to count the text without them by cutting before adding the colors.

Resize is handled by trapping SIGWINCH to force a refresh. POSIX sh supports the WINCH trap name on Linux and macOS, and I tested both.

The flicker is gone on the desktop. I recorded one minute of refreshes and the clear sequence count is now zero. The change is 22 lines in the pane script.

One open question is that the refresh still polls the folder every two seconds. A watch with fswatch would be better, but it is an extra dependency, so I left it.

summary: Replaced the two-second polling of the pane with a cheap check of the folder listing checksum so it redraws only when something changed
body:
Even after the flicker fix, the pane redrew every two seconds whether or not something changed. That is wasteful and also resets the cursor in some terminals.

I added a cheap change check. Each poll runs ls -l on the folder with the modification times and passes the output to cksum. If the number equals the one from the last poll, nothing is drawn.

This catches new files, deleted files, and edited files. It is also the reason I had to look again at the bug of three weeks ago: pulled files keep an old modification time. That fix touches the files after a pull, so the checksum changes. I tested a pull and the pane updated.

The cost of the check on the 5,000-entry journal was a concern. ls -l of that many files takes about 40 ms on the laptop. I limited it to the files of the last seven days with a name glob, since the pane only shows the latest entries. That brings it to 4 ms.

The glob uses the date prefix of the file names, so it needs the dates of the last seven days. I reused the date helper from the --since work. BSD and GNU date differ again, but the helper already handles both.

There is one limit. At midnight the glob changes, which changes the checksum and forces one redraw. That is harmless.

I measured CPU use over a minute with top. Polling with redraw used about 1.5 percent, and the new check used under 0.1 percent.

A test for the pane is hard because it is interactive. I split the check into a function that prints the checksum and tested that function: same folder gives the same number, a new file changes it.

The pane work is finished for now.

summary: Ran the recall eval on all three agents after the doctor and host changes and found the rules budget in Pi was down to 12 characters
body:
After adding the host filter and doctor, I wanted to know whether the rules had grown. They had not, since I never put the new commands in the rules, but the CLI version line that the Pi extension embeds got longer.

The eval runner has 13 questions and three runs per agent. Claude Code got 13 of 13 on all three runs. Codex got 12 of 13, missing question 13 once. Pi got 12 of 13 with question 9 missed in all runs, as before.

The length budget for Pi is checked by a test. It passed, but only with 12 characters to spare. The version line was the cause, because it now shows the git describe string and not just the number.

I shortened the line to the plain version number. That freed 19 characters, giving 31 again. This is the same margin as after the shortening of three weeks ago.

For question 9, the answer is in an entry that recall ranks eleventh. I tried raising the default limit to 12, which fixed it, but the output of each recall grows by two hits. Codex then started to run out of its context on the long sessions in the eval, which I could see in the transcript.

So I did not change the limit. A better fix is ranking. The entry has the search terms only in the body, and ranking counts hits equally in summary and body. A weight of two for summary hits would not help here, since the entry hits only in the body.

I wrote this down as an open item. The next idea is to count distinct terms before total hits, because the entry has all terms once while the top ten have a few terms many times.

I will try that ranking change tomorrow with the eval as a check.

summary: Changed recall ranking to prefer entries matching more distinct terms before total hits and measured the effect on the 13 eval questions
body:
Following yesterday's note, I changed the score in the recall awk program. It now sorts first by the number of distinct terms found, then by total hits, then by newest.

Since recall uses AND matching, every result already contains all terms, so distinct count is equal for all. That made my first version a no-op, and I wasted twenty minutes before seeing it. The real difference is only for the cases with a partial match, which recall excludes.

So the idea was wrong for this command. What matters is the distribution of hits. Entries with many repeated hits of one term outrank an entry with one hit of each term.

I tried a different score: the sum over terms of min(hits, 3). This caps the effect of a repeated word. Entries that mention a term once score the same as entries that mention it thrice, up to the cap.

On the eval, question 9 moved from rank 11 to rank 4. The other 12 questions kept their correct entries within the top three. I checked each by running the recall command from the question file and reading the order.

I also compared results on 20 queries of my own taken from the journal, looking at the top five before and after. 14 were identical. In 6 the order changed, and in 5 of those I found the new order more useful. In one it was worse, because a long entry with a generic word got capped and lost against a short one.

The cost in time is zero, as the cap is one comparison in awk.

I kept the cap at 3. A cap of 2 moved question 9 to rank 6, and a cap of 5 gave rank 8. The values are in a short table in the commit message.

Tests: a new fixture with one entry that repeats a term ten times and one that has each term once. The second must come first. It passes.

I will run the full eval on the agents later and look for regressions.

summary: Ran the full eval after the capped ranking change: Pi now passes question 9 on all runs, but Codex lost question 5 once
body:
I ran the eval with three runs for each of the three agents, using the capped hit score from this morning.

Claude Code scored 13 of 13 on all three runs. Pi scored 13 of 13 on two runs and 12 on one, and the miss was not question 9 any more. Codex scored 12, 13 and 12.

For Codex the misses were question 5 in one run and question 13 in another. Question 13 was a known miss. Question 5 was new, so I looked at its transcript.

Question 5 asks about the reason for the choice of awk over a small Go program. The agent ran recall with the terms awk and go. The entry with the answer has the words awk and portable, but go appears in it only as part of the word going. The agent searched for the plain word and got a ranking where the right entry was sixth, and then it stopped at the first three hits.

This happened before my change too, so I ran question 5 with the old ranking as well. The old order gave the right entry at rank 2. So the change did cause it, because the entry that was found earlier repeated awk and go-like words many times.

I looked at the new order. The top three were short entries that mention awk once and go once. They match the cap exactly while the real entry has more text around. This is the case I noted of the generic word.

One option is a cap of 4. I tried it and question 5 moved to rank 3, question 9 to rank 5. The remaining questions did not change.

With a cap of 4 I ran the eval again on Codex only, three runs: 13, 13 and 12. The last miss was question 13, as before.

I settled on a cap of 4. The tests use a fixture with 10 repeats and 1 repeat, and the fixture still passes since 4 is more than 1.

The finding I keep is that the eval needs more than one run per change, and that rank moves of a few places matter for agents that read only the first three hits.

The next step is to check whether the printing of the first body line under each hit helps the agent decide.

summary: Added a note in the recall rules telling the agent to read the top hit with --show when snippets look related, and kept Pi within its budget
body:
The eval showed that the agents sometimes answered from the snippet only. In the transcript of question 5 the agent had the right entry in the list, but the snippet cut before the reason, and the agent wrote an answer that was only partly right.

The rules already say to use --show, but in a sentence that I had shortened three weeks ago. I looked at the current wording: it said to show the entry when needed. Needed is vague.

I rewrote it as: when a hit looks related, run recall --show on it before answering. It is longer by 31 characters. The Pi budget had 31 characters free after the version line fix, so it would be exactly zero. That is too tight.

I cut other text. The sentence about the empty journal message was 58 characters, and the agent never needs it, as the CLI prints the message itself. I removed it. That gave 58 characters back.

The Claude Code rules and the Codex rules use the same shared text with agent-specific lines added, so the change reached all three. The budget test passed for each with margins of 89, 61 and 58 characters.

Then the eval, three runs each. Claude Code scored 13 on all three. Codex scored 13, 13, 13 for the first time. Pi scored 13, 13 and 12, with the miss on question 2, which I had not seen fail before.

I checked question 2 in the transcript. The Pi agent opened the entry with --show, but the answer asked for a number of seconds and it gave minutes. That is an agent mistake in reading the entry, not a problem of the rules. I ran question 2 five more times on Pi and it passed all five.

So the rule change looks good. The cost is one extra command per question, and the transcripts show about 800 more tokens per question on average.

I am keeping the change. The doctor and the host filter are not in the rules on purpose, because they are for the user, not for the agent.

I should add a line to the README about how the eval is run, since a contributor asked about it in an issue.

summary: Wrote the README section on running the recall eval and fixed the badges row so the CI badge points at the main workflow
body:
A contributor asked in an issue how the eval works and whether he could run it. The README said nothing about it, so I wrote a section called Evaluating the rules.

It explains in four sentences that the runner takes a file of questions with expected entry names, starts each agent in a temp folder with a copy of a fixture journal, and checks whether the answer contains the expected fact. It then gives the command and says each question should be run three times.

I also wrote down the cost: the full eval with three agents and three runs takes about 25 minutes and uses real agent calls, so it is not part of the CI.

While editing the top of the README I looked at the badges. The CI badge pointed to a workflow file name that I had renamed two weeks ago, so it showed no status. I changed the URL to the current file name and the badge shows passing again.

I also removed a badge for a package registry. The tool is not published there, so it showed unknown. Two badges remain: CI and license.

Then I read the whole README from the top as a new user would. The first paragraph says what the tool is, but not that the agents write the entries by themselves. I added half a sentence about it.

The install section is as I left it. The commands in the usage section match the help output; I checked each with a copy and paste. The recall --host flag appears in the list.

One error in the README remained: it said the pane refreshes every two seconds. It now checks every two seconds and redraws only on change. I fixed the sentence.

The fixture journal for the eval has 60 entries. A contributor might want to add questions, so I wrote where the fixture and the question file live.

I also thought about screenshots of the pane for the README. A picture would help, but a good one needs a real session. I will think about this over the coming weeks.

summary: Took two screenshots of the journal pane and list output for the README and checked they stay readable at the width GitHub renders
body:
I made two screenshots, one of the pane with six entries and one of a list output with the --utc flag. The terminal was set to 80 columns and a light font size so the text is sharp.

GitHub shows images at most about 880 pixels wide, so I resized to that. At this size the dim time column is hard to read, so I increased the contrast in the pane colors only for the screenshot by running without dim.

I did not add them to the README yet. They are in a temporary folder. The user wants to look at them before I commit the files, as the repository should not grow with large images. Both are under 60 KB as PNG.

summary: Fixed sync failing with a confusing git error when the journal folder had untracked files from a failed earlier run
body:
A user reported that sync stopped with the error: pathspec did not match any files. I could reproduce it by leaving a half-written entry file, with only the front matter and no summary, in the folder.

The sync script added files one by one with git add and a name list that it built from ls. A file that vanished between the listing and the add, which happened when the editor removed a swap file, produced the pathspec error.

I changed the script to build the list with git ls-files for tracked files and git ls-files --others --exclude-standard for new ones. Git itself then provides the names, so there is no race with the folder listing.

I also made the script skip files that do not end in .md. Swap files and the .DS_Store file had been added to commits before, and I found three such files in my own history. They are removed now with a normal commit, not a history rewrite.

A .gitignore with those names is created by the config step if it does not exist. That is a small addition of four lines.

One more point was the half-written entry. Sync now checks that each new file has a summary line in its front matter and skips those with a warning. This keeps incomplete entries from reaching the remote, where the other machine would show them in list with a blank summary.

Tests: a folder with a swap file, a folder with an incomplete entry, and a normal one. All pass.

The one-file-per-entry commit policy is unchanged.

summary: Looked into a report that Claude Code hooks fire twice after the plugin is installed both globally and per project, and made install detect it
body:
An issue said that the journal reminder appeared twice at the end of each turn. I asked for the settings files and saw the hook was listed in the global settings and in the project settings of the same repository.

Claude Code merges both and runs both. There is no deduplication, so the reminder ran twice. This was a setup problem, not a bug in the hook, but it is easy to run into, since the installer writes to the global file and some users copied the hook by hand into a project.

I made the status check look for the hook command in the project settings file of the current directory as well as the global one. If it finds both, it prints a warning with the two paths and says to remove one.

The installer does the same check before it writes. If a project file in the current folder already has the hook, it prints a notice and still installs globally, since that is the documented way.

I considered making the hook itself safe against double runs. A marker file with the session id would do: the first run creates it, the second sees it and exits. But the hook already uses a pending marker for Codex and Pi, and adding another one would make the logic harder to follow, so I did not.

I tested the check with a temp project folder and a temp HOME. Cases: only global, only project, both. The both case expects the warning and an exit code of 0, since a duplicate is not a failure.

I answered the issue with the explanation and the new warning. The reporter confirmed it was his copied hook.

One line about this went into the troubleshooting part of the README, which until now had only two items. It now has three.

summary: Added a journal sync step to the pane check so a failed pull shows a warning line instead of silently showing old entries, and measured the cost of the check
body:
The user asked why the pane looked fine while sync had been failing on the laptop for a day. The cause was that the pane only reads the folder and never looks at the result of the last sync. I added a small marker file, .sync-status, that sync writes with the exit code and the time of day after each run.

The pane now reads that file once per redraw and prints one dim warning line under the title when the code is not 0. The line says sync failed and gives the time of the last good run, for example 'sync failed, last ok 09:41'. Without a marker file the pane prints nothing extra, so machines that never use sync look the same as before.

Writing the marker needed care, because sync can be killed halfway. I write to a temporary file in the same folder and move it into place with mv, so the pane never reads a half-written line. I also made sure the marker is listed in the .gitignore that sync creates, since it must not be pushed to the remote.

I measured the extra read on the desktop machine with 5,000 entries in the folder. The redraw went from 11 ms to 12 ms, which is within the noise. Under NO_COLOR the warning line is printed without dim codes and starts with the word WARNING so that it still stands out.

I added three tests: a failed sync shows the line, a later good sync removes it, and a missing marker shows nothing. All three pass in the Vitest run next to the existing pane tests. Still open: the doctor idea from the notes could read the same marker, which would avoid a second git check. I will look at that next.

summary: Added the two pane and list screenshots to the README under a new Screenshots heading after the user approved them
body:
The user looked at the screenshots from two days ago and approved both with one change: the list picture should show the --utc flag in the command line, so the reader sees what produced it.

I retook the list screenshot with the command visible above the output. The PNG files went into a docs folder with the names pane.png and list.png. Their sizes are 54 KB and 41 KB.

In the README I added a Screenshots heading after the usage section, with the two images and one line of text each. I set the width attribute to 440 so they sit side by side on a wide screen.

The images show the light theme only. A dark version can wait for the better pictures that are planned.

summary: Made doctor-style sync check reuse the .sync-status marker and fixed the marker being written with the wrong time when TZ was set in the config
body:
This continued the marker work from yesterday. While testing on the laptop I saw the pane report 'last ok 03:12' for a sync that had run at 09:12. The marker was written with date in UTC, while the pane shows local times, and the tz config key was not applied in the sync script.

I changed sync to write the epoch seconds and let the pane format them. The pane already has the portable awk and date conversion from the list work, so it now uses the same helper and respects the tz key and the --utc setting. That removed the duplicate formatting code in sync.

I checked the result with tz set to a negative offset and to a half-hour offset, since those broke list before. Both showed the right local time. I extended the pane tests with these two cases and one with an old marker in the previous format, which is now ignored instead of printing nonsense.

The doctor command is not touched yet, but its sync check can now read the same file and report the age of the last good run. That is the next small step. The README mention of the warning line is also still to do.

summary: Planned an AGENT_JOURNAL_INTERVAL environment variable for the pane so the refresh poll can go below two seconds, and wrote the validation rules and tests first.
body:
The pane waits a fixed two seconds before it notices a new entry. That feels slow when watching it live, and impatient users have said the same. I spent the session preparing a way to shorten the wait and did not change the pane's behavior yet.

The plan is an environment variable named AGENT_JOURNAL_INTERVAL that the pane would pass to sleep. The default stays 2. A decimal such as 0.5 should work, and I checked that both GNU and BSD sleep accept decimals, on macOS and on Linux.

Input checking is the main design question. An empty, zero or non-numeric value would turn the loop into a busy wait or an error. I sketched a case pattern that allows digits and one dot, plus a small awk check that the number is at least 0.1. Anything else would fall back to 2 with a one-line warning at the start. I wrote the validator as a separate function in a scratch file so it can be tested alone.

I also considered a config key. Config keys are for things in the journal itself, like tz, and the interval is a property of one terminal, so an environment variable fits better. I settled on that.

I added test cases for the validator to the Vitest file: 0.5 passes, 0 falls back, abc falls back, empty falls back. They run against the scratch function, and the pane does not use it yet.

I took a first CPU measurement of the existing check loop, which is cheap. That makes me expect a short interval like 0.2 to be fine, but I want to measure it with the real variable before relying on it. Still to do: wire the variable into the pane, update its help text, and change the README line about the pane.

summary: Answered the user's question on which agents read the recall rules at session start, from the plugin entries and the three install paths
body:
The user asked whether all three agents get the recall rules at the start of the session or only after the first prompt. I read the plugin entries and the install code.

Claude Code gets them through the session start hook, which prints the rules into the context. Codex gets them from the instructions file, which Codex reads at start. Pi gets them from the extension, which appends them through the context field on session start.

So all three have them before the first prompt. The difference is the first action: Claude Code and Pi run list through the rules, while Codex needed the rule line moved to the top, as found in the eval weeks ago.

I told the user this and pointed out that the rules differ only in the agent-specific lines. No change in the code was needed.

summary: Started a lint pass over bin/agent-journal with shellcheck after the doctor and host changes, and fixed 11 quoting warnings that could break on folders with spaces
body:
The last few weeks added doctor, --host and the pane check, and each came with new shell code, so I ran shellcheck over bin/agent-journal and the plugin scripts for the first time. It reported 23 findings. Eleven were real quoting problems, mostly unquoted $dir and $file in for loops and in the checksum call of the pane.

I reproduced the worst one by setting the journal folder to a path with a space in it, "My Journal". list printed nothing and doctor reported the folder as missing, although it existed. After quoting the variables both worked.

The other findings were harmless. Several were SC2086 on purpose, where the awk option list needs word splitting, and I added a disable comment with a reason on each. Two were about `local` not being POSIX. I replaced them with function-prefixed variable names, because the script has to run under dash.

I ran the Vitest suite under dash and under bash as sh. All 94 tests passed in both. I added one new test that creates a journal folder with a space and runs list and doctor against it.

Not done: the plugin hook scripts still have 4 warnings about unused variables. I left them because the hooks are being touched later this week. Next I want shellcheck in the CI workflow, with a pinned version so new releases do not turn the build red by themselves.

summary: Added shellcheck to the GitHub Actions workflow with a pinned version, so quoting regressions in the CLI fail CI instead of reaching users
body:
I added a shellcheck step to the existing CI workflow, before the Vitest step. It runs on bin/agent-journal and on every script under the plugin folders. The version is pinned in the workflow file, so a new release cannot change the result without a commit.

The first run failed on the 4 unused variable warnings in the hook scripts that I had left yesterday. I removed two variables and renamed two that are used by the sourced rules file, with a disable comment saying so.

The second run was green. The step adds about 6 seconds to the job. I also documented in the README contributing part that `shellcheck bin/agent-journal` can be run locally. One open question is whether to lint the test fixtures too, but they are data and not scripts, so I skipped them.

summary: Found that recall --since accepted '3 days' but silently treated '3days' as no filter, and made unknown period strings an error with a usage hint
body:
The user pasted a recall call that returned the whole journal, although he meant only the last three days. The command was `recall --since 3days`. The period parser in the awk part only matched a number followed by a space and a unit, and anything else fell through to an empty cutoff, which means no filter.

I changed the parser to accept both forms, `3d`, `3 days` and `3days`, and to exit with 2 and a message when the string is not recognised: `recall: cannot read period '3dayz', try 3d, 2w or 1m`. The message lists the units that work.

Three new tests cover the accepted forms and one covers the error exit code. The existing tests for `--since` kept passing, so the stricter parse did not break the documented forms.

I also checked list, which shares the parser, and it got the same fix. The help text for both now shows `3d` as the example.

One behavior to watch: scripts that passed a bad string and relied on the silent fallback will now fail. I judged that acceptable, since no one can have wanted a filter that did nothing.

summary: Investigated why sync sometimes pushed an empty commit message on the laptop, traced it to an unset hostname in the message template, and added a fallback
body:
The user noticed commits in the journal remote with the message `journal: sync from ` and nothing after it. They all came from the laptop. I looked at the sync script and found the message is built from `$(hostname -s)`, with the host taken from the config key host first.

On the laptop, hostname -s printed nothing when the machine was on a captive network, because the name came from DHCP and was empty at that moment. The config key was not set, so the message ended up empty.

I added a fallback chain: config host, then hostname -s, then `uname -n`, then the word unknown. The same chain is now used when writing the host into new entries, which also fixes entries with an empty host line in the front matter. I counted them: 6 entries in the real journal have an empty host.

I did not rewrite those entries. The --host filter treats an empty host as no match, and that is the right behavior for old data. I wrote a test that runs the CLI with a stub hostname that prints nothing, and checks that the message contains `unknown`.

Next I want doctor to warn when the configured host is empty and the real one differs.

summary: Built an export command that writes selected entries as one Markdown file, with period and host filters, after the user wanted to share a month of work in a single document
body:
The user asked for a way to hand a month of journal entries to someone as one file. I added `agent-journal export`, which takes the same filters as recall: --since, --until, --host, and a project filter.

The output starts with a one-line header and then each entry as a level-two heading made from the summary, followed by the date line and the body. The front matter is dropped, since it is noise for a reader. Entries come in chronological order, oldest first, which is the reverse of list.

The parsing reuses the awk script of recall, so I moved the shared part into one function instead of copying it. That was the larger part of the work, as recall had grown some special cases for snippets. The export path now calls the function with a flag that turns off snippet cutting.

There are two choices to record. First, output goes to stdout, and the user can redirect it; I did not add an --output flag. Second, entries with a body that contains lines starting with # would break the heading structure, so export indents those lines by escaping the first character with a backslash.

I wrote 7 tests. They cover the order, the filters, the escaping, an empty result, which prints nothing and exits with 0, and a check that no front matter keys leak into the output. A run on the real journal of 410 entries took 0.4 seconds for the full export.

The help text has the new command with two examples. I did not touch the README yet. The Codex and Pi rules do not mention export either, and that is deliberate, because the rules budget in Pi is nearly used up and this is a command for the user, not for agents.

summary: Wrote the README section for export and rechecked the whole usage part against the real help output, fixing four stale flag descriptions
body:
After export landed this afternoon I wrote its README section: what it does, two examples, and a note that the output is a plain Markdown document. It sits after the recall section.

Because I was in the file, I compared the whole usage part with the output of `agent-journal --help` and each subcommand help. Four things were stale. The list section still described --host as planned. The recall section named a --days flag that was renamed to --since many weeks ago. The config section listed five keys but the CLI knows seven. And the doctor line said it checks three things, while it checks five.

I fixed all four from the real output, not from memory. For the config keys I ran `agent-journal config --list` and copied the key names exactly.

I also looked at the badges row. The CI badge is right, and the license badge pointed at a file name that exists. No change there.

A small idea came out of this: a test that extracts the flag names from the README code blocks and checks that the CLI accepts them. It would have caught the --days problem. I wrote it down as a task and did not start it, as it is bigger than a one-evening change.

summary: Started a README flag check test that pulls commands from code blocks and runs them with --help, and it found two more commands that no longer exist
body:
I started the test idea from last night. A Vitest file reads README.md, takes every fenced block that starts with `agent-journal`, and runs the first two words with --help to check that the subcommand exists.

The first run found two failures. One was `agent-journal pane --once`, which is a valid call but the test split it wrongly. The other was `agent-journal status claude`, which was an old form: status is now per agent, as `agent-journal status --agent claude`. Wait, the README install table uses the per-agent plugin command, so the README was right and my parser was wrong for that line.

I fixed the parser to take only the subcommand word. After that one real failure was left, an example of `agent-journal show` which was replaced by `recall --show` weeks ago. I corrected the README line.

The test runs in 0.3 seconds. I did not check option names yet, only subcommands.

summary: Extended the README check to option names, found --tz in an example that the CLI spells --timezone, and fixed the README line
body:
I extended the README test so it also takes every option that begins with two dashes in a command line and checks it appears in the help output of that subcommand.

It found one mismatch: an example of list with `--tz Europe/Berlin`. The CLI option is --timezone, and --tz only exists as an undocumented alias in an older version. I checked the list script, and the alias had been removed during the time zone work. I changed the README to --timezone.

There were two false alarms. Options inside quoted strings, such as a grep pattern in an example, were read as flags. I made the test skip text inside quotes.

The test now guards subcommands and options in 41 README lines. I added a short note in the contributing part that changing a flag means the README test will tell you where it is still named.

summary: Reproduced a user's issue where list shows entries twice after a sync merge, found duplicated files with different suffixes, and made list skip identical content
body:
A pull request thread from another person described entries showing twice in list. I reproduced it by syncing two clones that each wrote an entry in the same minute. Git kept both files, since the names differed by the session id, but a conflict copy also appeared with a `~2` suffix.

The conflict copy had the same content as the original. list reads every .md file, so it printed both.

I made list and recall compute a checksum of the front matter date, session and summary lines per file, and skip a file whose key was already seen. The cost on 410 entries is small, 30 ms more.

I added a test with a copied file. The `~2` files stay on disk, as I did not want the CLI to delete anything. I answered the thread with the cause and the fix.

summary: Made doctor warn about conflict copy files in the journal folder and print the command to remove them, so duplicates are visible and not only hidden
body:
Since list now hides duplicates, doctor should show the user that they exist. I added a check that looks for files ending in `~2`, `~3` and similar, and for files with the words `conflicted copy`.

If any exist, doctor prints a warning with the count and the names of the first three, and a line with the command to inspect them: `ls "$dir"/*~*`. It does not suggest rm, only inspection.

I wrote two tests, one with no copies, which shows a plain OK line, and one with two copies. The exit code stays 0 for warnings, as for the other soft checks.

The help text for doctor now lists the sixth check. The README line for doctor said five checks, so I changed it to six.

summary: Added a shellcheck-clean pass over the plugin hook scripts and the install script, fixing unquoted expansions and a broken test bracket that skipped the Pi folder check
body:
After the CLI lint pass of last week, the same shellcheck run was pointed at the scripts outside bin/agent-journal: the Claude Code hook scripts, the Codex notify script and install.sh. It reported 17 warnings in total. Most were the same kind as before, unquoted variables in paths that would break on a folder with a space in its name.

Three findings were more than style. In install.sh, a test used `[ -w $PI_DIR -a -d $PI_DIR ]`, which with an empty PI_DIR evaluated as a single-argument test and always succeeded. That meant the check for a writable Pi extensions folder, added a while ago, could pass when the folder variable was empty. I rewrote it as two separate tests with quotes, and ran install.sh with PI_DIR unset to confirm it now reports the failure and exits with 1.

The second real finding was a `cd` without a fallback in the Claude Code session end hook. If the journal folder had been removed, the hook kept going in the wrong directory and could have written the pending marker there. It now exits quietly with status 0 so it never blocks the agent. The third was a `read` without `-r` in the Codex notify script, which ate backslashes in summaries containing Windows style paths.

The remaining 11 warnings were quoting issues. I fixed them by hand and did not use a blanket disable comment, except for one `SC2034` on a variable that is read by the sourced config, where I added a comment explaining why.

Tests: the full Vitest suite passed. I added one test that runs the install script with a folder name containing a space and checks that the rules file lands in the right place. It failed before the fixes and passes now.

Next step is to make the CI shellcheck step cover these files too, not only the CLI.

summary: Extended the CI shellcheck step to cover plugin scripts and install.sh, using a file list from git so new scripts are picked up without editing the workflow
body:
The CI step added earlier only checked bin/agent-journal, so the fixes to the hook scripts and install.sh from this morning could regress unnoticed. I changed the step to take its file list from `git ls-files` and keep every file with a sh shebang or a .sh suffix. New scripts are then covered automatically.

I ran the new command locally first and it listed 9 files, including two test helper scripts that had never been linted. Those had four warnings, all about unquoted variables, and I fixed them in the same commit. The pinned shellcheck version stayed the same.

The workflow ran green on the push. I also checked that it goes red by temporarily adding an unquoted `rm $f` to a hook script on a throwaway commit, and then dropped that commit.

summary: Checked whether the Pi extension still fits its rules budget after the export command, and confirmed export is not in the rules, leaving 31 characters free
body:
The earlier eval found Pi down to 12 characters of budget, so I wanted to be sure export did not eat into it. The rules file for Pi is built from a shared part plus a Pi part, and I counted the characters with the status check.

Export is not in the shared rules, because it is a user command. The budget is 31 characters free now. The earlier 12 became 31 because of the wording cut in the recall note a few days ago.

I wrote down the numbers in the Pi plugin notes so the next change can compare. No code change.

One thing to watch: the doctor report text is also shown in the rules when the status check fails, and that could grow. I will check it when I touch doctor next.

summary: Added a --count option to recall that prints only the number of matching entries, so the user and scripts can check how big a result is before reading it
body:
The user asked how many entries mention the sync command without having to read the whole output. I added `recall --count`, which runs the usual filters and prints one integer.

The awk pass already knows the number of matching files, so the change was small: when --count is set, the printing part is skipped and the END block prints the counter. Terms, --since, --until and --host all work with it.

There was one detail with the ranking. Recall ranks entries by distinct term matches, and a term list means entries that match at least one term. --count follows that, and counts the same entries that a normal call would print. I checked this by running both on 12 queries and comparing the number of result blocks to the count.

I added 5 tests: no filter, a term, an empty result printing 0, combined with --host, and combined with --since.

Help text updated. I left it out of the agent rules for the budget reasons from this morning. In the README it is one line in the recall section. The answer to the user: the sync command appears in 37 entries.

summary: Reviewed the pull request from an outside contributor adding fish completions, found the generated list of subcommands was hard coded, and asked for it to come from the CLI
body:
A contributor opened a pull request with a completions/agent-journal.fish file. I read it carefully and ran it in fish 3.7.

The completions work for subcommands and for options of list and recall. The problem is that the subcommand list is typed into the file by hand. Since doctor, export and status were added in the last weeks, a hand written list will go stale again, as the README did.

I asked in a review comment for a hidden subcommand, `agent-journal completion-words`, that prints the subcommands and options per command, so fish can call it. I offered to add that part to the CLI myself if the contributor prefers.

A second point: the file uses `string match` with a regex that fails on fish 3.1, which is still on some distributions. I suggested a simpler test with `contains`.

Third, the pull request had no test. I said that a test that runs the fish completion is not needed, but one for completion-words is, and I would write it.

The contributor answered within the hour that they would try the first two points. So I implemented completion-words on my side in the meantime: it reads the same table of commands that the help text uses, so both stay in step.

The table is a plain here-document in the script, one line per command with its options. I moved the help text to be generated from it as well. That was more change than planned, but it removes one duplicate list. Tests: help output is byte equal to before for all 11 commands, and completion-words prints the 11 names.

I will merge the pull request when the contributor has pushed the update.

summary: Merged the fish completions after the contributor switched to completion-words, and added matching bash and zsh completion files built from the same output
body:
The contributor pushed the update this evening. The fish file now calls `agent-journal completion-words`, uses `contains` instead of the regex, and works on 3.1 in a container I tried. I merged it with a squash and thanked them in the thread.

Since completion-words exists, bash and zsh are cheap. I wrote completions/agent-journal.bash, which uses compgen with the words from the CLI, and completions/_agent-journal for zsh with _arguments and the same source.

In bash the first version completed options after a subcommand only when the subcommand was the first word. I fixed it to find the subcommand in the word list, so `agent-journal --host x list --<TAB>` also works.

The install script got a step that copies the completion files to the standard folders if they exist and are writable: the user bash-completion folder, the zsh site-functions folder in the home directory, and the fish completions folder. It prints one line for each file copied. If a folder does not exist, it skips it and says nothing, because most users only have one shell.

The install script has a flag --no-completions for people who dislike it. I added the flag to the usage text and to the test that checks the flags.

Tests: install into a temporary home, with and without the flag, and check which files exist. 6 new tests, all green.

README: I added a Completions part under the install section, with three lines, one for each shell. The README flag test passed, with the new flag found in the help.

Open: the zsh file was only tried in zsh 5.9 on the laptop. I would like to check 5.8 on the older machine.

summary: Checked the zsh completion on the older machine with zsh 5.8, found compinit was not loaded for a fresh user, and documented the one line to add
body:
On the older machine I installed the completions into a clean home and opened zsh 5.8. TAB did nothing for agent-journal.

The reason was not my file. A fresh zsh does not run compinit, so no function from site-functions is used. After adding `autoload -Uz compinit && compinit` to .zshrc, subcommands and options completed correctly.

I added a note with that line to the README Completions part, with a sentence that many setups have it already. The install script prints the same hint only when it copies the zsh file and `compinit` is not found in .zshrc.

The subcommand completion works on 5.8 and the option completion for --host also, but --host values do not complete, as the hosts are not in completion-words. That is fine for now.

summary: Looked into the user's report that recall --since misses entries written late in the evening, and found the cutoff was computed in UTC while entry times are local
body:
The user noticed that `recall --since '1 day'` did not return an entry he had written at around 23:30 the evening before. I reproduced it on the laptop by setting TZ to a zone several hours behind UTC and writing an entry with a local time late in the day.

The cause was in the period parsing. The cutoff timestamp was computed with `date -u`, while the dates in the entry front matter are written in the local time zone from the config. For anyone west of UTC the cutoff moved forward by the offset, so recent evening entries fell before it. For people east of UTC the opposite happened and the filter let in entries that were slightly too old, which is why nobody had noticed it earlier.

The fix was to compute the cutoff in the same zone as the entries. If the config has a timezone key, it is exported as TZ for the date call, and otherwise the system zone is used. This is the same rule the list command already follows since the time zone work earlier in the project, so I moved that small function into a shared file and made both commands call it.

Because BSD date and GNU date differ in how they subtract a period, the function has two branches. I checked both on the two machines. The GNU branch uses `date -d`, and the BSD branch uses `date -v`. The unknown period error from the earlier change still comes first, so a typo is reported before any date math.

I added three tests. One sets TZ to a zone behind UTC, one to a zone ahead, and one with the config key overriding the environment. Each writes an entry with a fixed local time near midnight and checks whether `--since '1 day'` finds it. All three failed before the fix and pass now.

The full suite passed on both machines. I also reran the recall eval on Claude Code, since its questions use periods, and the results did not change. I told the user what the cause was and that no entries need to be rewritten, because the stored times were always right and only the filter was wrong.

summary: Added a --until option to recall and export so a period can have an end as well as a start, reusing the zone-correct date function, with tests and README text
body:
Following the since fix of this afternoon, the user asked for a way to read only a past period, for example the week before last, without the newer entries mixed in. recall had only `--since`, so I added `--until` and made it work in export too, since export shares the same filter code.

The option takes the same period strings as `--since`, such as '2 weeks' or '10 days', and means everything older than that point in time. Using it together with `--since` gives a window. For example `--since '3 weeks' --until '1 week'` selects the two weeks in between. I reused the shared date function from today's fix, so the cutoff is computed in the configured zone and not in UTC.

The filter itself is done in the awk pass that already compares the entry time with the cutoff. I added a second comparison with the upper bound, passed in as another awk variable. When the option is not given, the variable is empty and the check is skipped, so the speed of the common case is unchanged. I timed recall on the 400 entry fixture folder and got the same 0.11 seconds as before.

Two edge cases needed a decision. If the window is empty because `--until` is older than `--since`, a quiet empty result would be confusing, so the command now exits with an error that says the end is before the start. And an entry exactly on the boundary is included for since and excluded for until, so that two neighbouring windows never show the same entry twice. I wrote this rule in the help text.

Tests added:
- window with both options returns only the middle entries
- until alone excludes recent entries
- reversed window gives the error and exit code 2
- boundary entry appears in exactly one of two adjacent windows
- export with until writes only the selected entries

All passed, and so did the existing suite. shellcheck is clean on the changed files.

I added a short paragraph to the README usage part with the window example, and updated the help output. The README check test that runs the code block commands with `--help` accepted the new option name on the first run. I did not touch the recall rules for the agents, because the Pi budget is tight and the user asked for this as a manual tool; I will look at whether the agents need it after the next eval.

summary: Reran the eval for Codex only with 10 runs after the help text change and got question 7 correct in all of them, so the fix holds
body:
The batch of 5 runs a few days ago could have been luck, so I ran Codex alone, 10 runs for each of the 13 questions. That is 130 answers.

Question 7 passed in 10 of 10. The other 12 questions also passed in every run, except question 4 once, where the agent gave a correct answer but without the file name that the check wants. I looked at that run and the agent had found the right entry, so I count it as noise, not as a regression.

The median number of calls per question was 3, as before. I recorded the numbers in the eval notes. No code change.

summary: Prepared a changelog and release notes for the next version from the journal entries of the last weeks, and found three user visible changes that were missing from the README
body:
I started the release work by building a changelog. The journal is the best source, so I used `agent-journal export --since 5w` and read the result from the top. It came to 61 entries, and I sorted them into added, changed and fixed.

Added: the doctor command, the --host filter, export, --count, completions for three shells, the hosts word list, the pane interval variable, the shellcheck step in CI. Changed: list and recall are a single pass and much faster, short terms match whole words, bad period strings are an error, the install script keeps a .bak of an edited rules file. Fixed: the host in sync messages, the duplicate entries after conflicts, list from the wrong host with clock differences, the pane flicker, and the sync error with untracked files.

While matching the list to the README I found three user visible changes that the README did not say. The first was the .bak backup of the rules file, which belongs in the install section. The second was the error for bad period strings, which belongs in the recall part, with the accepted forms. The third was the word boundary for short terms, which a user would otherwise find surprising.

I wrote the three paragraphs. The backup note is one sentence with the file name. The period note lists `3d`, `2w` and `1m`. The word boundary note says terms of 3 characters or less match whole words only, with the example of pi and pipe.

The README flag test still passed. I also looked at the screenshots, which show the pane with the older layout, because the warning line for a failed pull was added after I took them. The picture still looks right for normal use, so I left it and put a retake on the list for later.

The changelog got the format of short bullet lines under each heading, with no links to issues except for the one from the outside contributor, whose pull request I credited by name as they wrote it.

For the version number, there are new commands and no breaking change except the error for bad periods, so it is a minor version. The package file says 0.6.2, and I plan 0.7.0. I did not bump it yet, as the release is not today.

Still to do: run the full test suite on the older machine, look at the open issue about the pane under tmux, and decide about the screenshot retake. I wrote these three in the todo file of the repository.

summary: Looked at the open issue on the pane under tmux, reproduced wrong line positions when the window is resized, and fixed it by reading the size again on each redraw
body:
The issue said the journal pane drew lines past the bottom edge after the tmux pane was resized. I reproduced it with a split and `resize-pane -D 8`.

The pane script read the terminal height once at start, with `tput lines`, and used that number for cursor positioning. After a resize the number was wrong.

I changed it to read the size at the start of each redraw, which is cheap, and also to trap SIGWINCH so a redraw is forced when the size changes, even if no entry changed. The checksum check would not have redrawn.

I tested with the resize in tmux and in a plain terminal window. The lines now fit in both. A test for this is hard, since it needs a terminal, so I added a manual check to the release list instead. I replied on the issue with the cause.

summary: Ran the full test suite on the older machine and found two tests that fail there because its sort command orders names differently, so the tests now sort explicitly
body:
For the release I ran the Vitest suite on the older machine. 2 tests of 112 failed, both in the hosts word list and in list ordering for equal timestamps.

The cause is the locale. The older machine has a different default, and sort orders uppercase and lowercase names differently there. The code was right, but the tests assumed an order.

I set LC_ALL=C in the CLI where it calls sort, which makes the order the same everywhere, and set the same in the test helper. Both tests passed, and the full suite was green on both machines.

summary: Retook the two README screenshots with the current pane layout including the pull warning line, and checked how they render at GitHub width in light and dark mode
body:
The screenshots in the README were taken before the warning line for a failed pull existed, so I retook them. I used a terminal of 100 columns and the same journal of example entries as the first time, so the pictures stay comparable.

The first picture is the pane with six entries and, this time, one warning line at the bottom that says the last pull failed. That shows the user what the warning looks like. The second is the output of list with the --host filter, which was not shown before.

I took the screenshots at twice the pixel density and scaled them down in the README with a width attribute of 720. At that width the text is readable on GitHub. I checked in the preview at normal width and on a narrow window of 400 pixels, where it still can be read when zoomed.

The picture background is dark, and on the light GitHub theme this looks like a heavy block. I looked at a light terminal theme as well, but the colors of the warning line, yellow on white, were hard to read. So I kept the dark picture, and added a thin border with a margin through the surrounding HTML so it looks intended.

I compressed the files with oxipng, which cut the two files from 214 kB and 188 kB to 96 kB and 81 kB.

I considered recording an animation of the pane, since the user wants better pictures for the README, but that is a larger plan. For now I only noted in the todo file that the plan needs a tool decision and a test of a few tools on small things first.

The README flag test is unaffected. The alt text of the two pictures now describes what they show, which I had left as just the word screenshot the first time.

summary: Bumped the version to 0.7.0, finished the changelog, and ran the manual release checklist including the tmux resize check, before tagging
body:
I changed the version in the package file from 0.6.2 to 0.7.0 and in the line that `agent-journal --version` prints. The test that compares the two passed.

The changelog is in its final form. I added the fix for the tmux pane and the sort order fix for the older machine, which were new since the draft.

Then I went through the manual checklist: install in a clean home for each of the three agents, doctor with no warnings, the pane in tmux with a resize, export of the last two weeks, and a TAB completion in each shell. All of it passed.

CI was green on the main branch for the last commit. I created the tag v0.7.0 and the release notes from the changelog. No further steps are open for this release.

summary: Checked the README install section against install.sh after the 0.7.0 tag and found it still described a copy step that the script no longer does
body:
After the tag I read the README install section line by line next to install.sh. The text said the script copies the plugin folders into place, but since the Pi change it links them. I rewrote the paragraph and the two example commands.

I also ran the install into a temporary home folder to confirm the output matches the README sample. It did, apart from one extra line about the Pi folder. I added that line to the sample. Nothing else in the section needed a change.

summary: Looked into a report that sync fails when the remote has a different default branch name, reproduced it with a local bare repo, and added a branch lookup
body:
The report came as an issue from an outside user whose remote used trunk as its default branch. Sync ran git push origin main and failed with 'src refspec main does not match any'. I reproduced this with a bare repo created with --initial-branch=trunk in a temporary folder.

The sync command had main hard coded in three places: the pull, the push and the first-run setup. I replaced them with a lookup of the current branch through git symbolic-ref --short HEAD, with main as the fallback when the journal folder is not yet a repo. The setup path for a new folder still creates main, since there is no remote choice to follow yet.

I added a Vitest case that builds the bare repo with trunk, runs sync twice and checks that entries arrive on the remote. A second case checks that a folder with main still works. Both pass, and the full suite stays green.

I commented on the issue with the cause and said the fix will go out with the next release. Still open: a remote with no commits at all. Sync handles it today, but there is no test for it, so that is next.

summary: Started a review of how the Claude Code hooks behave when the journal folder is on a slow network drive, and measured the session start cost at 1.9 seconds
body:
The user mentioned that session start felt slow when the journal lives on a mounted share. I wanted numbers before changing anything. I timed the session start hook with the folder on a local disk and then on a simulated slow mount.

Local, the hook took about 60 ms. On the slow mount it took 1.9 seconds. I used strace-like tracing through sh -x with timestamps to see where the time went.

The hook did three things that touch the folder. It counted entries with a find, it read the newest five files for the rules context, and it checked the sync marker. The find walked the whole tree, which is the expensive part on a share with thousands of files.

The count was only used for a sentence in the rules text saying how many entries exist. That figure is not needed for the agent to work. I looked at whether the number could come from the .sync-status marker, but the marker does not store it.

I wrote down three options. First, drop the count from the rules text. Second, cache the count in a small file updated whenever an entry is written. Third, cap the find with a depth limit, which does not help because the files sit at one level.

The cache needs the write path to stay correct when sync merges bring in new files, so it could drift. Dropping the count is simplest and removes the risk. I leaned toward that but did not decide.

I saved the timing script in a scratch folder, not in the repo. Next I will ask the user whether the count in the rules text is something they use before removing it.

summary: Removed the entry count from the session start rules after the user said nobody reads it, which cut the slow mount start from 1.9 seconds to 0.4
body:
The user answered the question from the morning: the entry count in the rules text is not used and can go. I removed the find from the Claude Code session hook and the sentence that printed the count.

The Codex and Pi plugins build the same text, so I checked each. Codex had the same find in its start script. Pi computes the text in the extension code and had a similar directory read. I removed both.

Rules text size matters for Pi, since it has a character budget. The removed sentence freed 38 characters, so the margin grows from 31 to 69. I confirmed this with the budget test.

I then timed the slow mount again. The session start fell from 1.9 seconds to 0.4 seconds. The rest is the read of the newest five files, which cannot be avoided because the agent needs them.

The tests had two snapshot checks for the rules text that included the count line. I updated them and added one that asserts the text does not contain the word entries followed by a number, so the line cannot come back by accident.

I looked at whether the newest five files could be found faster than with ls sorted by name. Entry names start with the date, so the sort is correct and cheap. I left it alone.

The README mentions the count in one sentence of the how it works section. I removed that sentence and read the paragraph again to make sure it still flows.

The full test suite passes on the laptop. I have not run it on the older machine yet.

Next I will run the suite there, and then add a note to the changelog under unreleased.

summary: Ran the test suite on the older machine after the count removal, found it passes, and added the change to the unreleased part of the changelog
body:
I pulled the latest main on the older machine and ran the whole Vitest suite. All tests passed, including the two updated snapshot checks. The run took 41 seconds, about the same as before.

I also ran the Pi budget test there, since shells and node versions differ. It reports 69 characters free, the same as on the laptop.

The changelog had an unreleased section with the branch name fix for sync. I added a line for the faster session start on slow drives, with the measured numbers. I kept the wording plain, since people read the changelog to decide whether to update.

I reread the changelog entry for the sync fix and shortened it, because it explained the cause in more detail than users need. The issue thread has the detail.

Nothing else is pending from the slow mount topic. If the user sees it again with a different cause, the timing script in the scratch folder can be reused.

summary: Added a test for sync with a remote that has no commits yet, which passed without code changes and closes the gap left by the branch fix
body:
This was the open item from the sync branch fix. I created an empty bare repo and pointed a fresh journal folder at it. Then I ran sync with one entry present.

The push worked and created the default branch on the remote. The pull step before it printed a warning about no remote branch, which sync already ignores. I confirmed the exit code is zero.

I wrote this as a Vitest case next to the trunk cases. It checks the entry file is on the remote and that the second sync run changes nothing.

I also tried the case where the remote is empty and the local folder has no entries. Sync exits cleanly and prints that there is nothing to push. That matches what I want, so no change.

The suite is green. The test count is now 3 higher than at the tag.

summary: Reproduced the issue where recall with several terms returns entries matching only one term, and found the awk filter joined terms with or instead of and
body:
A user wrote that recall auth token returns every entry mentioning either word. The README says terms narrow the result, so this was a bug. I reproduced it on a small fixture with three entries.

The awk script builds a match flag per term. The loop set the flag to 1 on the first match and stopped checking, so one hit was enough. It should require every term to hit.

I changed the loop to count matched terms and compare against the number of terms. Matching is still case insensitive and still looks in both summary and body.

The existing tests only used single terms, which is why this slipped through. I added three cases: two terms in one entry, two terms split between summary and body, and two terms where only one exists. The first two should return the entry, the third nothing.

I also checked --count with several terms, since it shares the filter. It now gives the narrowed number.

All tests pass. I still need to check whether the rules text tells the agent that terms narrow, since it may have been working around the old behavior by running one term at a time.

summary: Checked the recall rules for workarounds to the old or matching and found one sentence telling agents to search one term at a time, which I removed
body:
After the and fix I read the recall section of the rules text in all three plugins. The Claude Code and Codex rules were identical. Both had a sentence saying to search one word at a time and combine the results yourself.

That sentence existed because several terms used to broaden the result. With the fix it only makes agents run more searches. I replaced it with one saying that several terms narrow the result and a single distinctive term is usually enough.

The new sentence is 12 characters shorter, so the Pi budget gets a little more room, 81 free now. The budget test passes.

I do not know how agents will react to the changed text. The eval of the recall rules can answer that, so I added a note to run it before the next release rather than guess.

summary: Built a small eval case for multi-term recall and ran it on Claude Code and Codex, finding both now answer from one narrowed search
body:
To check the rules change I wanted a question where the answer needs two terms. I picked a question about the zsh completion problem on the older machine, which needs both zsh and compinit to find the right entry.

I added it to the eval question file as question 12, with the expected answer being the entry from the older machine check. The grader looks for compinit and the one line fix.

I ran it 5 times on Claude Code. All five used a single recall call with two terms and found the entry. Before the rules change I did not record a baseline, so I cannot say how it differed.

Then I ran it 5 times on Codex. Four used one call with two terms. One ran two searches, one per term, and still got the right answer.

The average number of recall calls per run was 1.0 for Claude Code and 1.2 for Codex. Both answers were correct in all ten runs.

I looked at the Codex run with two searches. It searched zsh first and got a long list, and then narrowed on its own. That is acceptable behavior and not caused by the rules text.

I wrote the results to the eval notes file with the date left out, using the commit hash instead. I noted that the baseline is missing so later comparisons are not mistaken for improvements.

The eval harness took 14 minutes for both agents. That is fine for a pre-release check but too slow for every change.

Next I will run the older questions again to be sure the rules edit did not harm them. That is a bigger run and I will do it tomorrow.

summary: Wrote the README paragraph on how recall terms combine and added two examples that the README check test now runs against --help
body:
The README recall section did not say how several terms work. Given the bug, that gap probably confused people. I added a short paragraph saying terms must all match, in summary or body, ignoring case.
