I added two example commands in a code block: one with a single term and one with two terms plus --since. The README check test pulls commands from code blocks and checks the options exist, so both are verified.

The check passed, but I noticed it only tests option names and not the combination. That is fine.

I reread the whole recall section for consistency. It also mentioned --count, which was added later, in a different paragraph. I moved that sentence next to the new text so the options sit together.

I checked how it renders on GitHub in the preview. The code block is narrow enough not to scroll.

The badges at the top still show the old version. They read from the release, so they will update after the next tag.

summary: Ran the older eval questions after the rules edit and got the same results as before on Claude Code, with one flaky answer on Codex for question 4
body:
This was the bigger run planned yesterday. I ran questions 1 to 11 with 3 runs each on both agents.

Claude Code answered all 33 runs correctly. Codex answered 32 of 33. The miss was question 4, about the sync empty commit message.

I read the failing transcript. Codex found the right entry but answered with the fix for the hostname, and missed that the fallback is the folder name. The grader wants the fallback named.

This looks like answer detail, not a retrieval problem. Searching worked. I ran question 4 again 5 times and got 5 correct, so I put it down to noise.

I did not change the rules text. I noted the miss in the eval notes so a repeat can be spotted later.

summary: Fixed list so entries with a missing summary line show the first body line instead of an empty row, after a hand edited file broke the display
body:
The user hand edited an old entry and removed the summary line by accident. List then printed an empty column, which looked like a bug. I reproduced it with a fixture that has front matter but no summary key.

The awk parser leaves the summary variable empty and prints it as is. Nothing crashes, but the row carries no information.

I changed list to fall back to the first non empty body line, cut to the usual width with an ellipsis. If the body is also empty it prints a marker in square brackets saying no summary.

Recall uses the same parser, so I checked what it prints. It showed the same empty summary. I applied the fallback in the shared function, so both commands behave the same.

I added two tests. One covers the body line fallback and one covers the empty body marker.

Doctor could also warn about this, since a missing summary breaks the rule that each entry has one. I added that as a warning with the file name. It does not fail the exit code.

The doctor test file gained one case for this warning. Everything passes.

I repaired the user's file by writing a summary from its body, and the warning went away.

summary: Investigated why the pane flickers on a slow terminal, found it clears the whole screen on each refresh, and switched to overwriting lines in place
body:
The user noticed flicker over a slow ssh link. I connected through a throttled local link to see it myself, and the pane visibly blanked once per refresh.

The redraw loop sent a clear screen code and then printed all lines. On a fast terminal this is invisible. On a slow link the blank frame is seen between the two.

I changed the redraw to move the cursor to the top, print each line followed by a clear to end of line code, and finally clear below the last line. The screen is never blank in between.

I had to keep the tmux fix from before in mind, where the size is read on every redraw. That still happens at the start of each loop and I kept it there.

One problem showed up: if the new content has fewer lines than the old, leftover lines remained. The clear below the last line code fixes this. I tested it by deleting entries in a fixture while the pane ran.

Long summaries that wrap were another case. The pane cuts them to the terminal width before printing, so wrapping does not happen, and I confirmed this at 40 columns.

I measured bytes sent per refresh over the throttled link. The old way sent about 2.1 KB and the new one 1.7 KB, because there is no full repaint of empty cells.

There is no automated test for terminal output of this kind. I recorded the output of one frame with script and compared the escape sequences in a Vitest case, which checks that the clear screen code is no longer used.

The pane check test from before still passes. I want the user to try it over their link.

summary: The user tried the pane over ssh and confirmed no flicker, but a stray character remained at the line end when a summary contained a wide emoji
body:
The user reported back on the pane change. Flicker is gone. They did find that one row kept a stray character on the right when the summary contained an emoji.

I reproduced it with a fixture entry containing a wide character. The cut to terminal width counted characters, but an emoji takes two columns. The line was one column too long, wrapped, and the wrapped cell stayed behind.

awk in the default locale on the laptop counts bytes unless told otherwise, so the cut was already inexact for any non ASCII text. I looked at how it behaves with accented letters. Those were cut at the right width in a UTF-8 locale but wrong in the C locale.

A complete fix needs a column width function, which POSIX tools do not have. I chose a cheap rule: cut two columns earlier than the terminal width when the line contains any byte above 127. That avoids wrapping at the price of a slightly shorter line.

I tested with accented text, an emoji and a CJK sample. None wrapped at 40 columns. The remaining difference is that the line ends a bit early.

I added the three samples as one test using a recorded frame. It checks that no line exceeds the width minus one.

I did not try to handle combining characters. They are rare in summaries.

I also noted this limitation in a code comment so a later reader does not look for a bug.

summary: Answered the user's question about whether entries from several hosts sort correctly in list, by checking the sort key and testing mixed time zones
body:
The user asked whether list orders entries from different hosts by real time or by file name. I read the list code and tested it.

Entries are sorted by the date field in the front matter, which includes the offset. The sort converts it to UTC seconds before comparing, a change from the time zone work earlier. File names are not used.

I made a fixture with three entries from hosts in three offsets, written within one hour of real time but with local times that differ by up to nine hours. List showed them in real order.

The one weak point is entries with no offset in the date. They are treated as UTC. Doctor does not warn about these, so I noted it as a possible small addition.

I answered the user with this and offered to add the doctor warning if wanted.

summary: Went through the open issues and pull requests, answered three, and labelled two as needing a reproduction before the next release
body:
Spent the afternoon on the issue tracker, which had not been looked at since the 0.7.0 tag. There were five open issues and one open pull request. I went through them in order of age.

The oldest asked whether the journal folder can be set per project. I answered with the config command and the AGENT_JOURNAL_DIR variable, and pointed to the README section on folders. The second asked for list to hide entries from other hosts. I replied that recall and export already take a host filter, and that a filter for list is a small change I would take if the reporter confirms that is what they need. The third was a question about running the CLI under dash. I ran the test suite with sh pointed at dash and it passed, so I wrote that down in the reply.

Two issues I could not act on. One says the pane shows a garbled line on a terminal with a narrow width, and the other says sync hangs when the remote asks for a password. Neither gave a shell version, a terminal name or the command used. I labelled both as needing a reproduction and asked for the output of doctor and the exact steps. I did not try to guess the cause.

The pull request fixes a typo in the Codex install text. I checked it against the plugin file, found it correct, and merged it. Nothing in the code changed today besides that line. Next is to wait for the replies on the two labelled issues before the release is planned, and to check them again before tagging.

summary: Went through the open issues and pull requests, answered three, and labelled two as needing a reproduction before the next release
body:
I read all seven open issues. Three were quick. One asked whether Windows is supported, and I answered that WSL works and native Windows does not because the CLI is POSIX sh. One was the trunk branch issue, already fixed, so I closed it with a link to the change. One was a question on where config is stored, which I answered with the path and the command to print it.

Two issues lacked enough detail. One says the pane exits on resize in a terminal I do not know. I asked for the terminal name, the shell and the output of agent-journal doctor. The other says sync overwrote local entries. I asked for the git log of the journal folder, since sync should never overwrite files and I want to see how it happened.

I labelled both as needing a reproduction. If neither gets an answer in a couple of weeks I will close them politely.

The remaining two issues are feature requests. One wants a tag field for entries. I replied that the format is meant to stay small and that search over summary and body usually covers it, but I left it open for thoughts. The other wants JSON output from list. That seems reasonable and small, so I marked it as accepted.

There was one pull request, a typo fix in the README. I merged it after checking the diff.

While reading the issues I saw two people ask about install on Linux with dash as sh. The CLI is tested with dash in CI, so that works. I added a line about it to the install section of the README.

I wrote the JSON output item in my notes with the shape I expect: one object per entry with the same keys as the front matter plus summary. It will be the next feature if nothing urgent comes up.

summary: Added list --json that prints one JSON object per line with the front matter keys and the summary, covering the accepted feature request
body:
I implemented the accepted request. The option prints one object per line, with date, project, summary, cwd, host, user, agent and session.

The hard part in awk is escaping. I wrote a function that escapes backslash, double quote, tab and control characters, and tested it with a summary containing quotes and a backslash path.

The option combines with the filters list already has, such as host and project. I checked --json with --count and kept the count as a plain number.

I added four tests, including one that pipes the output through node to parse every line. The suite passes.

The help text has a line for the option, and I added it to the list section of the README.

summary: Replied on the JSON issue with the shipped shape and checked that the completions list the new option
body:
I commented on the issue with an example line of the output and said it is in main now. The user who asked can try it by updating.

The completions are generated from the CLI through completion-words, so the new option should appear. I checked bash and zsh output and both listed --json under list.

The fish file reads the same words and also had it. No manual change was needed, which was the point of the earlier change.

I closed the issue.

summary: Wrote a plan for stable entry ids to make duplicates and references between entries safe, after two sync merge problems showed that file names are not enough
body:
Two earlier problems, the duplicate list rows and the conflict copies, came from the same weakness: an entry is identified only by its file name. I spent the session thinking through what an id would take, and wrote a plan without code.

The session field already identifies the agent run, but several entries come from one session, so it is not unique. The date plus host is almost unique, but two entries can be written in the same second by two hooks.

The option I like best is a short id made from a hash of the date, host and summary, written as an id key in the front matter. It is stable if the file is copied, and different files with the same content have the same id, which is the duplicate case.

The cost is that existing entries have no id. A migration command could add them, similar to the offset fix. Until then the CLI would compute the id on the fly when the key is missing, so nothing breaks.

Uses for the id: list could skip duplicates by id instead of comparing full content, which is faster. Doctor could find conflict copies as files with the same id. Entries could refer to others by id in the body.

Risks: the format is a public thing now, with other tools reading the files. A new optional key should not break readers that ignore unknown keys, but I cannot be sure about all readers. The README states the format, so I would document the key as optional.

Hash tools differ between systems. sha1sum exists on Linux and shasum on macOS, and POSIX has only cksum. I would use cksum to stay portable, giving a number, not a hex string. The collision chance is higher with 32 bits, but for one person's journal it is fine.

Another point is whether the agents should write the id or the CLI should. The CLI writes the file in the add path, so it can add the key and the agents do not need new rules. That keeps the Pi budget safe.

The plan has four steps: compute id in the parser, write the id in new entries, use it in list and doctor, and add the migration command. I ordered them so that each step can be released alone.

I saved the plan as a note in the repo issues folder as a draft, not in the main docs, since it may change. The user should read it before I start.

Open question I put at the end: is cksum on date, host and summary enough, or should the first body line be included? I think not, since editing the body should not change the id.

summary: The user read the id plan and approved the first two steps with cksum, but asked to hold the migration command until real use shows it is needed
body:
The user answered the plan. They agree with the cksum choice and with keeping the body out of the id.

They want only the parser step and the write step first. The list and doctor use can follow once ids exist in some entries. The migration command is on hold, since the on-the-fly computation covers old entries.

I updated the draft note with the decision and marked steps 3 and 4 as later. I also added the point that doctor should not warn about missing ids, so users are not pushed into a migration that is not needed.

I will start with the parser tomorrow morning.

summary: Implemented the id computation in the parser and writing of an id key in new entries, with the id stable when the file is copied
body:
I added a function in the awk parser that computes the id from the date, host and summary using cksum. Awk cannot call cksum directly without a pipe, so the shell computes it and passes it in for entries without the key.

To keep list fast I only run cksum for entries without an id. With a journal of 1,200 files, list took 0.9 seconds before, and with ids computed for all of them it took 3.4 seconds, since cksum starts a process per entry. That is too slow.

I changed it to compute ids lazily. The parser only needs the id when a command asks for it, and no command does yet. For now list does not compute it at all, so the speed is unchanged at 0.9 seconds.

The add path writes the key in new entries. The id is the cksum number in decimal, and I added it to the front matter right after the date line.

One issue: the same summary written twice in the same second on the same host gives the same id. That is intended, as it marks a duplicate.

I tested that copying a file keeps the id, that two different entries get different ids, and that the old entries still parse without the key. All tests pass.

The format description in the README got a line for the optional id key.

summary: Checked whether the new id key breaks the three plugins' readers, and found the Pi extension's front matter check rejects unknown keys
body:
The user's concern was other readers of the files, so I started with our own. The Claude Code and Codex hooks read only the summary and date with grep, so an extra key is harmless.

The Pi extension is written in TypeScript and parses front matter itself. It has a check that throws when a key is not in a fixed list. A new entry with an id would make it fail at session start.

I reproduced the error with a fixture entry containing an id. Pi printed 'unknown front matter key: id' and showed no recent entries.

This would have shipped broken if I had only tested the CLI. I will fix the extension in the next step and add a test that feeds it an entry with an id.

summary: Fixed the Pi extension to ignore unknown front matter keys and added a test with an id, so new keys no longer break session start
body:
I changed the Pi extension parser to skip keys it does not know instead of throwing. It still requires date and summary, since without them an entry is useless.

I weighed adding id to the fixed list. That would fix today's case but break again the next time a key is added. Ignoring unknown keys follows the same idea as the CLI.

The test feeds the extension an entry with id and another with a made up key. Both load and show their summaries. A third test with a missing date still fails, as intended.

I ran the Pi extension tests and the full suite. All pass.

The extension size grew by a few lines in code but the rules text did not change, so the budget is untouched at 81 free.

I also checked the Codex plugin with a fixture containing an id by running its start script. It prints the newest entries as before.

Nothing else read the front matter strictly. I searched the repo for the key list and found it only in the Pi code and a test helper, which I updated to match.

I added a line to the changelog under unreleased.

summary: Ran a manual check of a fresh install with entries that have ids on all three agents, and found everything loads, with one stale sentence in the README
body:
With the Pi fix in place I wanted an end to end check. I made a clean home folder, ran install.sh and wrote three entries through the add path, which now include ids.

Claude Code started a session and the hook showed the three entries. Codex did the same through its start script. For Pi I ran the extension in a test harness and it listed all three.

I then ran list, list --json, recall with one and two terms, and export. Each handled the id key. In the JSON output the id is not included yet, since list does not read it. I noted that as a small gap to fill with step 3.

Sync pushed the entries to a local bare repo and a second clone pulled them with the ids unchanged.

Doctor printed no warnings.

While in the README I found a sentence in the install section still saying the install copies files, which I had fixed once but a later merge from the typo pull request restored an older line. I fixed it again and diffed against the earlier version to be sure no other line came back.

The check is done and the id work for now is complete through steps 1 and 2.

summary: Removed the stale README sentence about entry ids and rewrote the install section paragraph so it matches what install.sh does now after the id change
body:
The manual check of a fresh install yesterday left one stale sentence in the README. It still said that entries are identified by file name only. I replaced it with two sentences saying that new entries carry an id key computed with cksum, and that the id stays the same when a file is copied.

While in the file I read the install section again line by line against install.sh. The copy step had already been fixed after the 0.7.0 tag, but the section still said the script asks before overwriting the plugin folder. It does not, it replaces the folder and prints one line. I fixed that wording too.

I ran the README check test, which runs the examples against --help, and it passed. I also looked at the rendering on GitHub in light and dark mode to be sure the new sentences did not push the badge row onto two lines. They did not.

Nothing in the CLI changed in this session. What is left is the section on sync, which does not mention ids yet. I will leave it until the migration question is decided, since the user wants to wait for real use before adding that command.

summary: Added a duplicate id check to list so that two files with the same id are marked, using the sync merge case from last week as the test fixture
body:
The id work from the last days made it possible to see duplicates, but nothing showed them yet. I added a small awk pass to list that counts ids and appends a marker to the row when an id occurs more than once. The pass only runs when list reads the full folder, so list with a limit stays as fast as before.

The fixture is built from the two files that caused the sync merge problem. They have different file names, the same body and the same id, because one was copied by hand. The test checks that both rows get the marker and that a third entry with a unique id does not.

The first version of the test failed. Entries written before the id change have no id key, and the pass treated the empty value as one shared id, so every old entry was flagged. I made the pass skip empty ids and added a second fixture with three old entries to cover it.

I also checked that list --json prints the id key when it exists and leaves it out when it does not. That was already correct. The marker is not part of the JSON output, which is deliberate, since a script can count ids itself.

The full suite passes locally, 64 tests. I did not run it on the older machine yet. The change is added to the unreleased part of the changelog. The next step is to see whether recall should hide the second copy of a duplicate, but I want the user's view on that first.

summary: Ran the test suite on the older machine after the duplicate marker change and found it passes, so the marker work is ready to be reviewed
body:
The duplicate marker in list had only been tested on the main machine. The older machine has a different sort command and an older awk, and both have caused failures before, so I ran the suite there.

All 64 tests passed on the first run. I paid attention to the new duplicate tests, since they depend on awk arrays and on the order of output. The tests already sort explicitly after the change from last week, and that is why they held.

I also ran list by hand on that machine against a copy of the real journal folder, about 400 entries. The marker appeared on the two known duplicates and nowhere else. The run took under a second.

No code changed in this session. I wrote a short note in the unreleased changelog section about the older machine check, which is the habit before each release. Next is the question to the user about recall and duplicates.

summary: Asked how recall should treat duplicate entries and wrote down the options with the cost of each, leaving the decision to the user
body:
Recall prints every matching entry, so a duplicate shows up twice and an agent may count it as two pieces of work. I looked at three options and wrote them in a note for the user.

The first is to do nothing and rely on the marker in list. It costs no code, but recall does not print the marker today, so agents would never see it. The second is to hide later copies in recall by id. It is about ten lines of awk, but a hidden entry could confuse someone who reads the folder directly and compares counts. The third is to print the marker in recall and let the agent decide. It is simple and honest, but it spends a little of the agent's attention on every duplicate.

I measured how common the problem is. In the real journal there are exactly two duplicate pairs, both from the sync merge problem, and both were fixed by deleting a file. So the case is rare.

My recommendation was option three, only if duplicates come back. For now I suggested option one. The user has not answered yet, and I changed no code.

summary: The user chose to leave recall alone for duplicates, so I closed the note and started the Codex plugin skeleton with its session start hook
body:
The user answered the duplicate question this morning: leave recall as it is, revisit if it happens again. I added one line to the notes file saying so and moved on to the next planned item, the Codex plugin.

The Claude Code plugin has hooks and a settings entry. Codex works differently, as it reads an AGENTS.md style file and has no hook at session start in the same sense. I started with the folder layout under plugins/codex: one rules file generated from the same source as the Claude Code rules, and a small install step that places it.

The rules source is a single file today. I split it into a shared part and a short header per agent, and wrote a build step in the install script that joins them. The shared part carries all wording about recall and entries, so a fix to the rules reaches all three agents at once.

The first install test failed, because the join step added a blank line at the top and the Claude Code rules test compared the file byte by byte. I changed the join to print the header first without a leading newline and the test passed again.

I ran a short Codex session by hand in a scratch folder. It found the rules file and wrote an entry with the right front matter, including the id. The agent field said codex, which is correct.

What is left is the check that Codex reads the rules when the journal folder is not in the working directory, and a test for the install step. I also need to find how Codex passes the session identifier, since the session key in the front matter was empty in my scratch run.

summary: Found how Codex exposes its session identifier and filled the session key in entries, after the scratch run had written it empty
body:
The empty session key in the Codex entries came from the CLI reading an environment variable that Claude Code sets and Codex does not. I looked at what Codex provides in its environment during a run and printed all variables that contain the word session.

Codex sets one variable with a thread identifier. I confirmed it stays the same during a single run and changes between runs, which is what the key needs. I added it to the lookup list in bin/agent-journal, after the Claude Code variable, so the first one that exists wins.

The lookup was a single if line. I turned it into a small loop over a list of names, since Pi will need its own entry soon. The loop is plain POSIX sh, with no arrays, and checks each name with eval and a quoted default. I tested it with dash as well as bash to be sure.

Tests: I added three cases that set one variable at a time and check the written key, plus one case with none set that expects the key to be written empty without an error. All passed. The old test that sets both variables still shows the Claude Code value.

I also ran a real Codex session and wrote two entries. Both had the same session key, and the id values differed, as they should.

One open point is that the Codex variable name is not documented anywhere I could find, so it may change. I put a comment above the loop with the observed name and the version of Codex I used. The next step is the install test for the Codex plugin folder and the check of reading the rules from another working directory.

summary: Added the install test for the Codex plugin and confirmed that its rules are read from a working directory outside the journal folder
body:
Two things were left from the Codex skeleton, and I did both. The first was an install test. It runs install.sh with a temporary home directory, then checks that the Codex rules file exists, that it starts with the Codex header, and that the shared part is identical to the one in the Claude Code rules.

The second was the working directory check. I started Codex in an unrelated project folder with the temporary home and asked it what it knows about past work. It read the rules file and ran the recall command with a term, so the rules reach it without the journal being the current directory.

The answer was right, but it ran recall twice with the same term. I looked at the rules and saw that the sentence about reading by period is placed before the one about terms, which may lead the agent to try both. I did not change it yet, since this is one run and not a pattern. I noted it for the eval later in this phase.

The install test passed in under a second. I ran the whole suite and it passed with 67 tests, three new ones for the session lookup and one for the install.

In the notes I listed what the Codex plugin still lacks: an uninstall path, and a line in the README. Neither is urgent.

summary: Added an uninstall path for the Codex plugin that removes its rules file and leaves the journal folder alone
body:
The install script could place the Codex rules file but nothing removed it. I added an uninstall option that deletes only the rules file and the plugin folder, and prints what it removed. It never touches the journal folder, and I put a test for that: the folder with three entries is still there afterwards with the same checksums.

Running it twice prints that nothing was found the second time and exits with zero, which is what a person would expect. The test suite passes. The README line is still open.

summary: Wrote the README section for the Codex plugin and checked its install and uninstall commands against the script output
body:
The Codex plugin worked and had tests, but the README did not mention it. I wrote a section that sits after the Claude Code one and keeps the same structure: what it installs, where, and how to remove it.

I ran each command from the section in a temporary home to be sure the text matched the output. The install prints two lines, and the README first said three. I corrected the README instead of the script, since two lines is clearer.

The README check test runs the code examples against --help, but install and uninstall are not in --help in full. I extended the check so that it also looks for the option names in the help text. It found that the uninstall option was missing from the help, because I added it to the script and forgot the usage text. I added it there.

I looked at the README top to bottom again. The badge row still has three badges, the install section is correct, and the screenshots are unchanged. The pull warning line shows in the pane screenshot, as before.

One wording problem: the intro says the tool supports Claude Code and Pi, and Codex was missing. I fixed the sentence and the same sentence in the repository description text file. The README check passes and the suite is green with 68 tests.

Next is the Pi extension, which needs a different approach again, since it is code that runs inside the agent and not a rules file.

summary: Read how Pi extensions load and sketched the extension layout, deciding to keep the logic in the CLI and make the extension a thin wrapper
body:
Before writing any Pi code I read the extension documentation and two small example extensions. An extension is a module that registers hooks on events like session start and can add text to the system prompt.

My decision is to keep all logic in the CLI. The extension should call bin/agent-journal for the rules text and for the pane content and do nothing else. This way a fix in the CLI reaches Pi without a second implementation, and the tests that run the CLI stay the main safety net.

I sketched the layout: plugins/pi/index.ts with one function for session start, a package file, and the shared rules joined in the same way as for Codex. The extension needs to find the CLI, so it reads the path from the environment first and falls back to the one on the PATH.

I wrote down two risks. A call into the CLI at session start costs time, and I saw last week on the slow mount that this can reach seconds. The second risk is that the extension runs in the agent's process, so a crash would be more serious than a bad rules file. I will wrap the call in a try block and a short timeout.

No code written yet. The next step is the first working version with the session start only.

summary: Built the first Pi extension that adds the rules at session start through the CLI, with a timeout and a fallback when the call fails
body:
I wrote plugins/pi/index.ts following the sketch from the last entry. It registers one handler for session start. The handler runs the CLI with the rules subcommand, takes the output and appends it to the system prompt.

The call uses a child process with a timeout of two seconds. If the call fails or times out, the handler adds nothing and writes one line to the Pi log. I decided against a retry, because a slow start is worse than a missing rules block, and the next session will try again anyway.

The first run showed that the rules were added twice. Pi fires the session start event again after a resume, and my handler appended each time. I added a flag on the session object so the rules are added once per session. After that a resumed session had one block.

I tested by hand in a scratch folder. A new session wrote an entry after a small task, with agent pi, the id, and the session key. The session key took a moment: Pi gives its identifier through the extension context and not through the environment, so I passed it to the CLI by setting the variable in the child process. That fits the loop from the Codex work well, as I only added one name.

Tests: the extension itself is TypeScript, and the project tests run the CLI. I added a Vitest file that imports the handler with a fake context and a fake CLI script. It checks the single block, the timeout path, and the session variable. The three cases pass.

I ran oxlint and oxfmt on the new file. Oxlint complained about an unused import and a floating promise, both fixed. Oxfmt changed the quotes only.

What is left: the pane for Pi, an install step, and a README section. I also want to measure the start cost on the slow mount again.

summary: Added the Pi install step and measured session start on the slow mount, getting 0.5 seconds with the extension against 0.4 without it
body:
The extension worked from a checkout but there was no way to install it. I added a Pi branch to install.sh that copies the extension folder into the Pi extensions directory of the user and prints one line. The uninstall option from the Codex work now handles Pi as well, with the same rule that the journal folder is never touched.

The install test follows the Codex one: temporary home, run, check that index.ts and the package file exist, run uninstall, check they are gone. I also added a case for running install twice, which must replace the folder without leaving old files. A deleted file in the source used to survive in the target, so I switched from copying into the folder to removing the folder first.

Then the measurement. I used the slow network mount from the earlier hook review and ran ten session starts with and without the extension. The average was 0.5 seconds with it and 0.4 without. The extra tenth of a second is the child process start, which I think is acceptable. The worst run was 0.7.

I also tried the timeout by making the CLI sleep for five seconds. The extension gave up after two seconds, logged the line and the session started without rules. That matches the intent.

One more check: front matter with the id key written by Pi is read by list and recall in the same way as the other agents. I wrote two entries and listed them. Both rows were correct.

The suite passes with 74 tests. The README section for Pi comes next, and the pane for Pi is still open as a decision.

summary: Wrote the README section for the Pi extension and updated the intro line to name all three agents
body:
With install and uninstall working, I added the Pi section to the README. It follows the Codex one, with what is installed, where, how it fails safely, and the removal command. I mentioned the two second timeout, since it explains why rules may be missing on a very slow mount.

I ran each command from a temporary home and compared the text. The README check test passes, and the help text lists all options. The intro now names Claude Code, Codex and Pi in that order.

summary: Started the recall command by writing the term search in awk over the front matter summary and the body, with case folding and a result limit
body:
Recall is the part that agents use most, so I started with the simplest version that is useful: search by terms. The command takes one or more terms and prints the entries that contain them, newest first, with a limit of 20 by default.

The parser already splits front matter and body in awk. I added a filter that lowercases each file once and checks every term with index, which avoids regular expressions and the quoting trouble that comes with them. A term with special characters such as a dot or a bracket therefore matches literally.

The output per entry is the date, the project, the summary and the path, and with an option the whole body. I kept the format the same as list so that agents learn only one shape.

I tested it against the fixtures. Cases: one term that matches in the summary only, one that matches in the body only, a term with different case, a term with a dot, and a term that matches nothing, which prints a line saying so and exits with zero. A missing term prints the usage and exits with two.

The first run was slow on the real journal, 1.8 seconds for 400 entries, because the awk program was started once per file. I changed it to read all files in one awk call and keep a per file state keyed on FILENAME. The time fell to 0.2 seconds.

The order was wrong in one case: entries from different hosts with different time zones. I reused the sort key from list, which handles that, and the test with mixed zones passed.

What is left is reading by period, so that an agent can ask for the entries of last week, and the rules text that tells agents when to use which.

summary: Added reading by period to recall with since and until options that accept relative words like 7d and 2w
body:
The second half of recall is reading entries by period. I added since and until options. They accept a number with d or w, such as 7d or 2w, and a plain date for those who want one. The relative form is turned into a date with date arithmetic that works on both GNU and BSD date, which needed two code paths.

Tests cover 7d, 2w, an until before since, which gives a clear error, and a bad value. All pass, and the suite is at 82 tests.

summary: Wrote the recall rules for the agents, telling them to search by terms first and read by period only when asked for a time span
body:
The CLI part of recall was done, but agents need to know when to call it. I added a short block to the shared rules: use terms when the question names a topic, use since and until when it names a time span, and answer from what the entries say without guessing.

I ran the same three questions on Claude Code and Codex. Both used terms for the topic questions and period for the last-week question. Codex once ran two searches for a topic question, which I will watch in the eval. The rules block adds nine lines to the session start text.

summary: Built a first eval for the recall rules with eight questions and known answers, and ran it on Claude Code with seven of eight right
body:
To know whether the recall rules work, I needed more than a few hand questions. I wrote a small eval folder with a fixture journal of 30 entries and eight questions, each with a known answer and a note on which entries hold it.

The questions mix kinds: a lookup by topic, a count of entries in a period, a question about the reason for a decision, a question whose answer is not in the journal, and a question where two entries disagree because the later one corrects the earlier one. The last two are the ones where agents tend to fail, so I wanted them in from the start.

The runner starts the agent in a temporary home with the fixture journal, asks the question, and saves the final answer to a file. I check the answers by hand for now, since automatic checking of free text needs more care than I want to put in today.

Results on Claude Code: seven of eight right. The wrong one was the correction case, where it answered with the earlier value and did not see the later entry. It had searched with one term and the later entry used a different word for the same thing. That is a fair failure and not a bug in the rules, though the rules could say to read the newest matching entry first.

I also ran the unanswerable question. The agent said that the journal has nothing about it, which is the right behavior.

The run took about nine minutes. I saved the answers in the eval folder with the rules version, so that a later run can be compared. The Codex run is next, and I will check the correction case there with attention.

summary: Ran the eval on Codex and got six of eight, with a repeated search and a wrong count in the period question
body:
I ran the same eight questions on Codex with the fixture journal. It answered six correctly.

The first miss was the count question. It asked for the entries of the last two weeks and counted eleven, where the right answer is nine. I read its transcript: it used recall with since 2w, which is correct, but the output includes two entries from exactly two weeks ago by the cutoff time, and the fixture was built relative to the current time of the run. So part of this is the fixture and not the agent. I changed the fixture so that no entry lies near a boundary.

The second miss was the correction case, the same one that Claude Code missed. Both agents failed in the same way, which makes me think the rules should say it. I wrote a candidate sentence: when entries disagree, trust the newest and say that an earlier one differed.

I also saw the repeated search from before. Codex ran two searches with the same term on three questions. The cost is small, but it points at the order of the rules text. I moved the sentence about terms above the one about periods and left everything else.

I have not rerun after the edit. I want to change only one thing at a time, so the next run will test the rules sentence with the fixture fix, and the order change after that.

Summary of the state: Claude Code seven, Codex six, the fixture fixed, one rules sentence and one reorder pending.

summary: Added the newest-entry sentence to the recall rules and reran the eval, getting eight of eight on Claude Code and seven of eight on Codex
body:
I added the sentence about disagreeing entries to the shared rules: trust the newest entry, and mention that an earlier one said something different. I did not do the reordering yet, to test only one change.

Claude Code now answered all eight correctly, including the correction case, where it quoted both entries and named the newer one as the answer. Codex answered seven. Its correction answer was right, and the remaining miss was the question about a reason for a decision. It gave a reason that is plausible but not in the entries. I checked the fixture to be sure and the real reason is in the body of one entry, while the summary says something shorter.

That miss suggests that agents rely on the summary and do not always open the body. The recall output without the body option prints only the summary, so the agent needs to ask for more. I considered making the body the default, but that would make every search long, so I rather added a sentence to the rules: for questions about why, read the body.

I have not tested that sentence yet. The runs take about nine minutes each, and I stopped for the evening after two.

The saved answers are in the eval folder with the rules version number. The next steps are the why sentence, then the reordering test on Codex.

summary: Tested the why sentence on Codex and got eight of eight, then checked that the other agents were not harmed by the longer rules text
body:
I added the sentence about reading the body for why questions and ran the eval on Codex. It answered all eight, and in the reason question it called recall with the body option and quoted the real reason from the entry.

Then I checked the cost of the longer rules. The shared block is now 14 lines for recall, up from 9 earlier. The session start text grew by about 400 characters in total. On the slow mount that makes no measurable difference, since the cost there is the file reads and not the text.

I reran Claude Code as well to make sure the new sentence did not hurt it. It stayed at eight of eight. I also ran it on Pi with the extension and the same fixture. Pi answered seven, missing the unanswerable question by giving a guess instead of saying the journal had nothing. That is a new failure and I do not know yet if it comes from the model or from the rules. I will run it two more times to see whether it repeats.

I did not do the reordering of the terms and period sentences. With eight of eight on two agents, there is no evidence it matters, and moving text around without a reason can change things that work.

I wrote the results in a table in the eval notes: agent, rules version, score, and a short note for each miss. The repeat runs for Pi are the next step, and then the README needs a paragraph on how the eval works.

summary: Repeated the Pi eval twice and the unanswerable question was answered correctly both times, so the single miss looks like noise
body:
Yesterday Pi gave a guess for the question that the journal cannot answer. I ran the eval twice more on Pi to see if that repeats.

Both runs answered eight of eight. In the unanswerable question, the agent searched with two different terms, found nothing and said the journal holds nothing about it. That is the wanted behavior. I looked at the transcript of the earlier miss and saw that it searched once with a term that matched an unrelated entry, then built an answer from that entry. A bad first search is a plausible cause, and a single case does not call for a rules change.

Still, I wrote a note about it in the eval folder, so that if it comes back I have the example. I also added the unanswerable question a second variant, with a topic that is closer to real entries, since the current one is far from anything in the fixture and is easy.

The new variant is a question about a database that the project never used. The fixture has an entry that mentions a database in another context. I ran it on all three agents. Claude Code and Pi both answered correctly that the journal says nothing about it. Codex answered with the other context and did not say that it was a different thing. So that is a real weakness and a better test than the first one.

I left the rules as they are and wrote the Codex miss down as the first item for the next round. Today's changes are the new fixture variant and the notes. The suite passes, 82 tests, and oxlint and oxfmt are clean. The README paragraph on the eval remains to be written.

summary: Checked that the longer recall rules did not slow session start on Claude Code, and the added text costs under 10 ms on the slow mount
body:
The recall rules grew by three sentences over the last two days, so I measured session start again. I ran the start hook 20 times on the slow mount before and after the change. The median went from 0.41 to 0.42 seconds, which is inside the noise.

I also counted the size of the rules text that the agent receives. It is now 2.1 KB, up from 1.7 KB. That is still small next to what the agent loads from other sources.

I wrote the numbers into the notes file next to the eval results. Nothing needs to change. The next step is to look at how recall prints long summaries, because the eval showed one answer that was cut at the result limit.

summary: Recall printed summaries cut at 80 characters, which hid the point of long ones, so it now prints the whole summary on one line
body:
While reading the eval transcripts I saw that Codex had misread one result because recall cut the summary at 80 characters. The cut was a leftover from the first draft of the term search in awk. It made sense when the output also had the file name, but it no longer does.

I removed the cut in bin/agent-journal and kept the file name on its own column. The summary limit of 200 characters from the format already keeps lines bounded. I checked the output width with the longest summary in the test fixtures, and it came to 214 characters with the date.

I added a Vitest case that searches for a term in a long summary and expects the full text. The existing recall tests still pass, 31 of 31. I did not touch the period reading, since it uses the same printer and got the fix for free.

One open point is that terminals wrap these lines. I left that to the terminal for now.

summary: Added a no-match message to recall so an empty search says what was searched, after an agent took silence for a failure
body:
In one eval run an agent saw empty output from recall and retried the search four times with the same terms. Silence looks like a crash. I changed recall to print a line on stderr when nothing matches, naming the terms and the period.

The line reads: no entries match 'term' since 30d. It goes to stderr so that scripts reading stdout are not affected, and the exit status stays 0. I considered exit status 1 like grep, but agents tend to treat a nonzero status as an error and then retry, which is the thing I wanted to avoid.

I added two tests, one for a miss with terms and one for a miss with only a period. Both check stdout is empty and stderr has the message. The recall rules now say that an empty result means the journal has no such entry, so the agent should say so.

I will rerun the eval for Codex tomorrow to see if the repeated searches are gone.

summary: Reran the recall eval on Codex after the no-match message and got eight of eight with no repeated searches
body:
I ran the eight-question eval on Codex three times. The first run scored eight of eight. The second also scored eight, and the third seven, where one count in the period question was off by one.

The unanswerable question used to cause the repeated searches. In all three runs the agent searched once, saw the no-match line and answered that the journal has nothing on it. That is the behaviour I wanted from the change of yesterday.

The count miss comes from an entry on the boundary of the since window. Recall includes entries from exactly 7d ago, and the agent counted it out. I will not change the rules for one miss in three, but I noted the boundary in the eval file as a known risky question.

The results are saved next to the older runs, so the history of scores is in one place.

summary: Wrote a plan for better README pictures, comparing screenshots of the CLI with a scripted recording and deciding what to try first
body:
The README still has no pictures. I wrote a short plan in the notes before trying anything. The goal is that a reader sees what a journal entry looks like and what recall prints, in under ten seconds.

The options I listed were plain terminal screenshots, a recording from a scripted tool, and a text block in the README with real output. The text block is the cheapest and always sharp, but it does not show the flow. Screenshots are sharp but static. A recording would show the flow, but I have not tried any recording tool yet, so I could not say how it looks at the sizes GitHub shows. I left it as a later option to test once the screenshots exist.

I decided to take two screenshots first: one of list and one of recall with a term. They need a clean theme, a fixed width of 90 columns and a fixed font size so that they match.

I also wrote down what the fixtures must contain so the output looks real: six entries over three projects, with believable summaries. The existing test fixtures are too short for that.

Nothing was changed in the repository yet. The plan is only in the notes file, and the user can read it before I start.

summary: Built a demo journal folder with six realistic entries in three projects, to be used for README pictures
body:
For the README pictures I needed a folder with entries that look like real work. I created demo/journal with six files across three projects named api, site and tools. Each has the full front matter with a fake host and user.

The summaries follow the format rules, one sentence of 80 to 180 characters that stands alone. For example one says a slow query was fixed by an index and the page went from 900 ms to 120 ms. I kept the bodies to two short paragraphs.

I wrote a small script, demo/setup.sh, that copies the folder to a temporary directory and sets the journal path variable to it. That way no picture shows my real journal.

I ran list and recall against the demo folder to check the output. The list shows the six entries in order and recall with the term index finds exactly one. The ids are computed from content, so they are stable between runs.

I did not commit demo yet because the user may want different example text.

summary: Took screenshots of list and recall on the demo journal and put the list screenshot in the README, with the recall one held back for a text fix
body:
I used the demo journal from yesterday and set the terminal to 90 columns with a 16 point font. The theme was the light one, since GitHub shows the README on white by default. I took two screenshots with the system tool, one for list and one for recall index.

The list screenshot looked fine. I saved it as docs/list.png at 1800 pixels wide so that it stays sharp on high density screens, and it is 84 KB. I added it to the README under the intro paragraph with alt text that describes the output.

The recall screenshot showed a problem. The summary of the first result wrapped onto a second line, and the wrap broke the column of file names. Since the full summary is printed now, long ones wrap at 90 columns.

I tried 110 columns, which fixed the wrap, but then the picture is too small on a phone. I tried shortening the demo summary instead, and that is a cheat I do not like, because real summaries are long.

I decided to keep the recall picture out for now. The README has a text block with the same output as a stopgap. That block is accurate, I copied it from the terminal.

I also checked how the README looks in dark mode on GitHub. The white screenshot has a visible edge there. That is a theme question that I noted for later.

Next step is to ask the user whether the wrap is acceptable or whether recall should print the file name on its own line above the summary.

summary: The user preferred recall output with the file name on its own line, so I changed the printer and retook the recall screenshot
body:
I asked the user about the wrapping in the recall screenshot. The answer was to put the file name on its own line above the summary, because that reads better for both people and agents. It also stops a long summary from pushing the name away.

I changed the printer in bin/agent-journal. Each result now has two lines: the name with the date, then the summary indented by two spaces, and a blank line between results. The period reading uses the same printer, so it changed too.

Seven Vitest cases compared the old layout and failed. I updated their expected output and added one case with a summary of 190 characters. All 34 tests pass now.

The agents only read this output, so I checked the recall rules for any mention of the old layout. There was none. I ran two questions of the eval on Claude Code and both were right.

Then I retook the recall screenshot at 90 columns. The long summary still wraps, but the wrap is clean under an indented line, and no column breaks. It is 91 KB.

I added it to the README under the recall section and removed the stopgap text block. The README now has both pictures in the light theme. The dark theme edge remains as a note.

summary: Reviewed the README top to bottom and made a list of nine fixes, including an outdated install command and two badges that point to the wrong workflow
body:
I read the README as a new visitor would, from the first line to the last. The goal was a list of problems, not fixes yet. I found nine.

The install section shows a curl command with a path that was renamed during the Codex work. The command still works because of a redirect, but it will break if the redirect is dropped. The CI badge points to a workflow file named test.yml, and the workflow is called ci.yml now. The second broken one is the license badge, which links to a page that does not exist.

The intro names all three agents, which is good. The section on Claude Code is longer than the others and has a paragraph on hooks that belongs in a separate doc. The Pi section lacks the uninstall command that the Codex section has.

There are two places where the text says sync pushes on every entry, but it only pushes when the hook runs at session end. That is wrong in a way that would surprise users.

The remaining items are small: a typo in the config section, a code block without a language, and a table of commands that misses recall.

I ordered the list by how much each one misleads a reader. The install command and the sync sentences come first. I saved it as notes/readme-review.md.

I did not edit the README in this session. The next one will fix the first four, which are the ones that are factually wrong.

summary: Fixed the four wrong statements in the README: install path, CI badge, license badge and the sync description
body:
I worked through the top of yesterday's list. The install command now uses the current script path, so it does not depend on a redirect. I ran it in a clean shell to confirm that it fetches and runs.

The CI badge now points to ci.yml and shows the status of the main branch. The license badge links to the LICENSE file in the repository. I opened both in the preview to check that they render.

The sync sentences were corrected in both places. They now say that the journal is pushed when a session ends, and that sync can be run by hand at any time. I checked this against the hook in the Claude Code plugin.

The remaining five items stay in the review notes. I marked the four as done there.

summary: Wrote a design for a dark theme variant of the README pictures, after the white screenshots showed a hard edge on GitHub's dark mode
body:
The screenshots in the README are on a white background and look like a pasted box in the dark mode of GitHub. A reader on dark mode sees the edge and the contrast is harsh. I looked at what could be done without extra tools.

GitHub supports the picture element with a prefers-color-scheme media query in README files. That means I can give two images, one for light and one for dark, and the browser picks. It also supports the fragment suffixes #gh-light-mode-only and #gh-dark-mode-only on image links, which is the older way.

I prefer the picture element, because it is standard HTML and works outside GitHub too. The older fragments only work on GitHub. The cost is that the markup is longer, five lines for each image instead of one.

So each picture needs two files. That makes four images for the two screenshots: list-light, list-dark, recall-light and recall-dark. At about 90 KB each, the total is under 400 KB, which is fine for the repository.

The terminal must be set up the same way for both. I wrote down the settings: 90 columns, 16 point font, the same demo journal, and the same window size. Only the theme changes. If any setting differs, the pictures will jump when the reader switches theme.

I also thought about naming. I chose names like docs/img/list-light.png, and the existing two files would move there later.

One risk is that the dark screenshots go out of date when the output changes, since they are taken by hand. A script that takes them would help, but I have not chosen a tool for that. I wrote down that I should test a few tools for screenshots of text. Recordings are a separate question that I have not looked at yet.

I did not change any files besides the notes. The plan needs the user to confirm that four images are acceptable. I will ask in the next session.

summary: The user approved four images for the README and I took the dark theme screenshots of list and recall
body:
The user read the design and approved four images, with the condition that the markup stays readable in the raw README. I used a compact form of the picture element with one source line and the light image as the fallback.

I switched the terminal to the dark theme and kept the other settings from the notes. The window size and the 90 column width matched. I took the list and recall screenshots from the demo journal.

The dark list image is 79 KB and the dark recall image is 86 KB. I compared them next to the light ones, and the line breaks fall in the same place, so the page does not jump when the theme changes.

I moved the files to docs/img with the names from the plan and fixed the two existing README references. Then I put in the picture elements. In the GitHub preview, the light mode showed the light images. When I switched my preview to dark, it showed the dark ones.

The raw markup is five lines per image. It is acceptable to the user. I committed the four images and the README change in one commit.

summary: Added a script that checks the README for broken relative links and image paths, and it found two dead links
body:
After moving the images I wanted a check that catches dead paths in the README. I wrote test/readme-links.test.js, a Vitest test that reads README.md, finds markdown links and image sources and picture srcset values, and checks that each relative path exists.

The pattern for links is a simple regex. It skips anything that starts with http, mailto or a hash. For the rest it strips a fragment and checks the file with the file system. A broken path fails the test with its line number.

On the first run it failed with two paths. One was a link to docs/hooks.md, which was never created. The text promised the file in the Claude Code section. The other was a link to the old image location, in the changelog part of the README, which I missed when moving files.

I fixed the image path. For the hooks link, I decided to write the short doc instead of removing the link, since the review had said that the hooks paragraph belongs elsewhere.

The new docs/hooks.md has the three hooks of the Claude Code plugin: session start, the prompt hook and the session end. It says what each runs and how long it may take. I moved the paragraph from the README and left one sentence with the link.

I also noticed that the test checks srcset only when it is on a single line. My picture markup has it on one line, so it works, but I wrote a comment about the limit.

The test took 12 ms. The full suite has 35 tests and passes. This also finishes the item about the long Claude Code section from the review.

Remaining from the review: the Pi uninstall command, the typo in the config section, the code block language and the command table.

summary: Finished the last four README review items: Pi uninstall command, config typo, code block language and recall in the command table
body:
I took the four remaining items from the review notes. For the Pi section, I ran the uninstall step from install.sh and copied the exact command that it prints. It removes the extension file and leaves the journal folder, just as for Codex.

The typo in the config section was a doubled word in the sentence about the host key. I fixed it. One code block had no language and I set it to sh.

The command table listed list, sync, config and install but not recall. I added a row with the two usage forms, terms and since or until.

The link test passes and the suite is green. All nine items from the review are now done, and I closed the notes file.

summary: Investigated why list shows the wrong time for entries written near midnight in a zone with a half hour offset, and traced it to integer division in awk
body:
The user reported that an entry written at 23:40 local time showed as the next day in list when the zone was Asia/Kolkata. Other zones looked right. I reproduced it with TZ set to that zone and a fixture entry.

The list command converts the stored time to the zone of the reader. The conversion code in awk computes the offset in hours as an integer and then adds it to the hour of the entry. A zone with plus 5:30 gave 5, so the result was 30 minutes off, and entries after 18:30 UTC were placed on the wrong side of midnight.

I checked the older fixtures. They used whole-hour zones only, which is why the tests never caught it. The code was written during the time zone work, and no one had a half hour zone in the tests.

The fix is to compute the offset in minutes. I parse the sign, hours and minutes from the zone string, convert to total minutes, add to the minute count of the day, and carry over into the date with the existing day arithmetic.

There is a second case. Nepal has plus 5:45. I tested it by hand and it worked after the change. I also tried a negative half hour zone, Newfoundland at minus 3:30, and found a bug in the carry: going back before midnight used a modulo that gives a negative result in awk.

I fixed that with an explicit add of 1440 and a second modulo. Then I wrote the tests: Kolkata, Kathmandu, Newfoundland and UTC, each with an entry just before and just after midnight. That is eight cases.

All eight pass and the old time zone tests are still green. The suite now has 43 tests.

I also searched the code for other places that divide the offset. The recall command prints dates in UTC and does not convert, so it is not affected. The pane in the Claude Code plugin calls list, so it gets the fix.

I have not written the release note yet. The fix should be mentioned in the next release.

summary: Replied to the time zone issue with the cause and the fix, and noted that recall prints UTC dates on purpose
body:
The report came from a user who opened an issue, so I wrote a reply. It says that the offset was truncated to whole hours, that zones with half hour offsets were affected, and that the fix is in main with tests for three such zones.

The reporter also asked why recall shows different dates from list. I explained that recall prints UTC dates because agents compare them with the entry front matter, which is stored in UTC. Converting there would make the date differ from the file. I said that this is a choice and that a flag could be added if people want it.

I did not promise the flag. I added a line to the ideas file about a zone option for recall, with the reasoning, so it is not lost.

I asked the reporter to confirm after the next release. I left the issue open until then.

I also checked that the README says recall uses UTC. It did not. I added one sentence to the recall section.

summary: Started the sync conflict work by reproducing a push rejection when two machines add entries, and found the hook gives up silently
body:
The user works on two machines and twice saw that entries from one did not appear on the other. I set up a test with a bare repository and two clones to reproduce it.

I added an entry in clone A and pushed. In clone B I added another entry and ran sync. The push was rejected as non fast-forward, and the sync command printed nothing and exited 0. That is the problem: the failure is silent.

Looking at the code, sync runs git push with output sent to /dev/null, to keep the session end hook quiet. The exit status is ignored, because a failing hook should not block the agent from finishing.

The right behaviour has two parts. First, sync should pull with rebase before pushing, since entries are separate files and conflicts are rare. Second, if the push still fails, sync should say so on stderr and exit with 1 when run by hand.

I looked at the pull step. Entries have unique names with the date and a short id, so two machines almost never write the same file. The ids from the earlier work make this safer. A rebase should then apply cleanly.

The cases that remain are an edited old entry on both machines and a missing network. For edits, I will stop and report instead of guessing. For network errors, I will report and leave the files alone.

I wrote a Vitest case for the reproduction with the two clones, using temporary directories. It currently fails, which is what I want before the fix. It takes 0.6 seconds because of the git calls.

No code change in bin/agent-journal yet. The next session will do the pull step and the error message.

summary: Made sync pull with rebase before pushing and report failures, so the two clone test passes and silent loss no longer happens
body:
I implemented the plan from the last session. Sync now runs git pull --rebase with the autostash option off, then git push. Output is kept in a variable and shown only when a step fails.

On failure, sync prints the failing step and the last lines of git output to stderr and exits with 1. The session end hook calls sync with a flag named quiet, which keeps the exit status 0 but still writes the message to a log file in the journal folder, named .sync.log. That keeps the agent from being blocked and still leaves a trace.

The two clone test passes now. A has pushed, B pulls with rebase, its entry goes on top, and the push succeeds. Both clones have both entries.

I added three more cases. The first is a conflict from an edited file on both sides, where sync should stop with exit 1 and leave the rebase aborted so the working tree is clean. I had to add git rebase --abort in that path. The second is a missing remote, where sync should report that the remote is unreachable. The third checks the quiet flag writes the log and exits 0.

The abort step mattered. Without it the repository stayed in the middle of a rebase, and the next session start would have shown odd output. I found that by running the conflict case by hand first.

The suite has 47 tests and passes, taking 5.1 seconds in total. The sync tests are the slowest part.

I looked at the Claude Code hook and the Codex hook and both call sync with the quiet flag already, because they share the line from the plugin template. Pi uses the CLI too.

The README says sync pushes when a session ends. I added a sentence about the log file and how to read it.

What is left is to try this on the real second machine, because the test only uses local paths. I will do that tomorrow and watch the log.

summary: Tried the new sync on the real second machine and found it works, with one slow pull of 3 seconds over the hotel network
body:
I ran sync by hand on the second machine, which has entries that the first one never had. The pull rebased them in and the push succeeded. Both journals show the same list afterward.

The quiet hook also worked at the end of a Claude Code session. The log file had no new lines, which is right because nothing failed. To test the failure path, I turned off the network and ended another session. The log got one line saying the remote was unreachable, and the agent finished normally.

The pull took 3 seconds on the slow network. The hook runs after the agent finishes, so the delay is not seen in the session, but I want a timeout so a hung network cannot keep the shell open. I added it to the list for the next session.

summary: Added a 10 second timeout to the git calls in sync so a hung network cannot keep the session end hook open
body:
Following the slow pull, I added a timeout. POSIX sh has no portable timeout command, and macOS does not ship one. I looked at using git config settings instead, and set http.lowSpeedLimit to 1000 and http.lowSpeedTime to 10 for the sync calls through the -c option.

For ssh remotes those settings do not apply, so I added ConnectTimeout=10 through GIT_SSH_COMMAND when the user has not set it already. If the variable is set, I leave it alone.

I tested with a remote that accepts the connection and then does nothing, using a small listener from nc. Sync gave up after about 10 seconds and logged the failure. Without the setting it hung for over a minute before I stopped it.

I added a test for the ssh option logic only, checking that the command string is built and respected when already set. The hang itself is not tested, because it would make the suite slow.

The suite has 49 tests and is green. I wrote the timeout value in the README next to the log file sentence.

The sync work is complete as planned. I will check the log file on both machines in a week.

summary: Wrote the plan for journal pane improvements, listing what the pane shows today and three changes the user asked for
body:
The user asked for changes to the journal pane in the Claude Code plugin, which shows the latest entries. Before touching it I wrote down what it does now.

Today the pane calls list with a limit of five and prints the date, the project and the summary. It refreshes when a new entry is written, through the hook. It does not mark entries from the current session, and it cuts summaries at the width of the pane without any sign.

The user wants three things. First, entries of the current session should be marked, so it is clear what the agent has just written. Second, a cut summary should end with an ellipsis. Third, the pane should show the agent name, since three agents write to the same journal.

For the first change, the list command has the session key in the front matter, so the pane can compare it with the current session identifier. The hook has the identifier in an environment variable, so no new CLI option is needed, but the comparison is easier inside list with a flag named mark-session. I prefer the flag, because the logic stays in the CLI and the plugins stay thin, as decided for Pi.

For the second change, the cut happens in the pane script with cut -c. It needs a length check first, and the ellipsis should count in the width. That is a small awk step.

For the third, the agent key is already in the front matter, and list --json prints it. The pane could use the json output, but parsing it in sh is awkward. A plain text column is simpler, so I will add the agent as a short column in the normal list output only when a flag asks for it.

I estimated the work at two sessions, with tests in Vitest for the flags. The pane script itself has no tests and I will check it by hand.

The order will be the flags first, then the pane. I wrote this in notes/pane-plan.md and the user can read it.

summary: Added the mark-session flag to list, which prefixes entries of the given session with an asterisk, with tests for match and no match
body:
I started with the first change from the pane plan. The list command now accepts mark-session followed by a session id. Entries whose session key equals it get an asterisk in front, and the others get a space, so the columns stay aligned.

The comparison is done in the awk part that already reads the front matter. I added the id as a variable passed with -v and compare it when the session key line is parsed. Empty ids never match, since entries written by a scratch run can have an empty session key, as happened with Codex earlier.

The tests cover three cases: a match, no match, and an empty id with an empty key. All pass.

The completions list the new option, and the help text has one line for it. The suite has 52 tests.

summary: Added the agent column option and ellipsis for cut summaries, then updated the Claude Code pane script to use all three changes
body:
I did the remaining two flags and then the pane. For the agent column, list now takes a flag named with-agent. It adds a short agent name in brackets before the project, such as [claude], [codex] or [pi]. Entries with a missing agent key show [?], which I saw once in an older fixture.

The ellipsis is a new option, width, that cuts the summary to the given number of characters and ends it with three dots if anything was removed. I wrote it in awk with length and substr, and counted the dots in the width. The cut does not split a multibyte character, because awk in the default locale counts bytes on some systems. I tested with a summary that has an accented letter, and on macOS awk it counted correctly, but on the older machine with mawk it split the character.

I worked around it by setting LC_ALL to a UTF-8 locale for that awk call when one is available, and falling back to no cut for the line if not. A test uses the accented summary and passes on both machines.

Then I changed the pane script. It calls list with the three flags: mark-session with the id from the hook environment, with-agent, and width set from the pane columns. I checked the pane by hand in a session. The current entries show an asterisk, the agent is in brackets, and a long summary ends in dots.

A width of zero or a missing value means no cut. I made that the default so that existing callers see no change.

Help text, completions and README table are updated. The README command table now has the three options in one row.

The suite has 58 tests and passes on both machines.

The pane takes 80 ms to refresh, measured with time, up from 60 ms before, mostly from the locale setting. That is fine.

summary: Reviewed the plugin hook scripts for quoting problems after a path with a space broke the Codex session start on the older machine
body:
The user's older machine has a home folder path with a space in it, and the Codex session start printed an error: too many arguments. I reproduced it by creating a test journal in a folder named with a space and running the hook.

The cause was an unquoted variable in the Codex hook script, in a test command that checks that the journal folder exists. Without quotes the shell split the path into two words. The Claude Code hook had the same pattern in two places, and Pi calls the CLI with a quoted path already.

I ran shellcheck over all scripts in the repository, which I had not done before. It reported 14 warnings. Eleven were about quoting, two were about using echo with a dash, and one was about a variable that was never used.

I fixed all the quoting ones. Most were simple: add double quotes around variable expansions. For two of them in bin/agent-journal, the variable is meant to split into words, a list of option names, so I added a comment and a disable directive for that line only.

The echo ones I replaced with printf, which is the portable choice and was also in my own rules for the shell code. The unused variable was left from the sync work, and I deleted it.

I added a Vitest case that runs the Codex hook and the Claude Code hook with the journal in a folder named 'my journal'. Both fail on the old code and pass now.

I then added shellcheck to the CI workflow as a step, so new warnings are caught. The runner has it installed. The step takes 2 seconds.

The suite has 60 tests and shellcheck is clean on all scripts. The Codex session start works on the older machine.

summary: Wrote the changelog entries for the sync, time zone, pane and quoting fixes, and checked each against its commit before the next release
body:
