The next release will carry several changes from the last weeks, and the changelog had not been updated since the id work. I went through the git log and wrote the entries by hand, since a generated list would just repeat commit titles.

There are four groups. Fixed: list now shows the right time in zones with half hour offsets, sync no longer fails silently when the remote has new entries, and hooks work in folders with spaces in the path. Added: list options for session marking, agent column and width, and the recall message when nothing matches.

Changed: recall prints the file name on its own line above the summary. This one matters for anyone who parses the output, so I put it first and wrote that the JSON output of list is unchanged and is the stable choice for scripts.

I checked each line against its commit by reading the diff, and corrected two. I had written that the sync timeout is 10 seconds for all remotes, but it applies to http and ssh only, so I said that. The other fix was a wrong option name in the pane line.

I also listed the README changes in one line, since they do not touch behaviour: new pictures with a dark variant, fixed badges and a docs page for hooks.

The version number is not decided. The changes include one output change, so I suggested a minor bump instead of a patch, and left the choice to the user.

summary: Reviewed the plugin hook scripts and the journal pane after the sync work, and fixed a pane flicker plus a missing newline in the Claude Code pane output
body:
Today's session was a cleanup pass over the journal pane script for Claude Code, started because the user noticed the pane flickered each time a session ended and the sync hook ran. I reproduced it by running the pane script in a loop with a demo journal of six entries and watching the redraw. The script cleared the screen first and then called list, so the pane was empty for the time list took on the slow mount.

The fix was to call list first, store the output in a variable, and only then clear and print. With that change the empty gap went from about 120 ms to nothing that I could see. I also checked that the stored output keeps the asterisk prefix from the mark-session flag and the ellipsis on cut summaries, since command substitution can drop trailing newlines.

That led to the second problem. Command substitution removed the final newline, so the last entry ran into the shell prompt when the pane was closed. I switched to printf with an explicit newline at the end. A small test in the pane fixture now compares the last byte of the output.

I then read the other hook scripts again for the same pattern of clearing before printing. Only the pane had it. The session start hook prints the rules in one write, and the session end hook prints nothing but a status line on failure.

Things I checked:
- Pane output with zero entries prints the empty message, no error.
- Pane output with a summary longer than the pane width is cut with the ellipsis and does not wrap.
- The agent column option still lines up when the agent names have different lengths.

Nothing changed in the CLI itself, only in plugins/claude-code/pane.sh and its test. Left for later: the Codex plugin has no pane, so there is nothing to port, and the user wants to look at the pane on the older machine before the next release. I will ask for that result tomorrow and add a line to the changelog draft once it is confirmed.

summary: Fixed the recall period end bound by comparing the first ten characters of each timestamp, so entries from the last minutes of the end day are included
body:
I applied the fix chosen this morning. In the awk script of the recall command the comparison now uses substr on the entry's date field, so the end day counts completely. The start bound uses the same substr to keep the two sides symmetric.

The failing test with three entries on one day now passes with three of three. I added a second case where the period is a single day, start equal to end, which returned nothing before the change and now returns that whole day. A third case checks that an entry at 00:00 of the next day stays out.

I ran the whole Vitest suite. It showed 112 passing and one failure, in a fixture that relied on the old behavior: a recall test that expected the last-day entry to be missing. That expectation was a bug frozen into a test, so I changed the fixture and wrote a comment saying why.

I also checked the output on the real journal for last week. It now shows 14 entries, where before it showed 13. The missing one was the 23:5x entry the user had pointed out.

The agents' recall rules do not mention the end bound, so the rules text stays as it is. The help text still needs a sentence about inclusive bounds, and I left that for tomorrow with the other help fixes. Nothing was committed yet except the code and the tests, in one commit.

summary: Added tests for period edges in recall: single day, midnight and a reversed range, which printed nothing and now prints an error
body:
After the fix of this afternoon I wanted the period code covered at its edges, since it had been wrong without anyone seeing it. I added five tests to the recall test file.

The first is a single-day range. The second is an entry exactly at 00:00 that belongs to the new day. The third is an entry at 23:59:59 that belongs to the end day. The fourth is a range that crosses a month boundary, written with relative dates in the fixture so it does not depend on when the tests run. The fifth is a reversed range, start after end.

The reversed range was a surprise: recall printed nothing and exited with 0, so an agent would read it as no entries in that period. I changed it to print an error on stderr, reading start is after end, and exit with 2, the same code the CLI uses for bad arguments elsewhere.

I then ran the suite three times to check that the date-relative fixtures were stable. All three runs passed, with 118 tests.

One thing I decided against: accepting the reversed range by swapping the two values. That would be friendly, but it hides a likely mistake from the agent. The error message is better.

The help text sentence is still open and will be done with the next batch of small text changes.

summary: Updated the help text for recall to say that period bounds are inclusive and that a reversed range is an error
body:
I made the small help text change that was left over from the period fix. The recall section now says that both bounds are inclusive and are whole days in UTC. That last part matters because list shows local time and recall does not, as decided in the time zone issue.

I also added one line about the exit code 2 for a reversed range. The help text is now 4 lines longer, which still fits on a normal terminal screen with the rest of the usage.

The test that compares the help output to a snapshot failed as expected and I updated the snapshot after reading the diff. It only contained the new lines.

I checked that the README has no copy of that sentence. It only links to the help command, so nothing else needed to change. The period work is complete: bug, fix, edge tests and help text.

summary: Pi sessions wrote entries with an empty session field because the extension read an environment variable Pi does not set; found the real source in the extension context
body:
The user pointed out that two entries written by Pi had session: with nothing after it, so list with the mark-session flag could never mark them. I looked at the extension in the Pi plugin folder.

The extension passes the session id to the CLI through an environment variable named after the Claude Code one. I checked the Pi docs and the extension API, and Pi does not set it. The id is available on the session object that the extension receives in its start handler.

I wrote down what is known so far. The Claude Code and Codex hooks both pass the id correctly, as the earlier entries of their plugins show. Only Pi is affected. About a quarter of the entries from the last month came from Pi, so the number of entries with an empty field is not small. I counted them with grep and found 9.

The plan is to read the id in the start handler, keep it in a variable of the extension, and pass it as an argument on every write. The CLI should also warn when the session is empty instead of writing nothing silently. I will do both in the next session, plus a small command to fill in old entries if that looks safe.

summary: Fixed the empty session field for Pi by taking the id from the session object, made the CLI warn on empty ids, and filled in the 9 old entries
body:
I implemented the plan from this morning. In the Pi extension the start handler now stores the id from the session object. Each call to the CLI passes it with the session option, and the old environment variable code is gone.

In bin/agent-journal I added a check: if the session is empty at write time, the CLI still writes the entry, but prints a warning on stderr, session id is empty, and the agent sees it. I did not make it a hard failure, since losing an entry is worse than an empty field.

Tests came next. I added a CLI test for the warning, one for a non-empty session without warning, and a test for the Pi extension with a fake session object. The extension test runs in Vitest with a stub of the CLI that records its arguments. All three pass and the suite has 121 tests.

Then the old entries. The 9 files have a session line with nothing after it. Their ids cannot be recovered, since Pi never wrote them anywhere. I decided not to invent ids. Instead I made the session line say unknown, which at least marks them as not matching, and checked that list handles it.

I first tried this with sed on the files, and found that the in-place option differs between the macOS and GNU versions. I wrote it with a temp file and mv, the way the rest of the script does. I ran it on a copy of the journal first, compared with diff and then ran it on the real one.

A real Pi session wrote a new entry afterward and it carried the id. List with the mark-session flag then marked it with an asterisk, as it should. The user's own journal folder is committed in git, so the change shows up as 9 small diffs there.

What is left is to mention the unknown value in the entry format documentation. I will do it with the next README pass.

summary: Rewrote the install section of the README so that the one-line install comes first and the manual steps follow, after the user said newcomers got lost
body:
A person who opened an issue wrote that they could not tell which install path to use. The README had three: the install script, a manual copy and a per-agent plugin command, all with the same weight. I rewrote the section.

The new order is: one command with the install script, then what it does in three bullets, then a short block for each agent for those who want only one plugin. The manual copy moved to the end under a line saying it is for people who do not want to run scripts from the web.

I checked every command in the section by running it in a clean temp home. The install script worked, the Claude Code command worked, and the Codex one printed a path that I corrected, since the plugin folder had been renamed some weeks ago. That was a stale statement that the earlier README review missed.

The link checker script reported no dead links after the change. I also made the text shorter: the section went from 58 lines to 41.

I did not touch screenshots or badges. The user will read the new section tomorrow and may ask for changes. I replied to the issue with a short answer and a pointer to the new text once it is pushed.

summary: Added alt text to the four README images and fixed their widths, since the dark theme images were shown larger than the light ones
body:
While reading the README on GitHub's dark mode I saw that the dark images were wider than the light ones, so the picture jumped when the theme changed. The cause was that the picture elements had no width and the two files have different pixel sizes, 1480 and 1360 pixels wide.

I set a width of 720 on all four images. The image source files stay unchanged, so no new screenshots were needed.

The images also had no alt text. I wrote a short description for each: what the list command prints and what recall prints, in the light and dark variants. Screen reader users now get the same information, and if an image fails to load the text is shown instead.

I ran the link and image checker and it passed. The checker does not look at alt text, so I added a check to it: any image line with empty brackets is an error. It found none after my change, and it reported the right line when I removed one text on purpose.

The page looked the same in both themes in the preview. The user wants a better picture for the top of the README later, which is still being thought through.

summary: Planned animated pictures for the README: asciinema with agg first, what the script should show, size limits and how to judge the result
body:
The user wants a moving picture at the top of the README that shows an agent writing an entry and then another session finding it with recall. Static screenshots are in place, but they do not show the flow. I wrote the plan before recording anything.

The tool to try first is asciinema, with agg to turn the recording into a GIF. It is easy to install, records from a real terminal and the cast file is text, so it can be edited. A second option, which I note only for later, is a scripted tool that renders from a tape file.

The scene has four steps. First, a session ends and an entry is written with a one-line summary. Second, the list command shows it at the top. Third, a new session starts and the user asks about it. Fourth, recall prints the entry with the file name on its own line. I want it to be under 20 seconds.

To make the recording repeatable I will use the demo journal folder with the six entries from some weeks ago, and set the home and the prompt to something neutral. The shell prompt must be short and carry no host name or user name.

Size limits matter. GitHub shows images at most about 880 pixels wide in the README column, so the terminal should be around 90 columns by 24 rows with a large font. A GIF over 3 MB makes the page slow, so my limit is 2 MB.

I listed how to judge the result: text must be readable at 100 percent in the README preview, not only when zoomed; the colors must hold up in both light and dark mode; the loop must pause on the last frame for 2 seconds.

Possible problems: font rendering by agg, which uses its own renderer; the frame rate leading to large files; and timing of typed text looking robotic. I will test these in the first recording in the afternoon.

The cast script is written as a plain shell file with sleeps, so I can rerun it. It is in a scratch folder and not committed yet, since I do not know if this tool is the one to keep.

summary: After the blurry asciinema result I compared other recording tools on paper and checked that vhs installs and runs, without recording anything for the README
body:
The first attempt of this afternoon did not give a usable picture, as the entry before this one says. I did not want to keep fiddling with fonts, so I spent this session on what else exists.

The candidates are: a scripted renderer driven by a tape file, a screen recorder with a crop of the terminal window, and static screenshots with a fake typing animation made in a video editor. The editor path takes too much manual work and cannot be repeated when the output format changes.

The tape-based tool is vhs. It runs a real terminal in a headless browser and renders text with the browser's font engine, which is why its output should be sharper at small sizes. It needs ttyd and ffmpeg. I installed all three with the package manager and ran vhs --version to check. It worked after I fixed a path problem with ffmpeg on the shell startup file.

I wrote a tiny tape that only runs the help command and writes a PNG screenshot, to see if the toolchain works. It produced a file in about 6 seconds. I looked at it and the text was sharp, but I did not go on to make anything for the README. The user said that a further try needs a proper plan with the theme question settled first.

The notes for later: the tape file format is plain text, so it can live in the repo and be run in CI; the font has to be one installed on the machine; the theme is set in the tape, which helps with light and dark variants.

Decision: park the animated picture for now. The static screenshots stay in the README. I will return to this when other work is done, and the first thing to settle is the theme and the size.

summary: Took a fresh screenshot of the help output for the README command table, since the old one showed the removed sync flag
body:
While looking at the README I noticed that the help screenshot still listed a flag for sync that was removed a few weeks ago. I took a new screenshot of the help command in the same terminal settings as the other four images: 90 columns, the same font and the demo prompt.

I saved it as a PNG and made a dark variant the same way. Both are 1400 pixels wide, so the width of 720 in the README fits them.

I replaced the old file names in the README and ran the link and image checker, which passed. The new picture is 94 KB. The old ones are deleted from the images folder, so no unused files stay in the repo.

Nothing else in the README mentions the removed flag, which I checked with grep.

summary: The config command lost comment lines in the config file when setting a value; rewrote the update to change only the matching line and added four tests
body:
The user ran the config command to set the journal folder and found that the comments they had written in the config file were gone afterward. I reproduced it with a file that had two comment lines and three settings.

The config command reads the whole file with awk and prints it again to a temp file, and the awk program skips any line that does not look like key=value, so comments and blank lines were dropped. This went unseen because the tests used files without comments.

I rewrote the update. If the key exists, the awk program replaces only that line and prints every other line unchanged. If the key does not exist, the new line is appended at the end. The key match is exact, so setting a key named host does not touch hostname.

I wrote four tests. The first keeps comments and blank lines when a value changes. The second appends a new key. The third checks that a key which is a prefix of another is left alone. The fourth checks a value with an equals sign inside it, such as a URL with a query, which the old code cut at the second equals sign.

The fourth test failed on the first try of the new code, since I split on every equals sign. I changed it to split on the first one only, using index and substr instead of the field separator. All four tests pass and the suite has 125.

Another thing I looked at was the write of the temp file. If the process dies in the middle, the old file is still intact, since the mv comes last. I kept that. The temp file is created in the same folder as the config, so the mv is an atomic rename on the same filesystem, not a copy.

I also checked file permissions. The old code produced a file with the default umask, while the original might have been tighter. The config can hold a git remote with a token, so I now copy the mode of the original with a chmod from a stat call. Stat has different options on macOS and Linux, so I used ls -l and cut the mode, with a fallback to 600.

The config command in the README does not describe comments, so I added one line saying they are kept. Tomorrow I will check that the Codex and Pi plugins do not rewrite the file themselves.

summary: Checked that the Codex and Pi plugins never rewrite the config file themselves, and found that the Pi extension did a sed replace that would drop comments
body:
Following the config fix of yesterday I looked for other code that edits the config file. I searched all plugin folders and the install script for writes to it.

The Claude Code plugin and the Codex plugin only call the config command, so they are fine. The install script appends a default line if the file does not exist, which keeps nothing to lose. The Pi extension, though, had a function that set the journal folder with sed and a here-document, which replaces the full file when a key is found.

I replaced that function with a call to the config command, so there is one place that edits the file. The extension code is shorter by 14 lines.

I tested it by hand with a config with comments, and then added an extension test with the CLI stub that checks the arguments of the call: config, the key and the value. The suite is at 126 tests and all pass.

One more case to look at was a file that has Windows line endings, which a user mentioned once. The new awk code leaves the carriage returns alone, as it prints lines unchanged, but the replaced line has none. A mixed file works for the shell, so I did not add handling.

The journal itself is not affected. The question now is whether to document the comment behavior in the help text. I decided that the README line is enough.

summary: Added an agent filter to list so that only entries written by one agent are shown, and checked it against the agent column option
body:
The user wanted to see only the entries written by Codex when comparing the agents' summaries. List had a column for the agent but no filter, so I added an agent option that takes one name.

The filter is applied in the same awk pass that reads the front matter. It compares the agent field with the given name, exactly and without case folding, because the plugins always write the names in the same form: claude-code, codex and pi.

The count option is applied after the filter, so asking for 5 entries with agent codex gives the 5 newest Codex entries and not the Codex ones among the newest 5. I wrote a test that fails if the order is the other way round, with six entries from two agents.

Other tests: an unknown agent name prints nothing and a message on stderr saying no entries for that agent, which follows the no-match message of recall; and the filter combined with the mark-session option still marks the right lines.

The help text got one line and the usage line got the new option. I checked the Claude Code pane script. It calls list with its own options and does not need the filter, so I left it.

The suite has 130 tests, all passing. I ran the filter on the real journal and it gave 31 Codex entries in about 40 ms, so speed is no concern.

summary: Upgraded oxlint and oxfmt to the latest versions, fixed the two new warnings in the test files and kept CI green on the first push
body:
Both tools had new releases and the user asked to keep them current. I raised the versions in package.json and reinstalled.

oxfmt changed the format of long import lists in three test files. I ran the formatter and committed the result as its own commit, so the diff of the upgrade stays easy to read apart from the style change.

oxlint reported two new warnings: an unused variable in the Pi extension test, left over from the session id work, and a rule about a useless escape in a regular expression in the recall test. I fixed both by hand. The regular expression change did not alter what it matches, which I checked by running that test file alone.

I then ran the whole local check: lint, format check and the Vitest suite. Everything passed with 130 tests.

I pushed and watched the GitHub Actions run. It took about 1 minute 40 seconds, the same as before, and passed. There was one concern: the CI uses a cached install, and the cache key includes the lock file, so the upgrade created a new cache. The next run should be quicker.

Nothing in the shell code is checked by these tools, so the CLI itself was not touched in this work.

summary: Replaced the license and CI badges in the README with ones that load from the repo and added a short line about supported agents
body:
The two badges at the top of the README went through a third-party image service that was slow on the user's connection and once showed an error picture. I changed them to the badge that GitHub itself generates for the workflow, and the license one to a static text badge.

I checked the workflow file name in the badge URL against the real one in .github/workflows. It matched. A wrong name there was one of the earlier README review findings, so I wanted to be sure.

I also added a line under the badges: works with Claude Code, Codex and Pi. The user asked for it, since people could not tell at first sight which agents are supported.

The link checker passed. It cannot check remote images, so I opened the page in the preview and saw both badges load.

I did not add a badge for the version, because there is no release tag yet and it would show an empty value. That can wait for the release. The change is one commit with 6 changed lines.

summary: The Codex session start hook printed the rules twice when the journal folder was a symlink; found the duplicate through the path check and fixed it
body:
The user noticed that Codex showed the journal rules two times at session start on the older machine. That machine keeps the journal in a folder that is a symlink to a synced drive.

The hook finds the rules by looking for a rules file in the journal folder and also in the plugin folder, and it skips the second one if both paths are the same file. The check compared the path strings, so a symlink made them look different.

I changed the check to resolve both paths with cd and pwd -P, which works in POSIX sh without needing realpath, since realpath is not on every system. The hook now prints the rules once.

I wrote a test with a symlinked journal folder in a temp directory and counted how often a marker line from the rules appears in the hook output. It was 2 before the change and 1 now.

The Claude Code hook has the same structure, so I tested it with the same setup and it printed once already, because it uses only the plugin folder. No change there.

The suite is at 133 tests and passes. I added a line to the changelog draft for the next release.

summary: Wrote the full plan for the next release: which fixes go in, which tests to run on a second machine, the changelog order and what to leave out
body:
A release is coming in the next weeks and I used this session to collect everything that happened since the last tag, so that nothing is forgotten and nothing half-finished goes in.

I went through the git log since the last tag and sorted the commits into groups. The fixes: recall period end bound, Pi session id, config comments, Codex double rules. The additions: agent filter in list, the warning for an empty session, the reversed range error. The documentation: the README install section, badges and alt text, the help text lines.

Some things do not belong. The experiments with recording tools made no commits in the repo, which is right. One commit adds a helper script for the demo journal, and I decided to leave it in but not mention it in the changelog.

I listed the checks to do before tagging. First, the full test suite on a clean checkout. Second, the install script on a clean home folder for each of the three agents. Third, the sync between two machines, since it was changed some weeks ago and has had only short use on the second machine. Fourth, the help text read once more from top to bottom.

The changelog order will be: fixes first, then additions, then the documentation. Each line gets a short sentence in the user's voice, no commit hashes in the text.

I also thought about the version number. The changes are fixes and small additions with no change of format of the entries, apart from the session value unknown. Old tools read that value fine, so a minor version bump is right and not a major one.

There is one risk I wrote down: the warning on an empty session goes to stderr, and the Codex hook might show stderr to the agent in a confusing way. I will test that case on Codex before the release.

The plan is stored as a note in the scratch folder, not in the repo. Open question for the user: whether to wait for the new README pictures before releasing. My view is no, since they are independent of the code.

summary: Tested the empty session warning inside real Codex and Pi sessions and found Codex shows stderr as plain text, which the agent handled correctly
body:
The release plan listed one risk: the warning for an empty session id goes to stderr. I tested how each agent shows it.

For this I used a hidden environment variable that makes the hook pass an empty session on purpose. In a Codex session the entry was written, the warning appeared in the tool output as a line, and the agent mentioned it in one sentence and moved on. It did not try to write the entry again, which was my worry.

In a Claude Code session the same setup showed the warning in the hook output. The agent ignored it, which is fine, since the entry was written.

In a Pi session the id is now always passed, so I could not produce the warning without editing the extension. I made a temporary change to pass an empty value and saw the same behavior as in Codex. Then I reverted the change and checked with git diff that nothing remained.

I then counted what the warning costs: a few extra tokens in the tool output, about 15, only in the broken case. That is acceptable.

An important point is that the entry file is the same in all three cases. I opened the three files and each had session with an empty value, as expected, and no other field was missing.

One more question: should the CLI use the string unknown for an empty session when writing, as I did for the old Pi entries? I decided against it. An empty value shows a real problem, while unknown would hide new bugs behind a normal-looking word.

No code change came out of this session, only a note in the release checklist that the warning was checked on all three agents.

summary: Sync on the second machine failed with a lock file left by a killed session; added removal of stale git lock files older than a minute with a clear message
body:
The user's second machine reported that sync failed at session end with the message that index.lock exists. A session had been killed in the middle of a push, which left the lock behind.

I looked at the sync code. It calls git add, commit, pull with rebase and push, each with the 10 second timeout added some weeks ago. The timeout kills git with a signal, and git does not clean up its lock when killed this way. So the timeout I added earlier is probably what produced the stale lock, and I wrote that in the notes.

The fix checks for the lock file before the git calls. If it exists and is older than 60 seconds, the script removes it and prints a line saying it removed a stale lock. If it is younger, another sync may be running, so the script prints that and stops without touching it.

Finding the age of a file in POSIX sh is not simple. The find command with the -mmin option is not strictly POSIX, though available on macOS and Linux. I used find with -mmin +1 and tested on both.

Tests: a stale lock made with touch -t, which is removed; a fresh lock, which stays and gives the message; and no lock, with no message. The first test needed the touch -t value to be computed relative to now, so the test does not depend on a date. I wrote it with a shell expression that goes back 5 minutes.

I tried the case on the second machine in the evening by creating a lock by hand. The old lock was removed and the push worked, with the message shown once. The suite has 136 tests and passes.

summary: Added the sync stale lock fix and the other recent fixes to the changelog draft, checking each line against its commit
body:
With the release coming I updated the changelog draft. The sync lock fix of this afternoon was new, and I also went over the earlier lines again.

For each line I opened the commit and read the diff, to make sure the sentence describes what the code does and not what I intended. Two lines needed a change: the Pi session line said the id was fixed for all cases, but the old entries only got the value unknown, so I wrote that. The config line said comments are preserved, and I added that the file mode is kept too.

The new line reads that sync now removes a stale git lock older than a minute and says so. I did not claim anything about hung networks, since that is the older timeout change.

The changelog now has 11 lines, grouped as planned: fixes, additions, documentation. I read it aloud once for tone. The user writes short plain sentences and I matched that.

One thing I noticed is that the line for the agent filter in list does not say that the count applies after the filter. That is worth a clause, since it is the less obvious behavior. I added it.

Nothing else changed in the repo today beyond the changelog file.

summary: A user asked in an issue why recall prints UTC dates while list shows local time; answered with the reason and proposed a header line instead of a change
body:
A new issue asked why the same entry shows 22:40 in list and a different day in recall. This is the choice recorded in the time zone work, but a reader of the output cannot know it.

The reasoning for UTC in recall is that agents search across machines and zones, and the file names and front matter are in UTC, so the dates agree with what the agent can read in the files. List is for the user to look at, so it shows local time.

I did not want to change that. Instead I suggested in my reply to print a header line in recall output, such as dates are UTC, only when the output is for more than one entry. The user agreed with a small caveat: the line should not appear for a single entry, to keep the output short.

I checked how an extra line would affect the agents' use. The recall eval from a month ago counted entries in the period question, and a header line could be counted by a careless agent. So the change needs a rerun of the eval before it is released.

I wrote this into the issue, thanked the person and left it open for the implementation. I added a line to the notes for the next session of work on recall.

summary: Printed a UTC note line at the top of multi-entry recall output and made sure it is not counted as an entry by the tests
body:
I implemented the header line discussed in the issue this morning. When recall prints two or more entries, the first line is now a note saying that dates are UTC. A single entry prints without it.

The line starts with a hash character so that it is clearly not an entry. I weighed that against plain text, and the marker is what makes a count of entry lines unambiguous.

Several older tests counted lines of output and now failed by one. I changed them to count only lines that match the entry pattern, which is a better check anyway. Two new tests cover the header: present for two entries, absent for one.

The suite has 138 tests and all pass. I did not rerun the eval yet, which needs a session with each agent and will take the afternoon. The release waits for that result.

summary: Reran the recall eval on all three agents with the new UTC note line and got eight of eight on Claude Code and Codex and seven of eight on Pi
body:
The note line in recall output could confuse the count question of the eval, so I ran the eight questions on each agent with the current build.

Claude Code answered all eight correctly. Codex also got eight of eight, and neither made a repeated search. The period question, which counts entries, was right on both, so the header line was not counted.

Pi got seven of eight. The missed one was the question about a topic that has no entry, which Pi answered with a guess based on a similar entry. That is the same miss that appeared in earlier Pi runs, and it was judged noise then. I repeated that question five times on Pi and it was right four times, so the rate is not changed by the note line.

I also read the transcripts of the period question to see how each agent treated the note. Claude Code wrote that the dates are UTC in its answer, which is a nice effect. Codex ignored the line. Pi mentioned it once.

The numbers match the results from earlier in the project, so the change is safe to release. I wrote the results into the eval notes file with the date of the run in relative words only, as the other notes do.

One more idea for later is a ninth question about time zones, to see whether agents get the day wrong around midnight when told local times. That is not for this release.

The issue can now be closed with the implementation, and I will do that after the release is tagged.

summary: Went through the release checklist on clean homes for all three agents and on two machines, found one install script problem with a missing folder, and fixed it
body:
This was the full pre-release run from the plan. I started with a clean checkout and ran lint, the format check and the suite: 138 tests, all passing, in about 11 seconds.

Then the install script on a fresh home folder for Claude Code. It worked. For Codex it worked. For Pi it failed with a message that the extensions folder does not exist, because a new Pi installation has not created it yet.

The script had assumed the folder. I changed it to create the folder with mkdir -p before copying the extension, and print what it created. I added a test that runs the install against a temp home without the folder, which failed before the change and passes now.

I then repeated the three installs, and all worked. I also ran the uninstall for each, as the README describes, and checked that no files of the plugins were left. The Pi uninstall left an empty folder, which I think is fine, since the folder belongs to Pi.

Next the sync between the two machines. I wrote an entry on each, ended both sessions within a few seconds of each other, and watched the hooks. Both pushed, one after a rebase pull, and the log showed both entries on the remote. The stale lock removal did not trigger, as expected, because no lock existed.

I read the help text from top to bottom. It is consistent with the new options: agent filter, the inclusive bounds and the exit codes. One typo, a double space in the sync line, was fixed.

Finally the README: I followed the install section as a new reader would, with the one-line command, and it worked as written. The link checker passed.

The list of what is left before tagging is short: the final changelog read by the user, and the version bump in the package file. I did not tag anything yet. The release will follow when the user has approved the changelog, and I expect that to be in the next few days.

summary: Finished the work on release prep after the checklist run: fixed the install script folder problem, reran tests on both machines and trimmed the changelog to what shipped
body:
The release checklist of yesterday left three open items, and this session closed them. First, the install script problem with the missing folder was already fixed, but I wanted proof on a clean home. I created a fresh temporary HOME for each of the three agents and ran the install script from scratch. All three finished without an error and the journal folder existed afterwards.

Second, I reran the full Vitest suite on the main machine and on the older second machine. The main machine passed all tests in about 14 seconds. The second machine passed too, but one test for time zones was slow at 6 seconds because it starts the CLI many times. I left it as is, since it is not flaky.

Third, I went through the changelog draft line by line and compared each line to its commit. Two lines described work that was only planned: a note about a column width option and a note about a header for sync output. I removed both. One line said the stale lock fix removed locks older than a minute, which matches the code, so it stayed.

I also ran oxlint and oxfmt over the whole repo. Both were clean, and CI was green on the last push. The README was not touched in this session, only checked: the install section matches the script's real output.

What is left: tag the release after one more look at the Pi extension on a real session. I did not do that today because the Pi install on this machine needs an update first. The next step is that update, then a short real Pi session, then the tag.

summary: Updated Pi on the main machine and ran a real session; the extension wrote an entry with a correct session id and no warning
body:
Pi on this machine was two versions behind, so I updated it first. After the update I checked that the extension still loads: the startup output listed it and showed no error.

Then I ran a short real session that changed one line in a scratch folder and ended. The extension wrote one entry. The session field held the id from the session object, which is the fix from a few weeks ago, and the CLI printed no warning about an empty id.

I compared the entry to one written by Claude Code with the same CLI. The front matter keys are in the same order and the agent field says pi. The summary was a proper sentence.

I also ran list with the agent filter for pi and got the new entry on top. Nothing needed fixing. The release can be tagged once the changelog is read once more.

summary: Tagged the release after a last read of the changelog and checked that the install one-liner fetches the tagged version
body:
I read the changelog once more from the top and fixed two typos and the order of the lines, so that fixes come before small changes. Each line still matches a commit.

Then I created the tag and pushed it. CI ran on the tag and passed. I wrote the release notes on GitHub from the changelog text, without extra claims.

The install one-liner in the README points to the main branch, so I tested it in a clean temporary home. It installed the current script and the version command printed the new number. I decided not to pin the one-liner to the tag, because users would then stay on old versions without noticing.

Open: watch the issues for install problems in the next days. Nothing else is planned for today.

summary: A user reported that list shows the wrong order for two entries with the same minute; the sort was by file name only and now falls back to the full timestamp
body:
An issue came in: two entries written in the same minute appeared in the wrong order in list. I reproduced it with two fixture files that differ only in their session id.

The cause was that list sorted by file name, and the file name has the time to the minute plus a short hash. The hash is random, so the order of same-minute entries was random too. The front matter holds the full timestamp with seconds, so the fix was to sort by that value first and use the file name only to break ties.

In the awk part I added the timestamp as the first sort key and kept the old key as the second. The change is small, about six lines in bin/agent-journal.

I added a test with two entries ten seconds apart in the same minute, with file names that sort the wrong way. It failed before the change and passes now. I also ran the whole suite: all green.

I checked that recall uses its own sort and did not have the problem; its output for the same fixtures was in the right order already. I answered in the issue with the cause and the fix and said it goes into the next release.

One more thing I looked at was whether the mark-session flag is affected. It is not, because it only prefixes lines and does not change order. I will add a changelog line later, when the release is planned.

summary: Plan for the README pictures after the blurry attempt: screenshots for now, a short list of what each picture must show, and no recording until a better tool is chosen
body:
Since the asciinema result was too blurry, I wrote down what the README really needs before choosing any tool again. The README has four places where a picture would help: the list output, the recall output with terms, the journal pane in a Claude Code session, and the help text.

For each place I wrote what it must show. The list picture needs five entries with different agents and the agent column on. The recall picture needs one search term and two hits with the UTC note line visible. The pane picture needs the latest three entries cut with an ellipsis. The help picture is the command table.

I also wrote the limits. Text must stay readable at the width GitHub shows, about 830 pixels. Files should stay under 1 MB each. Both a light and a dark version are needed, because the README already uses the picture element for the screenshots.

For now the plan is to use plain screenshots in those four places, taken from the same fixture journal so that they match each other. The fixture journal needs its own folder with fake but believable entries, and no real paths of mine.

I started that folder and wrote eight entries with a mix of agents, one of them with a long summary to show the cut. The entries use the project name demo-app. I checked that list reads them with the fixture folder set through the config command.

Next step: take the four screenshots from this folder. A moving picture is a later question and depends on the tool.

summary: Took the list and recall screenshots from the demo journal in both themes and checked that they fit the README widths
body:
Using the demo journal folder from earlier today, I took the list and recall screenshots in the light and dark terminal themes. That makes four files.

I resized each to the same width of 830 pixels and ran an optimizer over them. The sizes ended between 60 and 110 KB.

In the README I swapped the old list and recall images for the new ones, kept the alt text and the picture element, and set the same width on all. I checked the rendering with a local Markdown preview. The dark and light ones now have the same size.

The pane and help pictures are still missing and are the next step.

summary: Went through the README top to bottom after the badge and install changes and fixed five stale statements, including a removed flag and a wrong default for the journal folder
body:
The README had changed in small steps over the last weeks: the install section, the badges and the screenshots. I read it from top to bottom once, with the CLI open next to it, and ran every command shown in it against the demo journal.

Five statements were stale. The command table still listed the sync flag that was removed two releases ago. The text on the config command said comment lines are dropped when a value is set, which the fix of last week made untrue, so I deleted that sentence. The default journal folder was described with the old path. The line on supported agents named two agents and not three. The recall section said period bounds are exclusive, while the help text says inclusive since the end bound fix.

I fixed all five in one commit and kept the wording short. For each change I checked the matching line in the help output, so the README and the help say the same.

I also checked the links. One link to the plugin folder of Pi pointed to a path that was renamed, and I corrected it. The badge images load from the repo as intended and the alt texts are still in place.

I did not touch the screenshots in this pass. They are planned as a separate step, and the command table screenshot will need a fresh take once the table text is final. The Vitest suite does not cover the README, so I only ran oxfmt on the changed file to confirm it does not complain.

Next is a short list of what each picture in the README must show, so the screenshots can be taken in one go.

summary: Took the pane and help screenshots, finished the README picture set and read the README top to bottom for stale statements
body:
I finished the picture set. The pane screenshot came from a real Claude Code session on the demo journal, with the pane showing three entries and one cut summary with an ellipsis. The help screenshot shows the current command table.

Both were made in light and dark themes and resized to the same width as the others. Total size of the eight pictures is about 640 KB.

Then I read the README from top to bottom. I found three stale statements: a sentence that said recall prints local times, which it does not since the UTC note; a mention of the sync flag that was removed; and a count of supported agents that said two.

I fixed all three. The recall sentence now says dates are in UTC with a note line at the top. The agent count says three and lists them.

I previewed the page in both themes and the pictures swap correctly. No moving pictures are part of this, by decision. The README is in good shape for now.

summary: Reviewed the install script for POSIX problems with shellcheck and found two bashisms that would fail on dash
body:
I ran shellcheck over the install script and the CLI, with the shell set to sh. The CLI was clean. The install script had two real findings.

The first was a double-bracket test in the part that checks whether the target folder is on the PATH. On dash that fails with a message that [[ is not found, and the script continued as if the folder was not on the PATH. The second was a use of the echo -e option for a coloured message, which dash prints literally as -e.

I replaced the double bracket with a case statement on the PATH string wrapped in colons, which is the usual portable way. I replaced echo -e with printf and a format string.

To test, I ran the install script with dash in a clean temporary home. Before the fix it printed the literal -e and a wrong hint about the PATH. After the fix the output is right in both dash and the default shell of the machine.

I added a test that runs the install script with sh pointing at dash when dash exists, and skips otherwise. The skip prints a clear reason in the Vitest output.

Shellcheck also gave a few style notes about unquoted variables in the plugin hook scripts. I looked at each one. Two were real and could break on a path with a space, like the earlier Codex problem, so I quoted them. The rest were intentional word splitting for a list of flags, and I added shellcheck disable comments with a reason.

All tests pass and shellcheck is now clean on every shell file. I want to add it to CI, but that is a separate change because it needs an install step.

summary: Added shellcheck to the GitHub Actions workflow as its own job, which found no issues on the current main
body:
Following the review earlier today, I added shellcheck to CI. It is its own job, so a style issue does not hide test results.

The job runs on the standard Ubuntu runner, where shellcheck is already installed. I list the files explicitly: bin/agent-journal, the install script and every script under the plugin folders. A find with a name pattern would also have picked up fixtures, which are not meant to be clean.

The first run failed because of one hook script in the Pi plugin that has no shebang line and is sourced. I added a shell directive comment at the top of that file instead of a shebang, since it is not executed directly.

Second run was green. The whole workflow takes about 50 seconds, and the shellcheck job about 12 of them.

I also checked that the job really fails when it should. On a scratch branch I mean a local change only, never pushed, I added an unquoted variable and ran the same command locally. It reported SC2086 and exit code 1, as expected, and I reverted it.

I added a short line to the contributing notes saying that shellcheck runs in CI and how to run it locally. Nothing else changed. Next is the changelog for these shell fixes.

summary: Added the list ordering, backslash and install script fixes to the changelog draft after checking each against its commit
body:
I added three entries to the changelog draft: the same-minute ordering fix in list, the backslash fix for summaries with the ENVIRON change, and the dash fixes in the install script.

For each one I opened the commit and compared the message to the claim. The ordering fix says list sorts by the full timestamp first. The backslash fix mentions list and recall both, because both changed. The install fix mentions dash and echo -e.

I did not add the shellcheck CI job, since it does not change anything for users. I put the three lines in the fixes section in the order of the commits.

The draft now has seven lines in total for the next release.

summary: Added plural matching to recall terms so that a search for 'sessions' also finds entries that say 'session', with tests and a note in the help text
body:
A user asked in an issue why a recall search for 'hooks' found nothing when an entry said 'hook'. The recall command matched terms as plain substrings of the lowercased entry, but the awk code compared whole words in the summary field, so the plural form missed. I reproduced it with the demo journal in two commands.

I looked at three options. Full stemming would be too much for a small awk script and would give surprising hits. Matching by prefix would find too much. A simple plural rule was enough: a term ending in 's' is also tried without the final 's', and a term without it is also tried with it. Terms ending in 'ss', such as 'class', are left alone so they do not turn into 'clas'.

The change is in the term normalizing function in bin/agent-journal, about twelve lines. Each term now expands into a small set of forms, and an entry matches the term if any form matches. Multiple terms still need all of them to match, as before.

I added six tests in the recall test file. They cover singular to plural, plural to singular, a term ending in 'ss', two terms where one is plural, a term that matches nothing in either form, and a term with a trailing 's' that is part of a name. All six pass, and the older recall tests did not change.

One case surprised me: the term 'status' lost its final 's' and found 'statu', which does not exist, but it still matched 'status' through the original form, so the result was right. I left it, since the extra form is harmless.

I added one sentence to the help text for recall that plural and singular forms both match. The README recall section got the same sentence. The changelog line will be written when I check the commits before the release.

Still open is whether the rules text for the agents should tell them they no longer need to try both forms. I will look at that with the next eval run, since the rules change affects the questions.

summary: Changed the recall rules text to say that a term and a period can be combined, with one example command, and reran the six new questions
body:
I edited the recall section of the rules that each agent gets at session start. It now says in one short paragraph that recall accepts a term and a period together, and gives a single example with both. I kept the text short, since the rules are printed at every session start.

I ran the six combined questions again. Claude Code got six of six, Codex got five of six and Pi got five of six. That is up from five, four and three.

The remaining Codex miss used the period only again on a long output. The remaining Pi miss was a question where the term appears in a different form, singular against plural. That is a search issue and not a rules issue, so I left it.

I also reran the older eight questions to be sure nothing got worse. The scores were eight, eight and seven, the same as before. The rules text grew by about 300 characters.

I will watch whether the Codex miss repeats before making the text longer.

summary: Fixed a backslash in a summary that was turned into a control character by echo on dash, by switching the writer to printf with a fixed format
body:
While testing the install script on the older machine I found a second POSIX problem, this time in the CLI. A summary with a backslash, such as one that mentions a path like C:\temp or the sequence \n, was written to the entry file with the backslash changed. On dash, echo interprets escape sequences, so '\n' became a real line break and broke the front matter.

I reproduced it by writing an entry with the summary 'Fixed the \n handling' under dash and under bash. On bash the file was right and on dash the summary field was cut after 'the' with the rest on a new line. The list command then showed a truncated summary and the next line was ignored.

The cause was three places in the write function that used echo with variable content. I replaced all of them with printf '%s\n' and a fixed format, so the content is never read as a format. I searched the whole script for other echo calls with user text and found two more in the error messages. Those were changed as well, because a file name with a backslash could do the same.

I added four tests. They write summaries with a single backslash, with '\n', with '\t' and with a double backslash, then read the file back and compare the summary field byte for byte. The tests run the CLI with sh, and I also ran them once with dash set as sh on the older machine. All four fail on the old code under dash and pass on the new code.

The awk parts were checked too. Awk reads the line as it is, but the -v option processes escapes in values. The list command passes the session id to awk with -v, and ids are plain, so no problem there. I moved the mark-session value to the environment anyway, to be safe for odd input.

The full suite passes on both machines, and shellcheck on CI is still clean. Entries written before this fix with broken summaries: I searched the demo and my own journal and found none, so no repair is needed.

The fix goes into the changelog draft after I check it against its commit.

summary: Looked into a Codex report that entries lose their cwd when the session starts in a subfolder, and found the hook used the git root instead of the real folder
body:
A user wrote that entries from Codex showed the repo root as cwd even when the session started in a subfolder. I reproduced it with a monorepo-like fixture with a packages folder.

The hook script computes the cwd with git rev-parse --show-toplevel and falls back to pwd outside a repository. That was written early, so that the project name would be stable, but it also overwrote the cwd field. The project field is meant to hold the stable name, and the cwd field is meant to be the real folder.

The fix keeps the git root only for the project name and writes pwd into cwd. I changed it in the Codex hook. Then I compared with the Claude Code and Pi plugins. Claude Code gets the cwd from the hook input and was right. Pi uses the session object cwd and was right too.

I added a test for the Codex hook script that runs it from a subfolder of a temporary git repository and checks both fields. Before the change cwd was wrong, now it equals the subfolder.

Existing entries are not changed. I counted how many old Codex entries could be affected, by comparing cwd and project in my own journal: 14 entries had a cwd equal to a git root where the session had started deeper, but I cannot know that from the file alone. So I left them.

I answered in the issue with the cause and said that old entries stay as they are. A changelog line is needed. I also noted for the next review that the three plugins compute the project name in three different ways, which could be unified later.

summary: Unified how the three plugins compute the project name into one CLI helper, so that Codex, Pi and Claude Code agree for subfolders and non-git folders
body:
Yesterday's Codex cwd fix showed that each plugin computes the project name on its own. This session moved that into one place: a new subcommand called project-name in the CLI that takes a folder and prints the name.

The rule is the same one the best plugin had. If the folder is inside a git repository, the name is the basename of the repository root. Otherwise it is the basename of the folder. If the folder is the home folder, the name is home, to avoid an entry with the user name as the project.

I wrote the helper in plain sh with git rev-parse and basename, and a case for the home folder. It handles a trailing slash and a path with spaces, which I tested.

Then I changed the three plugins to call it. The Codex hook replaced its own git call. The Claude Code hook had a version with sed that cut a path and failed for a repository whose folder name had a dot. The Pi extension had a JavaScript version using path.basename of the cwd only, which never looked at git, so a Pi session in a subfolder got the subfolder name as project. That was a real difference between the agents and probably explains why a few of my Pi entries had odd project names.

Tests: eight cases for the helper, covering repo root, subfolder, non-git folder, home, trailing slash, spaces, a dot in the name and a symlinked folder. For the symlink I decided to resolve it with pwd -P, matching the Codex symlink fix of last month.

I ran the plugin tests and the full suite and all passed. I also ran a real session in each agent in a subfolder of this repo, and all three wrote the project name agent-journal.

The Pi extension needed a small change in how it runs the CLI, using the same execFile call it already uses for the write command, so there is no new dependency.

Two things remain. Old Pi entries with a subfolder as the project are not changed, though I could list them with a filter in a later session. And the changelog needs lines for the Codex cwd fix and the new helper. I wrote both down in the draft already but not yet checked them against commits.

summary: Listed the old Pi entries with a subfolder as project name and decided to leave them unchanged, since the real project cannot be proven from the file
body:
After the project-name helper I wanted to know how much old data has the odd names. I wrote a quick awk one-liner, not committed, that compares the project field with the basename of the cwd field for Pi entries.

There are 63 Pi entries. For 11 of them the project differs from what the helper gives for the stored cwd. In nine of those the project is the name of a subfolder such as src or tests.

I considered rewriting the field. The helper needs the folder to exist and be a git repository, and several of those folders are on the older machine or were deleted. So I cannot prove the true name for all. Rewriting only some would leave the journal inconsistent.

I decided to leave all of them. The recall search also matches on cwd, so those entries are still found with the repo name in many cases. I wrote a short note in the docs folder under known issues listing the cause and the date range in relative words.

No code was changed in this session.

summary: Checked the changelog lines for the Codex cwd fix, the project-name helper and plural matching against their commits and tidied the release draft
body:
The release draft had grown to eleven lines. I went through the new ones and compared each to its commit before they stay.

The Codex cwd line said that entries now store the real folder. That matches the hook change. I added that old entries are not changed, because users will otherwise expect it.

The project-name line first said the helper is used by all plugins, which is true, but I also added that Pi sessions in subfolders now use the repository name. That is a visible change for Pi users, so it deserved its own mention.

The plural line said recall stems words. That is too strong, since it only drops a trailing s or es. I changed it to say that recall ignores a trailing s on search terms.

I also found that the ordering fix of list was listed twice, once from the issue and once from the commit message. I merged them.

Then I sorted the draft into fixes, changes and internal items. The shellcheck CI job and the shell fixes of the install script went into the internal section, except the dash fix, which stays under fixes because users with dash were affected.

Finally I counted the lines: five fixes, three changes and two internal ones, ten in total. The draft is ready for review when the release is planned.

summary: Planned the next release: which of the ten changelog lines need a second-machine test, the order of checks and a small list of things left out on purpose
body:
I wrote the plan for the next release in the docs folder, using the last plan as a template.

First, what goes in. All ten lines of the draft go in. Nothing else will be added now, to keep the release small. A few ideas were left out on purpose: unifying list and recall date handling, a config option for the UTC note, and cleaning old Pi entries.

Second, which changes need a test beyond the suite. The dash fix needs a run on a machine where sh is dash, and the older machine is one. The project-name helper needs a real session in each agent in a subfolder, which I already did on the main machine but not on the older one. The Codex cwd fix needs a real Codex session from a subfolder on the older machine as well, because the hook there runs with an older git.

Third, the order. Run the suite on both machines. Then the install script in a clean home on both. Then the three real sessions. Then rerun the recall eval, both the eight old questions and the six combined ones. Then the tag.

For the eval I set a rule for passing. The scores should not be lower than the last run: eight, eight and seven for the old set and six, five and five for the combined one. If one is lower, I read the transcript before deciding whether it is noise or a regression.

I also noted the risk with git on the older machine. Its git is old enough that rev-parse with some options may behave differently. The helper only uses show-toplevel, which has existed for a long time, so I expect no problem, but the check is on the list.

The plan has an estimate of about two hours for all steps. I will start with the older machine tomorrow.

summary: Ran the suite, the install script and three real subfolder sessions on the older machine; everything passed except the Codex session, which used a stale plugin copy
body:
On the older machine I pulled main and ran the suite. All tests passed, and the dash test ran for real since sh is dash there. The test output showed it as passed and not skipped.

The install script in a clean home also passed for all three agents. The PATH hint was right, which is what the dash fix was for.

Then the real sessions in a subfolder. Claude Code and Pi wrote entries with the repository name as project and the subfolder as cwd. The Codex session wrote the old values: the git root as cwd.

I first suspected the old git, but the hook script in the Codex plugin folder was an old copy. The install script copies the hook to the Codex folder, and I had not rerun it after pulling. After I reran the install, the Codex session wrote the right values.

This is a gap, though: a user who pulls the repo but does not reinstall gets the old hook without knowing. I do not think the CLI should update plugins silently. But I added a version stamp comment to each copied hook and a check in the CLI doctor-like output, where the version command now prints a warning line if the installed hook stamp differs from the repo version.

I wrote a test for the stamp comparison with a fake installed hook that has an old stamp. It prints the warning and exits with status 0.

It is a new feature, so it needs a changelog line and a README sentence in the update section. I have not written either yet. The eval is the next step.

summary: Reran the recall eval on all three agents for the release: old set eight, eight, seven and combined set six, six, five, so no regression
body:
I ran the eval as the plan said. The older eight-question set gave eight on Claude Code, eight on Codex and seven on Pi, equal to the last run.

The combined set of six questions gave six, six and five. Codex got one better than before, and the question it missed last time passed now. I looked at the transcript: it used both the term and the period this time, so the rules sentence probably helped, but one run does not prove that.

The Pi miss is the same one as before in both sets, in the old set it is a question about a sync detail where the entry has a very short summary. The agent found the entry and still answered from the wrong part of the body. That is an answer quality issue and not a recall issue, so I left it.

I saved the scores in the results file with the dates as relative words and the CLI version. Each run took about nine minutes in total across the agents.

The plan said that nothing lower than the last run is allowed, and nothing was lower. The eval step is done.

summary: Added the hook version warning line to the changelog and a short update note to the README, then tagged the release after a last green CI run
body:
Two things were left from the older machine session: the changelog line and the README sentence for the hook version warning.

The changelog line says that the version command warns when the installed plugin hooks are older than the CLI. I checked it against the commit and the test.

In the README I added a short paragraph under the install section, titled as plain text in bold and not as a heading, to match the style there. It says to rerun the install script after updating the repo, and that the version command shows a warning if a hook is out of date. I previewed the page in both themes and the paragraph reads well.

Then I waited for CI on main. All three jobs, tests, lint and shellcheck, were green. I created the tag, pushed it, and wrote the release notes from the changelog.

After that I ran the install one-liner in a clean home and the version command printed the new number without a warning.

The release is out with eleven changelog lines. Next, I will watch the issues for a few days.

summary: Wrote the release notes for the tagged version and checked that the install one-liner, the update note and the hook version warning all match what shipped
body:
After the tag of this morning I spent the session on the release notes that go on the GitHub release page. The changelog had ten lines, and I compared each one against its commit again so that nothing was claimed that was not in the tagged code.

The lines on plural matching, the Codex cwd fix and the shared project-name helper stayed as they were. The line on the stale git lock removal in sync got a rewrite, because the draft said all lock files and the code only removes those older than a minute. I changed it to say that.

The hook version warning needed the most care. When the hook and the CLI disagree about the version, the session start now prints one line on stderr. I ran it by hand with an old plugin copy and got: agent-journal: hook version 0.9 does not match CLI 0.10, run the update. The release notes quote this line exactly so that users can search for it.

I then fetched the install one-liner from a clean shell in a temporary home. It pulled the tagged version, and agent-journal --version printed the new number. The plugin files for Claude Code, Codex and Pi were all in place.

I also checked the README update note. It says how to update each plugin and mentions that old entries are not touched. One sentence still described the folder default from before the install script fix, so I corrected it.

Nothing is left open for this release. The next work is small bug fixes from the issue list, and I want to read the help text once for wording, since a user wrote that two flags sound alike.

summary: Read the help text of every command against the code and found three flags whose descriptions no longer match what they do
body:
I read the output of agent-journal help and of each command's help, line by line, and compared it with the awk and sh code behind it. The goal was to catch statements that went stale during the last releases.

Three problems turned up. The list help said --since takes only a number of days, but it has taken values like 2w for a while. The recall help described plural matching but not that it applies only to terms, not to project names. The sync help still said that a missing remote is an error, while the command now prints a hint and exits with zero.

I fixed the three texts and kept each line under the width of an 80 column terminal. There is a Vitest test that checks the help output for every command name, and I added a line to it that checks that --since and the 2w form appear together.

A user had written that two flags sound alike: --project and --cwd in list. I kept the flags but made the descriptions say what each matches. The first matches the project name from the front matter, the second the exact folder. I added an example for each.

The suite ran green with 64 tests. oxlint and oxfmt reported nothing. I did not change any behavior, only text and one test.

Next I want to look at what happens when the help is asked for an unknown command, since it prints the general help without a hint.

summary: An unknown command now prints a one line error with the closest known command name and exits with status 2 instead of dumping the whole help
body:
Following the help text review of yesterday I looked at what happens with a mistyped command. Running agent-journal lst printed the whole general help and exited with zero, which is bad in scripts and in hooks.

I changed the dispatch in bin/agent-journal. An unknown command now prints agent-journal: unknown command 'lst' on stderr, followed by a hint line with a suggestion when one known command starts with the same two letters. For lst it suggests list. The exit status is 2.

The suggestion is simple on purpose. I compare the first two letters in a case statement and do not compute distances, because that would need awk code that is not worth its weight here. If no command matches, there is no hint line.

I added three tests: a typo with a match, a typo without a match and a check of the exit status. The old test that expected the general help for a bad command was wrong in its intent, so I rewrote it.

The plugins call the CLI only with known commands, so I grepped the three plugin folders to make sure no hook relied on the old zero exit. None did. The suite is green, and the change goes into the changelog draft as a behavior change.

summary: Investigated a report that recall misses entries written in the last minutes of a day when the user asks for yesterday, and traced it to the UTC cut of the period
body:
A user opened an issue saying that recall for yesterday did not show an entry that they wrote at half past eleven in the evening. I first tried to reproduce it with the demo journal and a fake time zone.

The cause is in how the period is turned into a range. Recall computes the start and end of yesterday in UTC, which I documented in the UTC note line a few weeks ago. The entry was written at 23:30 in a zone that is two hours ahead, so its stored UTC time belongs to the same calendar day, but the user counted the day in local time. The entry was correct in the file but outside the range the user expected.

I wrote a test with TZ set to a zone ahead of UTC and an entry at 23:30 local. It showed the miss clearly: the entry appeared for today and not for yesterday in the local view, while recall used UTC and put it in the other day.

There are two ways to go. One is to switch the periods to local time, as list does. The other is to keep UTC and explain it. Switching is more natural for the user but changes the output of old queries and the eval questions that depend on periods. I did not want to change that without running the eval first.

So today I only added the test as a known case, marked as skipped with a comment, and wrote my findings in the issue. I asked the reporter whether a flag such as --local would be enough for them. The reply is open.

Next step is to prototype the local option and run the recall eval on all three agents to see whether the answers change.

summary: Prototyped a --local flag for recall periods and found that the agents ignore it unless the rules text mentions it, so the rules got one sentence
body:
Continuing with the issue from this afternoon I added a --local flag to recall. With it, the words today, yesterday and the forms like 3d are resolved in the local time zone, and the UTC note line says local time instead.

The code change was small. The function that builds the range takes an offset from date +%z and shifts the start and end. I kept UTC as the default so that old behavior stays the same. The skipped test from before now runs with --local and passes, and a second test checks that the default still gives the UTC range.

Then I ran a few real questions on Claude Code about the evening entries. The agent did not use the flag at all, which is no surprise, since the rules text never mentions it. I added one sentence to the recall rules: when the user talks about a day in their own words, add --local. I also put one example command beside it.

I reran the six combined questions on Claude Code and Codex. Both got six of six, and the answers about the evening entries were right this time. Pi will be run tomorrow, because that needs the older machine.

One worry is that the agents now add the flag too often. In the runs I checked, it was only used for questions that named a day. I will look at that again with Pi.

The reporter replied that the flag is enough for them, so I will answer the issue after the Pi run.

summary: Pi run of the recall eval with the new --local sentence gave six of six on the combined set and no flag in questions without a day
body:
I ran the combined recall questions on Pi on the older machine. The result was six of six, which is one better than the last Pi run for this set.

I checked the commands that Pi issued. In the two questions that named a day, it used --local. In the other four, which search by term or project, it did not add the flag. That is the behavior I wanted, so the sentence in the rules is not too strong.

I also reran the old set of eight questions to be sure nothing moved. Pi got seven of eight, as before, and it is the same question that fails every time: it asks for a count of entries and Pi estimates it from the first page of output instead of counting.

I left that question as it is. It is a weakness of the model in this test, not of the CLI, and a rule that tells it to count would add text to every session.

After the run I posted the answer in the issue and explained the flag, the default and the UTC note. I linked the commit and said it will be in the next release.

The skipped test marker is gone from the test file. The changelog draft has a new line for --local.

summary: Added the --local flag to the help text and the README recall section, and fixed the badge row after the CI badge pointed at a renamed workflow
body:
While writing the --local flag into the docs I found that the CI badge at the top of the README showed unknown. The workflow file had been renamed when I added the shellcheck job, but the badge still pointed to the old name.

I changed the badge url to the new workflow file name and checked it after a push. It shows passing now. The other badges, version and license, were fine.

Then the recall section of the README. It listed terms, periods and the plural matching. I added a short paragraph on --local with one example, and I changed the sentence about UTC dates so that it says UTC is the default and --local switches to local time.

The help text of recall got the same flag with one line. The help test that checks for names of flags now also looks for --local.
