I read the install section too, because it is the part users copy. The one-liner and the update note are right. One line said that the plugin folders are created by the script, but since the folder fix the script only creates what is missing, so I reworded it.

The suite is green, oxfmt had nothing to change in the shell tests, and the README renders correctly in the preview. No behavior was changed in this session.

summary: A contributor pull request added a --count option to list, and review found that it counted the header line and failed with an empty journal
body:
A pull request came in that adds --count to list, printing only the number of matching entries. I reviewed it in the main checkout by fetching the branch of the contributor and running the tests.

The idea is good and fits the tool, since agents often want only a number. Two problems showed up in the code. The count was taken from the number of lines of the normal output, which includes the header line, so the result was one too high. And with an empty journal the command printed nothing instead of 0, because the awk block that prints the sum only ran when at least one line was read.

I wrote both as review comments with the exact commands to reproduce them. For the first one I suggested counting entries inside the awk loop instead of counting output lines. For the second I suggested an END block that always prints the sum.

I also asked for a test of the combination with --since and --project, because the filters must apply before the count. The contributor had tests only for the plain case.

The style of the code was fine, and the shell was POSIX. shellcheck had no remarks. I did not push changes to their branch. I will wait for their update and then merge with a squash.

summary: Contributor fixed the --count pull request, I checked the new tests and merged it, then added the option to the help text and changelog
body:
The contributor updated the pull request within a few hours. The count now comes from the awk loop, and the END block prints 0 for an empty journal. They also added tests for --count with --since and --project.

I pulled the branch and ran the suite. All tests passed, 68 now. I tried a few cases by hand as well: an empty folder gives 0, a folder with a broken file without front matter gives the number of valid entries only, and --count together with --limit ignores the limit, which I think is right and wrote down in the help.

One small issue remained. The option was missing from the help text of list. I added it myself after the merge instead of asking for another round, because it was a single line.

I merged with a squash and edited the commit message so that it names the option and the issue it closes. The changelog draft got a line with a thanks to the contributor.

Then I added a short note to the rules text for the agents? I decided not to. The agents already read the help, and more rules text costs tokens in every session. If the eval shows that they never use --count, I will look at it again.

CI ran green on main after the merge. Nothing else is open from this pull request.

summary: Quick check that --count and --local are both in the changelog draft and that the draft lists no change that is not in main
body:
I went through the changelog draft once more in the evening. It has now twelve lines.

I matched each line with git log since the last tag. The --count line and the --local line are both there and both match their commits. The unknown command exit status line is listed as a behavior change, which is correct.

One line mentioned a fix that I had reverted in a later commit, so it was removed. Another line was a duplicate of the help text correction and I merged the two.

The draft is ready for review next time I plan a release.

summary: Fixed the recall --local period border for entries written right after midnight, which landed in the wrong day, and added tests for both sides of the border
body:
A follow-up to the clock change fix of the last days. While checking it by hand I found that an entry written at 00:03 local time was listed under the previous day when I asked recall for today with --local. The awk code that turns the border day into a UTC range used the offset of the day before midnight, so the first minutes after a shift were cut off.

The cause was in the helper that computes the border. It asked for the offset at 23:59 of the previous day and applied it to the start of the new day. On a normal day this gives the same result, which is why the tests did not catch it. On a day with a clock change, the offset at 23:59 and at 00:00 can differ.

I changed the helper to ask for the offset at the start of the border day itself, using the same date call as before but with the time set to 00:00:00. The end border now uses the start of the next day in the same way. That keeps the two borders consistent and means a period never overlaps or leaves a gap with the one next to it.

I added four tests to the recall suite. Two use a fixed TZ with a forward shift and two with a backward shift. Each test writes entries at 23:58, 00:00 and 00:03 around the border and checks which period returns them. Before the fix, two of the four failed with the 00:03 entry missing from today and present in yesterday. After the fix all four pass, and the full suite is green on the main machine.

I also ran the real command against the demo journal with TZ set to a zone with a clock change, for the days before and after the change. The counts matched what I counted by hand from the file names. The older machine is still to be checked, since it has a different libc date, and this goes on the manual list for the next release.

Nothing changed in the help text or the rules text, because the behavior now matches what they already say. I added one line to the changelog draft under fixes and checked it against the commit. Next is the manual time zone check on the second machine.

summary: Recall --local used the current offset for period borders and missed entries near a clock change, so it now uses the offset of the border day
body:
As planned after the list fix I looked at recall --local. It did have the same flaw, in a smaller form: the start and end of a period were computed with the offset of now, so a period that crosses a clock change had borders off by one hour.

I wrote a test first. With TZ set to Europe/Berlin, I asked for entries of a day just after the change, with one entry at 00:30 local time. Before the fix, the entry was missing from that day and showed up in the day before.

The fix reuses the cached offset helper from list. I moved it into a shared function in the CLI so that both commands call the same code, in line with the project name helper that I unified earlier. The border of each day now uses the offset of that day.

I ran the test and it passed. I ran the full suite too, 71 tests, all green. oxlint and oxfmt were clean.

I also tried the default UTC mode to be sure it was not touched, and its output was the same as before byte for byte on the demo journal.

The changelog got one line for both time fixes, since users will see them as one problem. I did not rerun the eval, because the questions use periods in a way that does not cross a change.

summary: Looked into slow session start on a large journal and found that the journal pane read every file twice, then cut the pane time from 1.6 to 0.5 seconds
body:
A user with about 4000 entries said that session start felt slow. I built a journal of that size from the demo entries and timed the pane command: 1.6 seconds, which is too long for a hook.

I looked at the code path. The pane first listed the files to find the newest ones, then called list, which read the same files again to parse the front matter. With 4000 files the double read was the main cost, plus a date call for every entry.

The file names start with the timestamp, so the newest entries can be found by sorting the names and taking the last ones. I changed the pane to take the last N names first and to parse only those. For N of 10 this means ten files instead of four thousand.

There was one catch. The sort by file name is wrong for two entries in the same minute, which was the bug of a few weeks ago, and it was fixed with a fallback to the full timestamp. I kept that rule by taking N plus a few extra names and sorting the small set by the timestamp. The extra count is 5.

Time after the change: 0.5 seconds, most of it the start of the shell and awk. I confirmed that the output is the same as before on the big journal and on the small demo journal by comparing them with diff.

I added a test for the same minute case in the pane, using two files with equal names except for the seconds. It passes. The list command itself is still slower than I would like on a big journal, but it is used less often.

summary: Wrote the plan for the next release: which fixes go in, what needs the second machine, and that the time zone changes need a manual check
body:
The next release will contain the unknown command exit status, --local, --count, the two daylight saving fixes and the faster pane. I wrote the plan down so that the checklist run goes smoothly.

The second machine needs the suite and three real sessions, one for each agent. The time zone fixes need a manual check with TZ set to a zone with a clock change, because the tests use fixed values.

Things left out on purpose: speeding up list for large journals and a rule about counting in the recall text.

Order of work: update the changelog, run the suite, run the checklist, tag.
